6a0be5398ce76b03: URDA: Shocked residents of Urda swung into action as soon as they heard about Wednesday's deadly train crash on the railway line a few kilometres from the normally sleepy Spanish town.
Urda's 78-year-old pharmacist said he was among the first on the scene, jumping into his car to help after his daughter told him about the crash involving two high-speed trains.
Antonio Garcia said the scale of the accident, which has so far left at least 68 people dead, became clear as he approached, with one carriage wedged inside another and scores of bodies.
"Just imagine what was inside," said Garcia, who brought first aid supplies, painkillers and tranquillisers from his pharmacy, as well as blankets to help treat the injured.
Garcia described how one passenger who had lost an arm in the crash was calmly asking for an ambulance, while another was saying his final goodbyes to his family.
"His last words were 'God is good'. For those of us who are believers, these are very beautiful words," said Garcia.
Other locals brought bottles of water for passengers evacuated from the two trains.
A few hours later, Urda was bustling with police, firefighters and emergency workers from across the region, and its local sports hall had been converted into a centre for survivors.
The local primary school was reserved for victims' relatives, where a volunteer psychologist from Madrid called Carmen said she had been helping since the morning.
"There were many mothers who found out their children had been killed. That was the worst of today. Telling a mother that her child has died in a train crash is devastating," she said.
Some relatives made the two-hour journey from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to search for family members.
A woman who gave her name as Ana said she had travelled to Urda after receiving a call from environmental police who had found her dog, Trece, which had been on board a train with her husband, Pepe.
Ana fought back tears as she described searching for her husband at the crash site, Urda's sports hall and the primary school, adding that his name was not on any list.
011875ffab44aa82: MOSCOW: US tech tycoon Elon Musk is "truly a genius" for deploying thousands of satellites into orbit, President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday, as Moscow seeks to develop its own satellite internet network.
The American tech tycoon owns SpaceX, which launches rockets for NASA and operates the Starlink communications network.
Russia, a spacefaring power, has long sought to develop its own satellite internet constellation for both civilian and military use.
Putin's comments come amid a dispute between Ukraine and the United States over access to Starshield, a military-grade satellite network powered by Musk's SpaceX.
"Elon Musk is a genius, truly a genius," Putin said while touring an exhibition on the sidelines of a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow.
"He has how many units in orbit...? More than 5,000. And we're taking our first steps," he added.
"We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr Musk, because it is crucial in orbit not to interfere with one another."
Ukraine began reporting problems using Starshield this month, following a row between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump over a US-Russia diesel deal.
Both Trump and Musk denied being responsible for the outages, although Musk later accused Ukraine of misusing SpaceX's Starlink internet service for military purposes.
Ukraine says the outages have frustrated its efforts to intercept Russian drones and slowed its logistics on the front line, as the Ukraine-Russia conflict grinds through its fifth year.

df9838d0c317b151: BRUSSELS, Oct 29 — President Donald Trump may be facing a political pounding at the US midterm elections next month — but in Europe expectations are low that a big Democrat win would change much.
From the battlefields of Ukraine to the boardrooms of Europe, Trump has sent multiple shockwaves across the continent since returning to power last year.
During a head-spinning 22 months, the mercurial leader has turned spectacularly on Kyiv, imposed tariffs on allies and threatened to take Greenland.
Ahead of the November 3 polls it looks like American voters could punish Trump’s Republican party and hand control of one or both of the US House of Representatives or Senate to the Democrats.
But while the hope may be that Trump could be reined in by a hostile Congress, multiple officials at the EU and Nato told AFP they doubt a big loss would muzzle him on the international stage.
“We don’t think the unpredictability is going to change,” said one senior EU diplomat.
Publicly the European Union is keeping its cards close to its chest.
“We will not comment on any elections in the EU or abroad. Let’s wait for those and we’ll see where it goes,” said European Commission spokeswoman Paula Pinho.
Behind closed doors as well, officials say that the midterms are not featuring much in the bloc’s internal discussions.

“I suspect because a) it is difficult to really predict the result, b) one wouldn’t want to get too high hopes for change and c) not sure how much even a Democratic wave would impact foreign policy issues,” said a second senior EU diplomat.
Ukraine, tariffs
Ahead of the midterms, Trump has rattled Europe by yet again lashing out at Ukraine and cosying up to Russia as Washington has renewed its push to end the fighting.
While a Democrat win could usher in a more vocal pro-Kyiv majority in Congress, the EU is not expecting US support for Ukraine to ramp up again.
Officials in Brussels say they are focused on plugging a 70-billion-euro hole in Kyiv’s finances next year.
And while they’re pushing other countries like Britain, Canada and Japan to do more, they are certainly not counting on the United States.
Meanwhile, there is equally little optimism for any major reversal on the tariffs Trump has slapped on Europe.
Diplomats and officials point out that it took months to get Democrat President Joe Biden to roll back tariffs on EU steel after Trump’s first term — and even then, limitations remained.
In a recent poll from the Washington-based Council on Foreign Relations, only one quarter of Americans backed removing all the tariffs on the EU.
US forces in Europe?
At Nato the story is much the same.
European allies are nervously waiting for the results of a Pentagon review of US forces on the continent that looks set to be unveiled in December.
The widespread expectation is that it will see the United States scale back its deployments, although the hope is the cuts will not be too severe.
Multiple diplomats at Nato said they didn’t envision the midterms having an impact on the review.

While a changed Congress could see US lawmakers more outspoken in support of the alliance, the direction of travel is already set with Europe stepping up efforts to take more responsibility for its defence.
“Whatever the outcome, we’ll keep going,” said one European diplomat.
Trump unleashed?
There is also a nagging fear that things could get worse after the midterms.
If Republicans cling on it could embolden Trump, meanwhile if they lose, he could seek to distract from his woes at home by stirring up things abroad.
“We have a history in America of presidents who get in trouble domestically turning more to the international stage,” said Bruce Stokes, a visiting fellow at the German Marshall Fund think tank.
From an escalation in the Iran war to a more concerted push on Ukraine, there are numerous ways the White House can keep worrying Europe.
“Trump has demonstrated they can’t stand not to be the centre of attention,” said Stokes.
“If that means he needs to do more on the world stage, positively or negatively, that may be what ends up happening.” — AFP
c70ac8461130cd89: TUSCON, Oct 29 — Christine, a retired widow in Arizona, placed food staples in her cart at a charity food distribution event — as she’s had to do monthly since the Trump administration slashed federal food assistance programmes.

“It’s just been hard. It’s been really raw,” the 67-year-old told AFP, declining to give her family name so that two children she cares for, ages nine and 13, would not discover how the refrigerator is stocked.
Until last year, Christine relied on the food assistance programme known as SNAP.
The few hundred dollars a month credited to a card she could use at supermarkets allowed her to supplement her modest retirement funds and keep her family afloat.
But in January many people saw this critical support vanish as cuts mandated by a major budget law championed by President Donald Trump went into effect.
The result: Five million Americans lost access to the programme.
“They don’t care about us,” Christine said, her eyes welling with tears. “The Trump administration doesn’t look out for the little people.”
Half of her retirement check goes to her rent.
And persistent inflation — fuelled by the president’s war on Iran, which has sent gas prices soaring — has proven disastrous for her.
Fuelling anger into votes?
At the food bank, Christine filled her cart with beef, tomatoes and zucchini.
Without this resource in the mid-sized city of Tucson, “we wouldn’t be able to eat meat anymore,” she said. “And we’d eat way less vegetables.”
The south-western state of Arizona has been hardest hit by cuts to SNAP. More than 465,000 beneficiaries, including 200,000 children, were stripped of programme access.
The situation has fuelled discontent that could influence midterm elections in the state, including two tight races for the House of Representatives, where the Republican majority is at risk.
“Many people are upset,” said Natalie Jayroe, head of the Community Food Bank of Southern Arizona. “Even people that voted for the Trump administration.”
Her network of food banks in the state’s south is serving 50,000 more people than usual this year, an influx largely driven by the federal cuts.
“If these people come out and vote, it could make a difference here in Arizona,” she said. “But the question is going to be, do they go to vote?”
Standing among crates of vegetables at the warehouse, Oscar Ochoa, 65, fumed.
He too has lost access to food stamps, and is incensed he has had to come out of retirement to work as a bus driver.
The military veteran has already mailed in his ballot, and said he voted “blue all the way” — down the line for Democrats.
‘Let our voice be heard’
Ochoa said Trump’s budget cuts only resulted in more wealth for the already rich, pointing out that the sprawling bill included tax cuts for billionaires.
It did not, he said, “benefit us poor people, or the average American.”
In the district covering part of the Tucson area, Democrat JoAnna Mendoza is campaigning on the issue of affordability, emphasising that she grew up in a family that relied on food stamps.
Her opponent, the incumbent Republican Juan Ciscomani, meanwhile is distancing himself from Trump, promising constituents that he’s “not a rubber stamp for anyone.”
“He’s a complete liar,” said Angelica Garcia, a 45-year-old hotel receptionist.
During a brief period of unemployment this past spring, Garcia should have been able to quickly access SNAP benefits.
But due to the stricter eligibility checks, her application took more than two months to process.
During that time, her daughters — aged 14 and 22 — subsisted primarily on rice, beans and pasta.
“I feel the Trump administration has put these walls in place for people to make it more difficult,” she said.
Prior to the policy changes, Garcia leaned left but followed politics only from a distance. She didn’t even know the name of her congressional representative.
Now she urges her neighbours to head to the polls on November 3: “We’ve gotta let our voice be heard.” — AFP
f922a5f70c805055: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — To most motorists, the SMART Tunnel is a way to bypass traffic congestion on the southern approach to Kuala Lumpur’s city centre. Its primary purpose, however, goes beyond moving vehicles.
The 9.7km Stormwater Management and Road Tunnel combines a 3km double-deck motorway with a flood-control system designed to divert excess water away from the city centre during heavy rain.
It channels water from the Klang-Ampang catchment to reduce downstream flood risks, including around the confluence of the Klang and Gombak rivers near Masjid Jamek.

According to Amanat Lebuhraya Rakyat (ALR), the holding company of the SMART Tunnel concessionaire and three other highway concessionaires, the system has a combined water-storage capacity of three million cubic metres and has recorded 685 flood-mode incidents.
Project documentation puts the overall cost at approximately RM1.93 billion.
Why was the SMART Tunnel built?
Kuala Lumpur has a long history of flooding, with major events recorded in 1926 and 1971.
In April 2001, floods inundated Jalan Ipoh, Jalan Gombak and Jalan Munshi Abdullah.
Further incidents in June 2002 and June 2003 affected areas around the Klang River, Jalan Gombak and Dataran Merdeka.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The 9.7km-long floodwater tunnel that channels floodwater to the Taman Desa holding pond. — Picture by Firdaus Latif
The SMART Tunnel idea emerged in 2001, when the government sought private-sector proposals to address recurring floods while easing congestion on the southern approach to the city centre.
How was the dual-purpose model developed?

Gamuda Berhad, working with engineering consultants Sepakat Setia Perunding Sdn Bhd and Mott MacDonald, developed a flood-diversion tunnel proposal before partnering MMC Corporation Berhad in 2002 to incorporate a motorway.
The project involved both the government and private sector, with the Department of Irrigation and Drainage (DID) and Malaysian Highway Authority among the agencies involved.
The government commissioned the stormwater management component to divert floodwater from the Klang-Ampang catchment through the tunnel and into downstream storage.
Meanwhile, the motorway was developed under a privatisation arrangement based on a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) model.
The private-sector joint venture formed Syarikat Mengurus Air Banjir dan Terowong Sdn Bhd to implement the project and operate the motorway concession.
Construction began in 2003, and the tunnel opened to traffic in 2007.
How does the tunnel work?
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The pump room located 30 metres below ground level. — Picture by Firdaus Latif.
The SMART Tunnel forms part of an integrated system that diverts excess water from the Klang and Ampang rivers towards downstream storage facilities.
According to ALR, the system has a combined capacity of three million cubic metres, equivalent to about 1,200 Olympic-sized swimming pools. This comprises:
Kampung Berembang holding pond: 600,000 cubic metres
SMART Tunnel: one million cubic metres
Taman Desa holding pond: 1.4 million cubic metres
During heavy rain, excess water is diverted into the system near Kampung Berembang and channelled towards Taman Desa for temporary storage before being released into Sungai Kerayong.
Two control centres oversee different aspects of the operation:
SMART Control Centre: Under DID, it monitors rainfall and river flows, issues flood warnings and directs water into the system.
Motorway Control Centre: Operated by ALR, it manages traffic diversion and clearing, as well as cleaning and restoring the road before reopening.

Safety features include 220 CCTV cameras monitored around the clock, variable-message traffic signs, 42 emergency telephones, 16 radio units, watertight doors and 10 emergency exits and escape routes.
There are four tunnel modes
Mode 1: Normal operation
During ordinary weather, traffic uses the motorway as usual, with no floodwater diverted through the tunnel.
Mode 2: Heavy rain

When water levels rise, excess water is diverted through the lower channel beneath the motorway, allowing traffic to continue. ALR’s operating matrix identifies a flow range of 70 to 150 cubic metres per second for this mode.
Mode 3: Motorway closure
When the flood model forecasts a flow rate of 150 cubic metres per second or more, the motorway is closed and cleared of vehicles in preparation for possible floodwater diversion.
The motorway compartments may not need to be flooded if conditions change.
Mode 4: Prolonged severe storm
If the storm persists, the motorway compartments are used to carry floodwater after all vehicles have been evacuated.
The motorway remains closed until the water has been drained and the road cleaned and inspected.
The distinction is important: a motorway closure does not necessarily mean the tunnel will be flooded.
Mode 3 prepares it for possible use as a floodwater channel, while Mode 4 involves diverting water through the motorway tunnel.
Closure of the SMART tunnel also meant that no tolls are collected throughout the flooding of the tunnel and recovery stages.
The numbers are an illustration only, not verified current losses.
Actual foregone revenue would depend on current toll revenue, traffic patterns, timing of closure, and whether traffic would otherwise have paid the toll.
What happens after the tunnel floods?
The tunnel cannot immediately reopen once a floodwater diversion operation ends. According to ALR, recovery involves six stages:
Stage1: Notification — DID issues a notification and monitors river flows and water levels.
Stage 2: Pumping — Floodwater is pumped out and the main flow checked.
Stage 3: Safety inspection — The tunnel is checked for gas and other potential hazards.
Stage 4: Cleaning — Machinery removes debris and sediment, with operations running around the clock.
Stage 5: System restoration — The tunnel’s systems are restored and checked.
Stage 6: Final inspection — Safety checks are completed before the motorway reopens.
This is a four-day reopening target, with an average recovery period of two days. The actual duration depends on the work needed to restore safe operating conditions.
Major maintenance may also be required after Mode 4, including replacing tunnel fixtures or repairing structural damage caused by floodwater.
How much flood damage has the tunnel prevented?
ALR reported 685 flood-mode incidents and estimated that the system had avoided RM4.94 billion in potential flood damage.
The incidents comprised 556 Mode 2 operations, 118 Mode 3 operations and 11 Mode 4 operations.

The estimates also cover areas and populations ALR said were protected during these operations. They represent potential damage avoided, rather than a direct accounting of losses that would certainly have occurred without the tunnel.

While the SMART Tunnel’s primary purpose remains flood mitigation, its motorway component also operates under a toll concession. Its financing and management arrangements have since changed as the government sought to reduce compensation payments, avoid toll increases and bring forward the return of the concessions to the government.
Why was the concession restructured?
The restructuring covered four Klang Valley highway concessions: SMART, KESAS, LDP and SPRINT.
Under the original agreements, the government faced compensation payments when tolls were kept below the rates concessionaires were contractually entitled to charge.
For SMART, ALR previously cited a contractual toll of RM5 for a Class 1 vehicle, compared with the prevailing rate of RM3 at the time. The contractual rate was scheduled to rise further.
The restructuring aimed to address three issues:
Reduce government compensation: The government had been paying concessionaires the difference between the tolls motorists paid and the rates stipulated in their agreements.
Avoid toll hikes: Without restructuring, the government would have had to continue paying compensation or allow toll rates to rise.
Shorten the concessions: Revenue would go towards debt repayment instead of shareholder dividends, allowing the highways to return to the government earlier.
ALR was established as a private, not-for-profit holding company to acquire the four concessionaires.
In October 2022, it issued RM5.5 billion in sukuk to finance the acquisition and refinance existing debt.
The SMART concessionaire, Syarikat Mengurus Air Banjir dan Terowong Sdn Bhd, became an ALR subsidiary.
ALR said it would not distribute dividends to shareholders, with revenue instead used to cover operating and maintenance costs and repay financing obligations.

The model was designed to maintain existing toll rates without government compensation under the restructured concessions, while directing funds towards debt repayment and an earlier return of the highways to the government.
The restructuring changed the financial and concession arrangements, not the tunnel’s flood-control function.
Who operates the tunnel now, and what happens next?
The SMART Tunnel concession is held by Syarikat Mengurus Air Banjir dan Terowong Sdn Bhd, which is wholly owned by ALR.
ALR aims to return all four highway concessions to the government by 2033, five years before the sukuk programme’s final maturity in 2038.
983923c235a84a32: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — On a daily basis, motorists driving through the motorway section of Kuala Lumpur’s SMART Tunnel may pass through without giving much thought to the two gates that remain shut beyond the familiar stretch of road.
Yet behind those gates lies another side of the tunnel — never seen by motorists.
During a visit to the facility, a current of air from the flood tunnel felt surprisingly cool against the skin, almost like a breeze offering relief from the heat outside.

This was coming from the 9.7km-long infrastructure beneath the city that is part of a flood-mitigation system designed to divert excess water from the confluence of Sungai Klang and Sungai Ampang at Kampung Berembang towards a holding pond in Taman Desa.
Only about 3km of the tunnel doubles as a motorway.

When heavy rain threatens to overwhelm the river system, that section can be closed to traffic so the tunnel can fulfil its other purpose: carrying floodwater away from vulnerable parts of Kuala Lumpur.
Constructing the tunnel required specialised underground engineering —a 13.2-metre-diameter Slurry Mix-Shield tunnel-boring machine (TBM) to excavate the passage beneath the city.
The machine was among the largest of its kind in the region at the time, helping create the stormwater tunnel that now serves two very different purposes, depending on the weather.
What happens behind the gates when the weather turns?
Two control centres, one flood threat
The first signs of a possible flood operation emerge well before water enters the motorway section.
The Department of Irrigation and Drainage (DID) monitors river conditions and water levels, assessing the threat posed by rising water and managing the diversion of excess flows.
Meanwhile, Amanat Lebuhraya Rakyat Berhad’s (ALR) SMART Traffic Control Centre oversees traffic operations, including traffic diversions and motorway closures.
ALR, is the holding company of the SMART Tunnel concessionaire.
When the threat of flooding requires the motorway to be closed, traffic must first be cleared and the road secured before the tunnel can be used for flood mitigation.

These warnings — through various channels, today via social media platforms — begin when Mode 3 is activated, as the motorway is closed and motorists are advised to avoid the SMART Tunnel and use alternative routes.
Mode 3 is a precautionary measure that places the tunnel on standby for possible flooding.
Although the motorway is closed, the traffic compartment is not necessarily flooded at this stage.
Only if heavy rain persists, Mode 4 is activated and the motorway compartment is used to trap floodwater.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Amanat Lebuhraya Rakyat Bhd group chief executive officer Muhammad Nizam Alias speaks during a visit and media briefing at the SMART Tunnel in Kuala Lumpur on October 21, 2026. — Picture by Firdaus Latif.
What happens behind the gates?
Under normal conditions, the motorway remains open and the gates stay shut.
Most motorists have little reason to think about what lies beyond them.
The tunnel is designed to operate in four modes, depending on rainfall and flood conditions.
Under Mode 1, the motorway operates normally, with no floodwater diverted through the tunnel.
In Mode 2, excess water is channelled through the lower section while the road remains open to traffic.
When a more serious storm threatens, the system moves to Mode 3, then subsequently, Mode 4 is activated if the rain arrives at a threatening stage.
For the first time in nearly 20 years, the gates were opened for viewing to the press, offering a glimpse of the tunnel’s interior.

Once diverted, excess water is channelled towards Taman Desa Pond, where it is temporarily stored before being released into Sungai Kerayong through a separate, approximately 500m-long twin box culvert.
The gates are only one part of a system that also relies on river monitoring, traffic control, water diversion and storage.
Since the tunnel began operating in 2007, Mode 4 has been activated 11 times, turning the motorway into a flood channel when heavy rain threatens Kuala Lumpur.
When the rain stops, work continues
After a Mode 4 operation, floodwater must be pumped out and debris removed before the tunnel can be restored for traffic.
About 30m underground, seven floors below ground level, there is the Pump Room that houses five large pumps.
These large pumps are responsible for draining water that’s been trapped in the tunnel.
Floodwater can leave behind mud, sediment, driftwood and other debris, while the force of the water may also damage lights, signboards and other tunnel fixtures.
Crews must check for gas and other potential hazards before proceeding with cleaning.
The recovery process is estimated to take an average of about two days, with a reopening target of up to four days after closure.
RM500,000 in average repair costs
The physical damage caused by floodwater also carries a substantial cost and could be estimated at RM500,00 each time Mode 4 was activated.

There is also a financial trade-off when the motorway closes. During Modes 3 and 4, vehicles cannot use the motorway section, meaning toll collection through that section stops while the road is unavailable to traffic.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A general view of the SMART Tunnel during a visit and media briefing in Kuala Lumpur on October 21, 2026. — Picture by Firdaus Latif.
Awaiting the next storm
For motorists, the SMART Tunnel may be little more than a few kilometres of road beneath Kuala Lumpur. Its other function is largely invisible during ordinary journeys.
Behind the closed gates is a system that must be monitored and prepared before floodwater can be diverted, then drained, cleaned and repaired before traffic can return.
Ventilation, pumping and maintenance all play a part in keeping the infrastructure ready for the moment it must change purpose.
The cool breeze ends once the visit was over, it was lights-off and the tunnel was left in pitch darkness, awaiting the next time it would be called into service.
1348742610e80ed2: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — Malaysia’s recent haze episode carried an estimated RM8 billion in welfare losses, while short-term exposure to fine particles from fires may have contributed to about 1,700 deaths, according to a report commissioned by the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers (FMM).
The report valued the health burden of estimated premature deaths at between RM3 billion and RM15 billion, using standard benefit-transfer methods.
It said this represents what people would be willing to pay to avoid the risk of premature death — not lost economic output — and should not be added to other economic losses.
The haze also disrupted manufacturers indirectly through staff absences and school closures.

Among 59 sites reporting some operational impact in FMM’s survey, 81 per cent said they experienced more sick leave or health-related absence, while 63 per cent said school closures affected staff availability.
The report also highlighted that, at 14 per cent of affected sites, staff shortages disrupted shifts, production or deliveries.
Overall, 37 per cent of sites reporting an impact said output fell, and 27 per cent temporarily shut down at least one operation.
The survey received responses from 86 FMM member sites, including 81 manufacturers.

More than two-thirds reported some operational impact, while 26 per cent said disruption was moderate or significant. The report cautioned that the survey was not representative of all manufacturers; most responses came from Selangor and Penang, and only two came from Sarawak.
School closures during the haze affected an estimated 8.4 million to 13.4 million student-days, the report said. It did not assign a monetary value to any loss in teaching quality.

FMM president Jacob Lee Chor Kok said the haze should no longer be viewed exclusively as an environmental issue but also a matter of public health, labour productivity, economic sustainability and regional competitiveness.

“Manufacturing industries are increasingly interconnected through regional and global supply chains. Environmental disruptions in one country can affect economic activities and business operations across national boundaries.

“Preventing haze is therefore not only an environmental responsibility but also an investment in economic resilience, sustainable industrial development and the wellbeing of future generations,” he added.
The report also estimated 1,700 deaths related to the haze, with a 95 per cent interval of about 1,300 to 2,300, which covers the period from July 1 to Oct 22.
About 1,600 were attributed to smoke from fires outside Malaysia, the report said.
The report stressed that the figures are statistical estimates of deaths brought forward across the population, not individually identified cases.
If fire smoke is assumed to be no more toxic than other fine particles, the estimated toll falls to about 600.
The main estimate also carries uncertainty because the health-risk study used did not include Malaysian cities and was based mostly on forest fires rather than peat fires.

The research paper, titled “The 2026 Fire Season and Transboundary Haze in Malaysia,” covers the period from 1 July to 22 October 2026. It draws on satellite observations, air-quality monitoring, atmospheric modelling and findings from FMM’s member survey to assess the sources, severity and consequences of prolonged haze exposure.
The study was undertaken by Piyu Ke, Chief Scientist of Carbon Spur Sdn Bhd.

The study combined multiple scientific approaches to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the haze problem, including the cumulative effects of prolonged pollution exposure rather than focusing solely on peak air pollution readings.
d70ee8722ff53b80: BRUSSELS, Oct 29 — Canada and the EU will lay the groundwork for a sweeping new partnership aimed at better navigating a world dominated by the United States and China at a Montreal summit this week.
Already enjoying a free trade pact and a defence procurement programme among other deals, Brussels and Ottawa hope to deepen cooperation in other areas.
Here are some of the issues on the table:
Associated membership
European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen raised the prospect of Canada becoming the 27-nation bloc’s first “associate member” in September.
This raised a few eyebrows as the title doesn’t exist in the EU treaties. Some EU states oppose the term being used before its meaning is properly defined.

An EU official speaking on condition of anonymity admitted it was “uncharted territory” for the bloc, but the term underscored the ambition to create a close partnership with Canada just short of membership.
This would entail aligning policies in areas such as climate, energy, and artificial intelligence, letting Ottawa participate in some EU programmes, and creating a common governance structure.

The latter would “build on” the invitations Canada recently received to take part in EU summits and ministerial meetings, Jozef Sikela, the EU commissioner for international partnerships, told the European Parliament last week.
Some EU lawmakers have also argued for the creation of an inter-parliamentary body to hold regular exchanges.
Minerals
Canada is rich in rare earths and critical minerals needed for green technologies like batteries and wind turbines that Europe currently sources mostly from China.

But mining in Canada is yet to take off, with operators looking for investments and commitment from buyers to enter a market dominated by Beijing, said Noah Gordon of the European Council on Foreign Relations think tank.
The summit could lead to an agreement allowing the European Investment Bank to put money behind Canadian critical minerals projects.
Brussels and Ottawa were also looking at joint stockpiling, the anonymous EU official said, referring to the practice of storing materials to stabilise supply and support demand.
Digital, space
A digital trade deal allowing for faster and cheaper online transactions is expected to be unveiled in Montreal.
An early draft of a joint statement for the summit seen by AFP also envisaged deeper cooperation on both artificial intelligence infrastructure and regulation.
The summit should launch work to pave the way for Canada to join the EU’s Galileo programme and IRIS² project.

The first is a global navigation satellite system that offers an alternative to the United States’ Global Positioning System (GPS), and the second aims to equip Europe with a substitute for Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite constellation.
The EU also recently unveiled plans to connect the EU’s mainland with Greenland, Canada, Japan and South Korea via a submarine cable system that would bypass the United States.
“We need to develop our stuff and take care of our own,” said a European diplomat.
People

Ottawa and Brussels are understood to be working to have Canada participate in the EU’s popular Erasmus youth mobility programme, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad among other things.

The draft statement also discussed “enhancing labour mobility, with a focus on reducing barriers for young people and highly skilled workers and promoting greater recognition of professional qualifications”.
“Treaties and institutions are important, but the real foundation of the EU-Canada alliance is people-to-people contact,” said Tobias Cremer, a centre-left EU lawmaker from Germany.
Ukraine and more
Brussels is hoping to secure additional financial support for Ukraine from Canada to cover Kyiv’s budget shortfall.
And scientific cooperation could be boosted by allowing Canada into Horizon Europe, the EU’s flagship funding programme for research.
The EU official said Europe was ready to open its supercomputing infrastructure to Canadian researchers.
The two parties want to strengthen energy ties, with the draft statement mentioning exports of Canadian liquefied natural gas to Europe and the development of renewables.
Plans for the joint purchase of 50 water bombers made by Canadian firm De Havilland — something that also appeared in the early draft — have instead been shelved.

The EU’s commissioner for crisis management Hadja Lahbib told the AFP the bloc had already ordered 24 of the planes in 2024 — and no new purchases were possible as member states negotiated the EU’s next long-term budget.
The idea had faced some opposition in Europe, where some countries would rather EU money be spent on alternative aircraft made by European firms. — AFP
3f40214d76a7be3b: SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 29 — No startup has ever grown so fast. In five years, Anthropic has become an AI giant valued at US$1 trillion (RM4.08 trillion), and it is now aiming for a record-breaking stock market debut.
But it faces three threats: rivals that are catching up, prices that are collapsing, and bills that keep climbing.
Anthropic spells out the risks in its Wall Street prospectus, published Monday.
The first is commoditisation: “the degree of differentiation among advanced AI models may narrow,” the company warns.

The San Francisco-based firm also says “substantially all of our revenue” comes from its AI tools. Unlike Google or Meta, it has no advertising empire to fall back on if business takes a hit, and no cloud business like Microsoft’s or SpaceX’s.
Investors have already grown nervous. In mid-August, shareholders were floating a valuation of US$2 trillion.
But quarter-on-quarter growth slowed from 145 per cent in the second quarter to 45 per cent in the third, cooling expectations to around US$1.5 trillion.
Cheap and open
So-called open AI models, which anyone can download and modify, are close behind closed models such as Claude or ChatGPT, which are available only through their owners’ paid services.
The performance of open models trails by only about four months on average, according to research institute Epoch AI.
They include Kimi K3.1 Pro from Chinese company Moonshot, which costs half as much as Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic’s current flagship.
And among paid models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, none has stayed on top for long.
Anthropic also acknowledges it is holding itself back: its safety measures “could slow our capability gains relative to competitors that do not adopt similar constraints.”
Still, the company says each new version of Claude has boosted sales. More than 80 per cent of its revenue last quarter came from models less than six months old.
Prices collapsing

When products look alike, prices fall. According to Morningstar, the price of having AI process the same amount of text, at the same level of performance, has dropped 97 per cent, from US$17 at the end of 2024 to 50 cents today.
Anthropic itself cut the price of Claude Opus by 20 per cent in September, and OpenAI cut the price of one of its flagship models by a factor of five in July.
The effect is already visible at Vercel, a developer platform that routes requests across AI models.
In August, more than half of the text it handled was processed by open models, up from 13 per cent in April.
Even so, Anthropic still captured nearly two-thirds of spending on the platform.
Even a 90 per cent price cut would not shrink total spending on AI as long as usage keeps growing at its current pace, said Malik Ahmed Khan, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Traffic transits past Anthropic’s headquarters in San Francisco, California October 27, 2026. — Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images/AFP pic
‘Triple whammy’
Anthropic’s costs, by contrast, are largely locked in. To stay ahead, each new Claude model has to be bigger than the last, trained on more data using more computing power.
Since late 2025, the company has committed to paying at least US$417 billion to rent chips and servers.
That is nearly 13 years of sales at its first-half 2026 pace, and the total could nearly double if cancellable or planned contracts are included.
These commitments are due no matter the state of its business, Anthropic warns.
The bet involves the entire industry: Google and Amazon are at once Anthropic’s shareholders, its suppliers and its resellers.

If AI turns out to be less profitable than expected, the International Monetary Fund fears a “triple whammy” from these intertwined investments: falling stock prices, debts that are harder to repay, and promised revenue that never materialises.
The independent research firm New Constructs called the listing “an unprecedented test of investor gullibility.”
To pay these bills, Anthropic is counting on money from the stock market, which is not unlimited.
SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company, raised record sums there in June, while Google and Meta, which are pouring fortunes into data centres, are also seeking fresh capital.
OpenAI, whose chief Sam Altman called a listing “ill-advised” this year, has chosen to wait until 2027, giving it time to see how Wall Street treats its big rival. — AFP
fee575ecacd13739: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — The recent haze has cost some Malaysian businesses additional haze-related expenses of at least RM280,000, according to a report commissioned by the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers (FMM).
The report said 45 sites provided estimates of extra spending in FMM’s survey of 86 member sites, 81 of them manufacturers.
Almost all respondents who reported an operational impact said they had incurred additional costs, mainly for masks and medical expenses.
Among the 59 sites reporting some impact, 92 per cent said they had spent more.
Masks were cited by 76 per cent and medical costs by 58 per cent, the report said.
The survey covered the effects of haze from October 5 onwards, with responses collected between October 12 and 21.
More than two-thirds of all responding sites reported some operational impact, while 26 per cent said disruption was moderate or significant.
FMM said the survey results describe only the responding sites and should not be treated as representative of all manufacturers.
Most respondents were in Selangor and Penang, and only two were in Sarawak, which the report identified as the worst-affected state.
The report also noted that extra spending across the wider economy, including on protection, was not valued because public data for this season were unavailable.
FMM president Jacob Lee Chor Kok said that transboundary haze has become a recurring regional challenge that requires more decisive and coordinated action.

“Year after year, Malaysia and neighbouring countries continue to experience the consequences of transboundary haze. Beyond environmental degradation, haze affects people’s health, workers’ wellbeing, industrial productivity and economic activities.

“For manufacturers, prolonged haze can result in employee illness, absenteeism, disruptions to production and deliveries, and additional expenditure on protective measures and healthcare. These costs ultimately affect business competitiveness and economic resilience,” he added.

The federation urged regional leaders to give greater attention to transboundary haze pollution at the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meetings and Asean meetings, including through the relevant environmental, economic and ministerial cooperation mechanisms.

“Transboundary haze does not recognise national boundaries. Its consequences are shared by neighbouring countries, their populations and their economies. Therefore, its prevention cannot be the responsibility of any single country alone.

“FMM appeals to Apec and Asean leaders to place greater emphasis on this recurring challenge and strengthen regional cooperation in scientific research, environmental monitoring, early warning systems, sustainable land management and fire prevention,” said Lee.
According to the report, Malaysia recorded 422 city-days with an API above 100 across 13 cities between July 1 and October 22, compared with 207 in the same period of 2019.
West Sarawak experienced 63 days of haze episodes.
School closures during the season amounted to an estimated 8.4 million to 13.4 million student-days.

30ce619fb9a51a86: NEW YORK: Alvin Hellerstein, the US judge overseeing the case against deposed Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro, has died aged 92, an official said on Wednesday.
As one of the oldest US federal judges, questions had been raised about whether he was the right judge to preside over what could be a prolonged trial of Maduro on drug trafficking charges.

Hellerstein's lengthy career included overseeing civil cases arising from Al-Qaeda's Sept 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on New York and Washington, often rejecting deals he considered unfair to complainants.

His death was confirmed by the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, where he presided. A court filing showed that the case had been reassigned to Analisa Torres, who was born in 1959.
Hellerstein also clashed with Donald Trump, rejecting a request by the US president to have his New York hush money case moved to federal court.
Last year, he blocked the Trump administration from deporting alleged Venezuelan gang members without a court hearing.
In a notable 2015 ruling, Hellerstein ordered the US government to release a trove of photos depicting the abuse of detainees in Iraq and Afghanistan.

He also presided over a trial last year in which a jury found that French banking giant BNP Paribas's work in Sudan had helped prop up the regime of former ruler Omar al-Bashir, awarding US$20.75 million in damages to three plaintiffs from Sudan.
Hellerstein handled the sprawling drug trafficking case linked to Maduro for more than a decade. It has already seen the conviction of Venezuela's former intelligence chief, Hugo Armando Carvajal.
Maduro was seized by US forces in January in a military raid on his compound in Venezuela.
A graduate of Columbia University law school, Hellerstein served as a lawyer in the US Army from 1957 to 1960 before entering private practice.
He was nominated by then-president Bill Clinton in 1998 to serve as a district court judge for the Southern District of New York.

707cbb2c82137463: WASHINGTON: Shares in Google parent Alphabet fell more than 10 per cent in after-hours trading on Wednesday as the company reported lower-than-expected profit and a slowdown in its advertising business while maintaining heavy spending on AI.
Net profit fell 25 per cent from a year earlier to US$26.2 billion in the July-to-September period, or US$2.12 per share, well short of expectations among analysts surveyed by FactSet.
Alphabet booked an US$8.7 billion loss on its equity investments, which it attributed to its stake in SpaceX, the Elon Musk-led company whose shares have struggled since it went public in June.
Revenue rose 25 per cent to US$127.6 billion, slightly below the roughly US$128 billion analysts had forecast.

Advertising revenue grew 11 per cent to US$82.0 billion, falling short of expectations. Revenue from Google's search business, still the company's largest source of income, rose 12 per cent to US$63.4 billion, slowing from 17 per cent growth in the previous quarter.

YouTube, now the most-watched content provider on American TV screens, saw advertising revenue grow nine per cent to US$11.2 billion, down from 13 per cent growth in the previous quarter. YouTube Music and Premium surpassed 150 million subscribers worldwide, including trial users.
Google Cloud, which rents computing power and AI tools to businesses, saw revenue jump 103 per cent to US$30.7 billion, ahead of analysts' expectations.
The company said sales of its in-house AI chips, known as TPUs, contributed significantly to that growth. Operating income for the unit tripled to US$11.1 billion.
Google is also selling its TPU chips to outside companies, posing a growing challenge to market leader Nvidia. OpenAI plans to buy some of the chips, according to media reports this week.
Alphabet's "Other Bets" division, which includes robotaxi company Waymo, posted revenue of US$372 million and an operating loss of US$2.0 billion.
Waymo now provides more than 500,000 paid rides per week across 15 US metropolitan areas and aims to reach one million weekly rides by the end of the year.
'Long-range planning'
Alphabet spent US$51.4 billion on capital expenditure during the quarter, mostly on data centres and AI chips, more than double the US$24 billion spent a year earlier.
Its latest forecast puts capital expenditure for 2026 at between US$195 billion and US$205 billion.
The company said it would continue to increase capital expenditure significantly in 2027.
"I would broadly think of all of this as a long-range planning process, not a short-term allocation exercise," Google chief executive Sundar Pichai told analysts of the company's investment splurge.
The company's spending, which included a fine paid to the European Union, outstripped the cash generated by Alphabet's businesses for a second consecutive quarter, leaving a US$9.1 billion gap.
During the quarter, Alphabet raised US$28.7 billion by selling bonds and US$12.4 billion by issuing new shares to help fund its AI ambitions.
Google has stepped up the pace of its AI releases since a delay to a flagship model in July raised questions about whether it was falling behind rivals OpenAI and Anthropic.
It launched Gemini 4 at the end of September and later released a version focused on cybersecurity.
The Gemini app has reached one billion users. Google's AI models now process nearly 32 billion tokens, or units of text, per minute, more than four times the level of a year ago, the company said.
Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is also one of Google's largest cloud customers. It has committed to using up to one million Google AI chips.
In September, a US judge declined to order Google to sell off parts of its advertising technology business, imposing restrictions on how it operates instead.

ef016c6396d52f41: SAN FRANCISCO: Microsoft shares popped more than 5% Wednesday afternoon after it reported better than expected revenue and profit, fuelled by its Azure cloud computing division which grew by 48% in the September quarter.
"We are delivering greater capability, choice, control, and cost efficiency for customers across our entire stack," Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said in a statement.
The technology giant recorded US$92.3 billion in total revenue and more than US$36.6 billion in profit, the company said in a securities filing Wednesday.
Analysts had expected around US$90.6 billion in revenue and US$35.1 billion in profit, according to FactSet.

The quarterly earnings report comes just days after Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence investments.
It's the second voluntary buyout offer that Microsoft has offered employees this year, after giving seven percent of its US workforce the option to retire early in April.
Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings.
Earlier this month, Microsoft also announced a new Surface Ultra laptop that runs on Nvidia's artificial intelligence chips and will cost more than US$2,500.

The launch is part of a broader push by tech companies to release hardware that can handle more AI computing on-device and offline, so users do not have to rely solely on remote cloud data centers, where running AI is slower and more expensive.
Microsoft will hold a call with analysts on Wednesday afternoon to discuss its quarterly results.
AI spending
One of the big questions looming over tech earnings is whether the industry's heavy AI spending is paying off.
Analysts are expecting US$51 billion in overall spending by Microsoft from July to September, according to FactSet.
Microsoft nearly doubled its spending on "property and equipment" to US$39 billion compared to the same period last year, according to a press release.
It competes with Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google parent Alphabet for cloud computing services customers.
AWS has dominated the sector and remained number one globally by revenue in the second quarter of the year, according to Synergy Research Group.
Microsoft is number two globally, followed by Google.

However, Google on Wednesday reported that revenue from its cloud division doubled to US$30.7 billion during the quarter, bringing it closer to Microsoft's Azure revenue, which reached US$33.2 billion in the same period.
Alphabet also recently raised US$85 billion through equity offerings to fund its AI data center expansion.
On Monday, Facebook parent company Meta said it would raise US$35 billion through a stock offering to fund its own AI investments.
Tech companies are expected to collectively spend hundreds of billions of dollars on AI-related expenses this year.
c5ac4b7e4c57c4ed: SAO PAULO: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who arrived in the United States on Wednesday, has declared himself the rightful leader of Brazil, alleging an electoral coup d'état had been carried out by the country's Supreme Court and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who won the presidential election by more than four million votes.

Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday's election and left Brazil for Miami, where he and his family received US visas, thanked Argentine leader Javier Milei and US President Donald Trump for helping him leave his country and welcoming him.

In an initial open letter posted on X, Bolsonaro declared himself "the elected president". He then deleted that version and replaced it with another letter in which he said he was the rightful "leader" of Brazil.

"I want to say, not only to my 60 million voters but to the Brazilian people, that I am the leader and that the criminals who stole Brazil's election are part of a criminal organisation that has established a tyranny," he said in the updated version.
Asked by reporters at Joint Base Andrews about Bolsonaro's comments, Trump declined to comment, reiterating his earlier view that it was "a very strange election".
Bolsonaro's comments pose a problem for Washington as it seeks to navigate a rift with Latin America's largest country, which is home to the world's second-largest reserves of rare earths.

Lula has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaro family to help return them to power. Ahead of Sunday's election, Reuters reported on a US State Department campaign to restore the Bolsonaros to office.
Washington has denied trying to interfere in Brazil's domestic affairs. Trump has previously alleged that Flavio's father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution.

Jair Bolsonaro travelled to the United States after refusing to concede defeat to Lula in 2022. He eventually returned to Brazil but was sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.
There was no immediate response from the State Department.
Neither Lula's office, the federal electoral court nor the Supreme Court immediately responded to requests for comment.
Lula, who was himself jailed on corruption charges that were later overturned, said this week that it was "shameful" Bolsonaro had not stayed in Brazil to prove his innocence.
No proof

Bolsonaro and his family arrived in Miami on Wednesday, leaving Brazil after he refused to comply with a Brazilian Supreme Court order to surrender his passports. He left under a shroud of secrecy following the court order, which relates to a money-laundering investigation in which he denies wrongdoing.

Bolsonaro, who had been widely expected to win Sunday's election but suffered a shock defeat, did not provide evidence for his allegations of electoral fraud. International observers have found Sunday's vote fair.

Bolsonaro based his rejection of the result on the fact that a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice had extended voting by two hours on Sunday following allegations by Lula's campaign of voter suppression in left-leaning northeastern states.
However, Bolsonaro's campaign also sought an extension because of rain in conservative southern states.

Bolsonaro lost to Lula by around 4.5 million votes. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or about 0.03 per cent of the total, were cast during the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.

The scale of Bolsonaro's loss to Lula — more than twice his father's losing margin — and the fact that his campaign also requested an extension because of rain in the conservative-leaning south make any annulment of the election unlikely, analysts said.

In his letter, Bolsonaro denied fleeing Brazil, saying he had left to protect himself and his family and avoid becoming the victim of a witch hunt he accused Lula and the Brazilian Supreme Court of carrying out.
"I want to make this clear: I did not flee Brazil," he said. "I left Brazil, but I did not abandon the Brazilian people."

0fb60d4598bf4b71: KUALA LUMPUR: It was never enough for Tony Warren to sing a Tom Jones song. He wanted you to believe you were watching the Welsh superstar himself.
There was the powerful voice, the swagger and those hips that seemed to have a life of their own.
But Warren could also switch to Elvis Presley or Engelbert Humperdinck, tackling three very different styles with a flair that made the act his own.
For more than five decades, the Ipoh-born entertainer took his show from Malaysian nightspots to stages overseas, building a career that outlasted changing musical fashions.
Warren died in his sleep yesterday, aged 81. His son, Andrew Warren, 54, a live audio engineer and production manager, said his father was found in his favourite chair at home by his wife, Cecilia.
Before the bright lights and late nights, however, Warren had a classroom to attend.

He began singing at 17 with a band called The Socialites in Ipoh. He later taught English and history at schools in Kepong, Rawang and Tanjong Malim, balancing his job with performances and the demands of raising a family.
By day, he was Mr Warren or Cikgu Warren, the teacher and discipline master. After hours, he pursued his passion for music.
His breakthrough came in 1969, when he performed at a talent show at Stadium Negara in Kuala Lumpur.
Warren earned a standing ovation. The emcee introduced him as the “Tom Jones of KL”, a nickname that eventually became the “Tom Jones of Malaysia”.
He worked hard to earn that billing, studying Jones's recordings, vocal delivery and stage movements to capture not just the sound but also the swagger.
Yet Jones was only part of the show. Warren also tackled the songs of Presley and Humperdinck, bringing three distinctive musical styles to a repertoire few local entertainers could match.

During the 1980s, he became a fixture of Kuala Lumpur and Petaling Jaya's nightlife, performing at venues including the Copper Grill at The Weld, Yuyi Kitchen, the Royal Selangor Club at Dataran Merdeka and the PJ Hilton.
Audiences came for the familiar hits, but Warren gave them a show, complete with cheeky humour, energetic moves and the confidence to command a room.

His reputation soon travelled beyond Malaysia. A talent scout who watched him perform in Kuala Lumpur invited him to Perth, Australia, where he appeared at a Channel 7 telethon and Burswood Resort and Casino.
He also performed in Singapore, Jakarta and Cambodia, released three CD compilations featuring songs by his musical heroes and other artistes, and opened for international pop act Air Supply in 2009.

Retirement from teaching did not end his stage career. Warren continued entertaining at corporate functions and performing for royalty and visiting English Premier League football clubs, keeping his beloved repertoire alive for audiences across generations.
A son joins the show
For Andrew, though, his father was more than the entertainer who could channel three musical legends.

His father's work kept him busy during Andrew's younger years, leaving them with limited time together. That changed after Andrew completed his SPM, when he joined Warren on the pub and hotel circuit, playing keyboards alongside him for the next five years.
The experience brought father and son together through music. Andrew saw first-hand how his father could command an audience and move effortlessly between three very different musical styles.
“He was a one-of-a-kind entertainer, had a voice like no other that could handle Tom Jones, Elvis Presley and Engelbert Humperdinck at the same time,” Andrew said.
After his father's death, Andrew paid tribute to him on Facebook, reflecting on the different roles Warren had played in people's lives.
“To some of you, you would have probably known him as Mr Warren or Cikgu Warren, the teacher, discipline master from school, and to others, Tony Warren (Tom Jones of Malaysia), the entertainer.
“But to me and my sister, he was simply ... Daddy. May he rest in eternal peace as he makes his way home,” he wrote.
Warren leaves behind Cecilia, Andrew, daughter Lisa and five grandchildren.

His funeral Mass will be held at 10.30am today at Jesus Caritas Church in Jalan Burung Hantu, Taman Kepong, Kuala Lumpur, followed by cremation at the DBKL Crematorium in Jalan Kuari, Taman Pertama, Cheras.

c65342f42e85a766: WASHINGTON: Shares in Google parent Alphabet fell more than 10% in after-hours trading Wednesday as the company reported lower-than-expected profit and a slowdown in its advertising business while it maintained big spending on AI.
Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to US$26.2 billion in the July-to-September period, or US$2.12 per share, well short of expectations by analysts surveyed by FactSet.
Alphabet booked an US$8.7 billion loss on its equity investments, which it attributed to its stake in SpaceX, the Elon Musk-led company where shares have struggled since going public in June.
Revenue rose 25% to $127.6 billion, slightly below the roughly US$128 billion analysts had forecast.

Advertising revenue grew 11% to US$82.0 billion, short of expectations. Revenue from Google's search business, still the company's largest source of income, rose 12% to US$63.4 billion, slowing from 17% growth in the previous quarter.

YouTube, now the most-watched content provider on American TV screens, saw advertising revenue grow 9% to US$11.2 billion, down from 13% growth in the previous quarter. YouTube Music and Premium passed 150 million subscribers worldwide, including trials.
Google Cloud, which rents computing power and AI tools to businesses, saw revenue jump 103% to US$30.7 billion, ahead of analyst expectations.
The company said sales of its in-house AI chips, known as TPUs, contributed significantly to that growth. Operating income for the unit tripled to US$11.1 billion.
Google is also selling its TPU chips to outside companies, in a growing challenge to market leader Nvidia. OpenAI plans to buy some of the chips, according to media reports this week.
Alphabet's "Other Bets" division, which includes robotaxi company Waymo, posted revenue of US$372 million and an operating loss of US$2.0 billion.
Waymo now provides more than 500,000 paid rides per week across 15 US metropolitan areas and aims to reach one million weekly rides by the end of the year.
'Long-range planning'
Alphabet spent US$51.4 billion on capital expenditures during the quarter, mostly on data centres and AI chips, more than double the US$24 billion a year earlier.
Its latest forecast for capex spending is between US$195 billion to US$205 billion in spending for 2026.
The company said it would continue to increase capex spending significantly in 2027.
"I would broadly think of all of this as a long-range planning process, not a short-term allocation exercise," Google CEO Sundar Pichai told analysts of the company's investment splurge.
The company's spending, which included a fine paid to the European Union, outstripped the cash generated by Alphabet's businesses for a second straight quarter, leaving a US$9.1 billion gap.
During the quarter Alphabet raised US$28.7 billion by selling bonds and US$12.4 billion by issuing new shares to help pay for its AI ambitions.
Google has stepped up the pace of its AI releases since a delay to a flagship model in July raised questions about whether it was falling behind rivals OpenAI and Anthropic.
It launched Gemini 4 at the end of September and later released a version focused on cybersecurity.
The Gemini app has reached one billion users. Google's AI models now process nearly 32 billion tokens, or units of text, per minute, more than four times the level of a year ago, the company said.
Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is also one of Google's largest cloud customers. It has committed to using up to one million Google AI chips.
In September, a US judge declined to order Google to sell off parts of its advertising technology business, imposing restrictions on how it operates instead.
8cc8ce868171fc62: ROME: Inter reclaimed top spot in Serie A with a nervy 2-0 win at Venezia on Wednesday, while Samuel Mbangula's hat-trick inspired Bologna to a 4-2 victory at AC Milan and Juventus stumbled again at Genoa.
Champions Inter drew level with Lazio on 25 points at the top ahead of a hotly anticipated Milan derby meeting with their rivals on Saturday.
Ruben Amorim's side will go into that game on the back of their first league defeat of the season after Alphadjo Cisse's double was not enough to avoid a loss that left the Rossoneri fifth.
Inter coach Cristian Chivu admitted that an unconvincing performance was not the perfect derby preparation for his team either.
"We go into that game with eight wins and a draw and are aware that it is a derby," Chivu told Sky Sport.
"We need to regain mental and physical energy - I'm referring to some of the guys I had to sacrifice at half-time as a wake-up call. If I could have, I would have changed the entire team."

Fresh off a pulsating stoppage-time turnaround against Fiorentina on Sunday that marked their fifth comeback win of the season, Inter thought they would have to fight back from behind once again when Lion Lauberbach fired home, but he was offside.

Venezia have picked up just three points all season but looked the likelier to make the breakthrough as Ivan Provedel diverted a shot onto the bar before Akor Adams rounded Provedel to score, only for the offside flag to save Inter again.

However, Matias Moreno and Redouane Halhal diverted dangerous deliveries into their own net in the space of two minutes to ensure Inter returned to the top of the standings and Venezia remained rooted to the bottom.
Mbangula magic downs Milan
At San Siro, a lengthy injury list featuring the likes of Adrien Rabiot, Diego Moreira and Mario Gila restricted Amorim's options for the first midweek round of the season.
Mbangula, making his full debut for Bologna, swept home the opener inside eight minutes, but the visitors were soon pegged back when an Arthur Theate error gifted Cisse a simple finish.

The Milan teenager struck again in the 27th minute, volleying home a Fikayo Tomori cross, but the game was turned on its head once again in the space of two second-half minutes to stun the San Siro crowd.
The unfortunate Davide Bartesaghi turned a free-kick into his own net before Mbangula struck again with a composed finish in the box just after the hour mark.
The 22-year-old then completed a memorable night when he beat Mike Maignan for a third time.
"A lot of games, a lot of players out," Amorim told DAZN.

"I felt from the first minute that the team was a little bit tired and without much energy. We conceded two goals quickly; we tried to come back, and we had a great opportunity with (Francesco) Camarda. This number of games was hard for us, with so many players out."
Juventus slip up again
Juventus's shaky start continued with a 2-0 defeat away to Genoa, while Napoli thrashed Monza 4-1.
Luciano Spalletti's inconsistent side have not won back-to-back league games since the opening two weeks of the season and were deservedly beaten at the Stadio Luigi Ferraris.
Kingsley Ehizibue struck early with an angled strike before Tommaso Baldanzi doubled Genoa's lead in the 28th minute.
Next up for the Turin club is the visit on Sunday of Napoli, who dispatched Monza to go sixth, level on 14 points with Juve.
Head coach Massimiliano Allegri was suspended after being sent off during a 3-3 draw with Roma, but Napoli produced their biggest win of the season in his absence.

Rasmus Hojlund's early opener was cancelled out by Serie A top scorer Gustavo Varela's clever header just before the break, while there were concerns when Napoli midfielder Stanislav Lobotka was stretchered off.
Napoli pulled away in the second half as Matteo Politano, Rafa Marin and substitute Kevin De Bruyne struck.
Elsewhere, Adrian Bernabe had a penalty saved by Maduka Okoye as struggling Parma and Udinese played out a 0-0 draw.

3cf4a8f883316650: BERLIN: Newly-crowned Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane was left on the bench as Bayern Munich sailed to a 6-1 win over second-tier Magdeburg in the German Cup last 32 on Wednesday.

Bayern had no difficulty without their star striker, with Michael Olise grabbing a double and Ismael Saibari, Alphonso Davies, Nathaniel Brown and teenager David Santos Daiber also getting on the scoresheet.
Kane received a guard of honour from his Bayern teammates before kick-off as the 75,000 fans at the Allianz Arena saluted the Ballon d'Or winner, two days after his triumph in London.
Bayern got some more good news pre-match, with coach Vincent Kompany discharged from hospital, five days after collapsing at training on Friday.
Olise tapped in an excellent Saibari assist from close range after 10 minutes but the unfancied visitors levelled five minutes later through Mateusz Zukowski.
Olise returned the favour by setting up Saibari midway through the opening half and added a third from the spot early in the second half, with regular penalty-taker Kane still on the bench.
Teenage forward Lennart Karl set up goals for Davies and Brown before Santos Daiber added more gloss to the victory with a stoppage-time goal.
Kane remained on the bench for the entire match, with Saturday's home Bundesliga clash with Borussia Dortmund in mind.
Bayer Leverkusen came from two goals down to win 5-2 against Nuremberg, with defender Edmond Tapsoba netting twice and Patrik Schick, Jonas Hofmann and Lucas Vazquez scoring goals.
Earlier on Wednesday, Germany forward Deniz Undav's 90th-minute strike took Stuttgart to a 1-0 win at 10-man Paderborn.
Stuttgart, finalists in 2025, had a one-man advantage after Laurin Curda's 37th-minute red card but could not break down a stubborn Paderborn.
After striker Ermedin Demirovic had two efforts saved, Undav took matters into his own hands and turned in a Chris Fuehrich cross with extra time looming.
"The win is what matters most," Undav said. "I honestly don't care whether I'm the one who scores, and that's the truth. We won, we're through to the next round - on we go."
Japan forward Keisuke Goto scored twice in the final 15 minutes to overturn a 2-1 deficit as Freiburg won 3-2 at home against Wolfsburg.
Goto's Japan teammate Kento Shiogai also bagged a brace, while Freiburg's Igor Matanovic opened the scoring.
Elsewhere, second-division sides Dynamo Dresden and Hertha Berlin both won 2-0 against Schalke and Jeddeloh respectively, while Kaiserslautern eliminated Hannover.

f24cafac704dde64: UNITED NATIONS: UN rights chief Volker Turk said Wednesday he hopes a new Israeli government will "change course massively" and respect international law, as the country's political future hung in the balance after hard-fought elections.

"The message is: don't continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that's what we have frankly seen in the current environment," he told reporters in New York.

Earlier this week, Turk warned that Israel's military occupation in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron, launched after a deadly attack by Palestinian gunmen, raised serious concerns of "ethnic cleansing".

3f479e95f7d38311: BASEL: Novak Djokovic dug deep to overcome Ugo Humbert in three sets in his opening match in Basel on Wednesday, keeping his bid to qualify for the season-ending ATP Finals on course.
The 39-year-old Djokovic dropped the first set but recovered to beat the French left-hander 4-6, 6-3, 6-4 on his first appearance in Basel since 2011.
"It was a super tight match, very intense from the beginning," said Djokovic.
"I was under attack from the very first point. I had to weather the storm, but I managed to find my rhythm at the beginning of the second set.
"After that, I started feeling a bit more comfortable with his tempo. Overall, it was a huge challenge. I succeeded in managing to find the solutions in a tough match today."
Djokovic strengthened his chances of a record 19th qualification for the ATP Finals by winning the China Open in Beijing earlier this month, the 102nd title of his career.
That was followed by an early exit at the Shanghai Masters, with the 24-time Grand Slam champion accepting a wild card into the Swiss event after slipping to 11th in the Race to Turin standings.

Djokovic is a seven-time winner of the ATP Finals, but he did not compete at either of the past two editions because of injury. Only the top eight players qualify for the November 15-22 showpiece, although Jannik Sinner has already pulled out due to a knee problem.
Fourth seed Djokovic takes on Germany's Jan-Lennard Struff in the next round in Basel. He holds an 8-0 record against Struff.

LONDON: France captain Kylian Mbappe apologised to China on Tuesday after a fierce backlash over his comments referring to late Chinese leader Mao Zedong as a dictator, underscoring how swiftly global celebrities can come unstuck.
In a video on a French podcast that has since been taken down, Mbappe is heard discussing a funny meme where his face had been photoshopped onto that of "some guy — I think he's a Chinese dictator."
"During a recent interview, I reacted to an image of myself," Real Madrid forward Mbappe said in a statement.
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world.
"I apologise to everyone my words have upset," added Mbappe, who has ties with firms including Swiss sportswear brand On Holding, hotel chain Accor and Lego.
"This was absolutely not my intention."

The backlash highlighted the risks for athletes and brands in the lucrative China market, where satire about Mao, modern China's founding leader who ruled the country from 1949 until he died in 1976, remains a social taboo.
La Liga president Javier Tebas said he met the Chinese ambassador in Spain to resolve the fallout.

"Our commitment is to keep working together so that an individual episode does not harm the important advances achieved nor affect the millions of Chinese fans who follow our competitions," Tebas said in a statement posted to social media.
"China is and will continue to be a strategic partner for La Liga."
Brands including dairy companies Mengniu and Shanghai Milkground Food Tech, as well as Eastroc Beverage, said they were ceasing all cooperation with Mbappe effective immediately.
The companies said they "firmly oppose and have zero tolerance for any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people."

State television has stopped broadcasting matches and programmes involving La Liga and Mbappe, while all advertisements featuring the player have been taken down, state-backed news outlet The Paper reported on Tuesday.
"Mbappe's team knew, or should have known, what the true cost of Chinese brand endorsements was all about," said Terrence Burns, sports sponsorship expert and CEO of the T. Burns Sports Group.
Swiss-based On Holding, which signed Mbappe in September after he had spent two decades at US rival Nike, welcomed his apology and said it had "deep respect" for China.

Chinese state media outlet China Daily said Mbappe's remark had "triggered a backlash among his Chinese fans, threatened his lucrative commercial relationships and offered a sharp reminder of the limits of celebrity influence."
"What did he say? Many Chinese would rather not repeat it," the state-backed Global Times added.
"The message from Chinese consumers is clear: Respect is not optional; one doesn't get to profit from China while disrespecting it. Not a chance."
On Chinese social media platform Weibo, one user wrote about the apology: "Not accepted. Not forgiven!!".
State broadcaster CCTV struck a more conciliatory tone, saying it would listen to what Mbappe had to say after his apology and "even more importantly" watch what he does.

Singer Shila Amzah believes joining music competitions remains the best platform for artistes to push their boundaries and discover hidden potential within themselves.
But the 36-year-old acknowledges that contestants naturally face immense pressure and tight deadlines to deliver top-notch performances.
"Every time you join a competition, you discover something new about yourself.

"Things you previously thought you couldn't achieve suddenly become possible because you are working under pressure and driven by a strong desire to deliver your absolute best," she shared in a Threads post.
Shila said aspiring artistes must build both physical and mental strength to succeed in the entertainment industry.
"Anyone participating in a competition must ensure they have mental and physical endurance.
"Don't skip your workouts because they build stamina and keep your mind sharp. Memorising lyrics, new musical arrangements and choreography in just a few days is no mean feat."
Reflecting on her early days as a contestant on 'One In A Million', Shila recalled how different the challenges were compared to today's tech-driven era.
"No matter your age, knowledge today is literally at your fingertips. Back when I competed in 'One In A Million', we had to cut our own music tracks and finding reference material was tough.
"Luckily, I was deeply passionate about it and working with music director Aubrey Suwito was an unforgettable experience."
For Shila, true artistic satisfaction comes from delivering an outstanding performance rather than fixating solely on winning.
"Towards the end of a performance, there is always a deep sense of satisfaction in knowing you gave it your all. Hard work never lies.
"What sets you apart from other contestants isn't just talent, but the effort you put into enhancing the song and bringing creativity onto the stage."

SYDNEY: Australian mushroom murderer Erin Patterson will learn tomorrow if she has succeeded in overturning her conviction for killing three people with a poisoned beef Wellington lunch.
Patterson, 52, was found guilty last year of murdering her husband's parents and an elderly aunt in 2023 by serving them a beef-and-pastry meal laced with lethal death cap mushrooms.
A judge sentenced her to life imprisonment, eligible for parole after 33 years.
In August, her lawyers argued before the Court of Appeal in Melbourne that she had suffered a miscarriage of justice.
They alleged a litany of irregularities in the trial, including an "oppressive" cross-examination and unfair decisions on the admission of evidence.
Prosecutors also appealed, however, saying her 33-year non-parole period was "manifestly inadequate" — and she should never be allowed to walk free.
Tomorrow morning, the Court of Appeal will hand down its decision on both appeals, officials said.
On the conviction, the judges must decide whether there are even grounds to give her leave to appeal.
If they agree to do so, the judges may dismiss the appeal or uphold it, in which case they may order a new trial or acquit her.
On her sentence, the court will either dismiss the prosecution's appeal or uphold it and re-sentence her.
Patterson was not expected to attend in person.
Her trial last year drew podcasters, film crews and true crime fans to a courthouse in the rural town of Morwell, a sedate hamlet in Victoria better known for its prize-winning roses.
Audiences from New York to New Delhi followed every twist of what many now simply call the "mushroom murders".
The motive of the killings remains a mystery.

A 12-person jury found Patterson guilty in July last year of murdering her husband Simon's parents, Don and Gail Patterson, as well as his aunt, Heather Wilkinson, at her home in the Victorian farming village of Leongatha.
She was also found guilty of attempting to murder Heather's husband Ian, a pastor who fell gravely ill but eventually recovered.
