623841ef72de0a54: THE reason why migrant workers, refugees and asylum seekers desperately enter Malaysia by any means necessary is also why they attract human smugglers.
Human trafficking is a burgeoning business because of Malaysia's strategic location, reliance on migrant labour and vulnerabilities in law enforcement and border control.

In one clean sweep, Malaysia is a lucrative source, transit hub and destination country for criminal syndicates. The coastline, including the Strait of Malacca, is riddled with smuggling entry points while the dense forest shared with Thailand is ideal cover for refugees and migrants from Myanmar and Bangladesh to enter Perlis, Kedah, Perak and Kelantan.
Because of stringent labour policies and expensive work permits, labourers and employers sidestep legal immigration red tape, fuelling the black market for smuggling operations.

The United States Department of State's Trafficking in Persons Report designated Malaysia at Tier 2, which meant that Malaysia has yet to meet minimum international standards to eliminate human trafficking.

Border control is managed by dedicated enforcement officers, unsung heroes whose feats are barely understood by the general public. But a tragedy highlighted just how crucial their jobs are: on Oct 27, Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency sailor Mohd Roshaimi Mohd Ridzuan was killed and three colleagues injured while pursuing a boat carrying illegal migrants.

Their patrol boat collided with a coastal seawall at Sungai Padang during a high-speed pursuit. There were previous incidents: last year, a boat carrying illegal immigrants off Tanjung Kling rammed into an enforcement patrol boat, injuring two MMEA officers.

The incidents reflect the volatile and dangerous night surveillance and sea chases against heavily armed rogue operators. That's not all: MMEA officers have survived machete attacks. Roshaimi's tragic death in the line of duty must strengthen, not weaken, Malaysia's resolve to dismantle these smuggling syndicates.

While we pay tribute to the fallen sailor, we must acknowledge the risks faced by the MMEA. The best tribute we could offer is the funds and resources for a better-prepared, better-equipped and intelligence-led enforcement.

In the meantime, we must remove and indict compromised border control officers through continuous spot checks at border checkpoints and visa-processing agencies. Make it mandatory for employer-pays mechanisms to prevent migrant workers' accruing massive debts to third-party agents.

Businesses using unauthorised sub-contractors or ignore illegal workforce must be subjected to punitive penalties. Deploy drone patrols, thermal imaging and biometric tracking and train enforcement officers to distinguish deliberate illegal immigrants from coerced or deceived victims.
133598f3f99fbe16: Donate to our Justice as infrastructure Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!

All images via Canva or fair use. Screenshots of Peacekeeping circle (bottom left) and Duterte protest (top center) via YouTube. International Criminal Court building (top right) via Wikimedia CC BY-SA 4.0. St. Louis courthouse under construction (center middle) via Picryl CC0 1.0.

Often portrayed as abstract, large, formal, distant, and quite technical, justice is a moral and ethical area, tied to institutions and legal statutes, and can seem a long way from mundane daily experience. But it is also a deeply practical underpinning for how most societies function. Without justice systems that work and are understood at the most fundamental level, economic mobility is threatened, socially marginalized groups have no recourse, and lack of trust hampers institutions and interpersonal interactions alike.

Justice is the grease in the motor of social functioning. Nobody will contest the importance of justice to holding people to a collective moral code of conduct, but the often overlooked next-level function justice plays is that, when justice is fair, fast, and reliable, it makes everything in a society run better. It allows for a society to fulfill its economic, social, and creative potential. Copyright law protects ideas and innovation; land law protects resources and livelihoods; labor law supports humane and effective use of our work — as long as those laws are enforced. When you know that it will be straightforward and predictable to get all the permits, you are more likely to start a business. When you know that fraud will be punished, you are more likely to invest your capital. When you know that you will be caught, you’re less likely to evade taxes. When you know that there will be fair and fast prosecution, you are more likely to report injustice and less likely to perpetrate it.

In this spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to make visible the ways in which justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society, and how countries with a justice deficit can work towards stronger protections that will enable economic and social benefits.

f2369deb6850e771: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysian creators must understand that copyright protects original work expressed in material form, not ideas alone, an intellectual property lawyer said.

Speaking on Beyond the Headlines in conjunction with World Animation Day, Mahendra Balakrishnan said original work must be expressed in a tangible form, such as a drawing, script, photograph or film, to qualify for copyright protection.
He advised creators to keep records of their work, store files securely and limit the sharing of concepts and designs before taking steps to protect them.
He also urged creators to understand their contractual rights, particularly the distinction between licensing and assigning copyright, before allowing others to use their work.
"Always put it down on paper or put it down on a sketch, put it down on a dated document with a time stamp where possible," he said.
Licensing allows another party to use the work under agreed terms, while assignment transfers the copyright or rights specified in the agreement, Mahendra said.
He urged creators to be aware of unauthorised commercial use of their work, including reproductions and adaptations of existing characters or designs.

On generative artificial intelligence (AI), Mahendra said Malaysia's copyright framework was human-centric, with authorship and human contribution remaining important considerations in determining intellectual property rights.
He said proposed amendments to the Copyright Act 1987 were expected to address emerging issues, including generative AI.

Meanwhile, WAU Animation co-founder and Agent Ali creator Muhammad Usama Zaid said building a successful animation property involved more than producing a series or film, as its characters and stories could be extended into merchandise and other commercial ventures.
"The idea is always to tell the right story, create the right character, and then once you have the visibility, we can extend from there," he said.
Usama said he had initially aspired to work for internationally renowned animation studios such as Pixar, Disney or DreamWorks while studying animation.
However, an opportunity to develop a local animated feature redirected his focus towards building Malaysia's animation industry.
Less than a year after graduating, he and several friends had the opportunity to establish a studio and work on Geng: Pengembaraan Bermula, which he described as a catalyst for Upin & Ipin.
His experience in the industry also influenced his approach to developing Agent Ali, with the team recognising the potential for an animated property to expand beyond television and film.

Usama said the studio had to tackle the unauthorised distribution of Agent Ali The Movie 2, including recordings made in cinemas that were later shared on Telegram or edited into shorter clips for TikTok.
He said the studio worked with fans to identify the material before its digital team pursued takedowns.
Unauthorised merchandise was another concern, particularly when sellers downloaded existing images of Agent Ali characters and reproduced them on clothing, bags and other products for sale.

Usama distinguished such commercial activity from fan art, in which artists create their own interpretations of the characters. While fan art could reflect appreciation for the property, selling products featuring copied images could generate revenue without the studio's authorisation, he said.
On AI, Usama said his concerns extended beyond copyright infringement to the technology's potential impact on the creative process.
He said relying on AI without developing the underlying skills could deprive people of opportunities to learn through experimentation, problem-solving and refining their work.
Usama also cautioned creators against becoming so protective of their ideas that they avoided seeking feedback.
When developing Agent Ali, the team built a circle of trusted people who could offer candid feedback and identify weaknesses in the work, he said.
He added that the series had undergone numerous revisions, feedback sessions and brainstorming exercises before its first episode was released.
"Don't create in a silo," he said.
Usama said young artists should be valued for their work even before their creations became commercially successful, adding that creative disciplines were often treated as secondary to other fields.
World Animation Day is observed annually on Oct 28.

33c673a8d5cb4cdb: A cartoon from an ex-Google software engineer, titled “Welcome to Google,” made the rounds a while back. It featured two diverging roads, neither passable. One was the main road, marked as deprecated (“don’t even think about it,” the sign read). The new road, however, was marked as still under construction (“Danger”), and so was unusable as well.

That was the no-win choice two million frontend developers faced in 2014, when Google unexpectedly deprecated its popular JavaScript framework, AngularJS, in favor of Angular 2, which had a radically different architecture, a confusing name, no upgrade path, and wasn’t even fully released yet.
So, many developers turned the wheel and headed to Reactville or Vuetown instead.

How Google botched the Angular upgrade provides timely lessons in how not to update a software package, which former Google Developer Advocate Stephen Fluin outlined in a talk at the All Things Open conference last week.
“Uncertainty kills motivation,” said Fluin. “When you're taking away everything [developers] know and love, they're going to feel disheartened.”
Fluin is now head of developer relations for Buildkite, but he worked for Google from 2016 to 2021 on the Angular project.

“Things were a little bit rough at the time. It was a bit of a death march,” he told the audience. “We had no idea when Angular 2 was going to come out, and the core fundamentals of Angular kept changing.”
From AngularJS to Angular 2
Google had good reasons for updating Angular.

The AngularJS team had been snatched from Google’s infrastructure division and placed under its ad division, where the software could be more fully exploited. To support operations of that size, Angular needed greater rigor.

The original AngularJS was launched in 2009 as a side project of Google engineer Miško Hevery, who wanted to extend HTML. Google pulled AngularJS into an internal project because Google developers found it easier to work with than the Java-based Google Web Toolkit (GWT).
The framework quickly caught on with outside web developers too, who readily understood the angle brackets of HTML (hence the name) and wanted more interactive components.
Hevery built AngularJS 1.3 with a traditional controller model, which handled all user input, logic and data transport under the JavaScript $scope object.

Angular 2, announced at the ng-europe 2014 conference, was a major shift in architecture. It shifted to a component model, with each HTML template enjoying its own class properties. After a forced, unhappy dalliance with Google's Dart, the team rewrote Angular completely in TypeScript, with no backward compatibility whatsoever.

It was a lot to take in, and the introductory talk at ng-europe seemed to spook Angular developers more than inspire them. For each discarded feature, the speakers displayed a graphic of a tombstone (“RIP Controllers”) and played a recording of a church bell tolling in the background.
“That talk is still infamous today for what it did to the community,” Fluin said. “All these things that you know and love about AngularJS are gone. They're dead. And nobody knew this was coming.”

In general, it was not a good time for software migrations, Fluin noted in his talk. Python was having a rough time migrating from version 2 to 3, as was the KDE desktop moving from version 4 to version 5. And the rocky transition from GNOME 2 to 3 still loomed in the rearview mirror for many.
What's in a name?
“If you're trying to bring your developers with you, give them a path. Don't just kill your old thing and then not have a new thing ready,” Fluin advised.
Many devs defected to React and Vue.js, two other JavaScript frontend frameworks that also embraced the component model and were already in production.

In the 2016 State of JS Survey, React was the most popular frontend framework, with 53 percent of JS devs reporting that they had used it. Angular’s audience was heavily bifurcated; 30 percent still used the classic version while only 13 percent used Angular 2. Ten percent of users adopted the still up-and-coming Vue.

Angular 2 was finally released in September 2016, followed by Angular 4 the following March. Version 3 was skipped entirely for no discernable reason. Meanwhile, AngularJS classic, which was not formally retired until the end of 2021, was updated to version 1.5 in the spring of 2016, introducing components.

Muddying the waters further was the naming of the frameworks, which confounded many casual observers. Was AngularJS different from Angular 2? And was the “2” part of the Angular name, signaling the complete architectural shift, or its version number?

Getting the public to understand the name change turned out to be a major quagmire. Fluin said: “We had to fix public communication guidelines. We had to train experts. We had to fix Google's knowledge graph,” which is Google’s database of facts about the world.
“Naming and versioning matter,” he told the audience. “They don't matter in a pure technical sense, but they matter to human beings because it's human beings you're trying to keep up to date with.”

It would be easy to blame the Google brass for nearly shipwrecking Angular, but it has been a success at meeting Google’s needs. Today, the component-driven Angular powers Gemini’s user interface, Google Analytics, and countless other Google apps. It is now converging with Google’s internal Wiz high-performance framework, originally designed for the ill-fated Google+ social network.

Angular has also settled into a more predictable and user-friendly update pattern. Updates have a routine release cadence, currently twice a year. They dutifully follow semantic versioning guidelines, with major version numbers signifying breaking changes. Google tests each new version of the framework on its own apps before releasing it publicly. Any feature slated for removal is deprecated for a year first.
But in retrospect, Google may have been better off giving Angular 2 an entirely different name, even if it meant building up a new user base from scratch.
“JavaScript developers loved trying new frameworks. So, pretending to be a new framework might have been better,” Fluin told The Register. ®

f945cf98ce47877f: URDA: A high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed 64 people and injured scores more on Wednesday, with the toll likely to rise, authorities said in one of Europe's deadliest such disasters this century.
AFP reporters on the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha saw one train embedded into another after the second such accident to strike Spain this year.
Some carriages were lying on their side in tangles of metal debris at the bottom of an embankment, while dozens of emergency services vehicles were racing to and from the site.

"We are speaking of approximately 64 (dead), but this is probably going to grow even more," Castilla-La Mancha's leader Emiliano Garcia-Page told reporters at the scene, raising a previous toll of 31.
A spokeswoman from the Castilla-La Mancha government told AFP that more than 100 people had been injured. Of them, 58 had been taken to hospital, with 15 in a critical condition.
Helicopters hovered above the site during a frantic search for survivors, while several black vans arrived from a funeral parlour.

State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.
Iryo said in a statement that its train, which was carrying 147 passengers and five staff including the driver, "was hit from behind" by the Renfe service.
A visibly shaken Manuel Ortiz, 49, who lives in the nearby village of Urda, around 130km south of Madrid, told AFP he had been transporting survivors all morning in his car.
Ortiz added that the passengers of the Iryo told him their train was stationary when the collision happened, describing a "horrific, horrible" scene that "smelled of an accident, of metal".
Rail safety under scrutiny

The accident comes one month before Socialist prime minister Pedro Sanchez, who faced heavy criticism for this year's first disaster, seeks to overturn unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership in an early general election on Nov 29.
Sanchez's office said he was heading to the scene. The premier had said on X that he was "shocked" by the accident and sent "my love, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families".

Condolences flooded in from across Spain and Europe. The Spanish royal household said on X it was "shocked and concerned" by the accident, conveying its support to the victims, their loved ones and the emergency services.
An EU spokeswoman said the bloc was "ready to help Spain if needed", while European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said "Europe mourns" with the victims after the "devastating news".
The Spanish football federation postponed 24 matches in the first round of the Copa del Rey "as a mark of respect and solidarity".
Spain's high-speed rail network has received huge investment in recent years, growing to become the world's second-largest after China and a source of national pride.

However, Wednesday's accident comes after another collision between two high-speed trains outside the southern village of Adamuz in January left 46 dead, which raised major questions about safety on the country's railways.
That crash was Spain's deadliest train accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela.
Both of this year's accidents happened on the line linking Madrid to the southern city of Seville.

The cause of the latest disaster, which happened on a straight stretch of track in sunny, dry conditions, was unknown. Five people wearing white overalls were examining the tracks and taking photographs, AFP saw.
One of the country's busiest routes, it was Spain's first high-speed line when it opened in 1992 to coincide with the Seville universal exposition.

b65bd78dcb9b0242: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Earlier this month, Meta updated its commercial terms of use for business accounts to allow it to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products.

Many artists and small business owners that rely on Instagram and Facebook are livid at Meta granting itself permission to use their content, including from websites simply connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. But for users in the United Kingdom and European Union, for now, there’s a way to object.

Meta buried this change in its Commercial Terms, and Nieman Lab first reported on the change. The update was originally set to go into effect on October 30, but following backlash, Meta changed the effective date to November 20. Adding to the confusion, Meta then removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, Nieman Lab reported, and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products. Those terms still allow Meta plenty of leeway for scraping users’ data to develop its products, however.

EU users’ personal data rights are governed by the General Data Protection Regulation and the AI Act. GDPR, which became enforceable in 2018, requires explicit consent to use personal data. This includes the right to object to one’s data being used. The AI Act, which went into effect in 2024, dictates how AI companies can use personal data, and how people can opt in or out, stating that they can withdraw consent at any time. The UK has its own version of the GDPR. The European Commission states: “The GDPR rules only apply to personal data about individuals; they do not govern data about companies or any other legal entities. However, information in relation to companies may constitute personal data where it allows the identification of a natural person.”

Several users based in the UK and EU have explained how to object on Instagram. Instagram user bookish.sil posted a walkthrough of how they did it on mobile: by clicking the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center, and clicking “object,” which goes to a form that asks users to write why they are objecting to their data being used. They received an email from Meta saying their objection was approved. Instagram user jenniqueart posted a similar walkthrough with the same results.

My Meta accounts are based in the US, but using a VPN to locate my IP address in London, I could see options in my Meta privacy settings that would let me object to the use of my information by Meta AI. To get there on desktop with a VPN on, I went to my account privacy center, clicked “Submit a privacy rights request” at the bottom, selected Instagram, clicked “How can I object to the processing of my information?” and got to a page where I could choose to object to the use of my information for Meta AI or third parties, which were two separate options.
When my location is based in the US, these options don't appear.

When I clicked through the option to “object to the use of my information for Meta AI,” however, it returned an error page that said “This form is only available to people in certain regions.” GDPR is meant to apply to wherever someone is located at the time, but since this objection applies to the preferences of one account, it might be based on where the account was created. I tried again located in Belgium and got the same results. I’ve asked Meta to clarify.

As many have already pointed out in the comments on UK and EU users who’ve posted walkthroughs, these objection steps aren’t available to people outside of those countries, and as Meta continuously changes its platform, these steps might not work for everyone always. Unless something changes before November 20, the rest of us are screwed.
6b3a7de94c538112: Trillium Asset Management wants Microsoft to explain how it will meet its 2030 greenhouse gas (GHG) emission targets, and is backing a shareholder proposal to request this information at the firm’s next shareholder meeting.

The cloud and software biz set itself lofty environmental goals back in 2020, aiming to be become "carbon-negative" by 2030, and to have removed the equivalent of all the carbon it has ever emitted by 2050.

But since the start of the decade, an explosion in AI development and demand for ever more complex models has seen a boom in demand for high-performance compute infrastructure and a construction wave to deliver new datacenters to house it all in.
Microsoft is one of the firms to profit from this huge demand, with its cloud division making $214.4 billion in revenue for the fiscal year 2026 ended June 30, a 27 percent year-on-year increase.

This has also caused Microsoft’s emissions to head in the wrong direction, with figures from the company’s most recent Environmental Sustainability Report showing that these have increased from 13 million tons of CO2 equivalent in 2020 to 20 million tons in 2025.
However, Microsoft estimates that without the carbon reduction initiatives it has already put in place, emissions would now be much higher, somewhere near 34 million tons.

The increase is largely accounted for by indirect emissions (Scope 3) from the construction and provisioning of datacenters to meet that demand for cloud services and AI training. But as The Register pointed out, 2025 saw a growing contribution from Scope 2, due to generation of energy the company purchased. This represents 13 percent of total emissions – up from 2 percent in 2024.

Now Trillium Asset Management, financial advisors specializing in sustainable and responsible investing, is urging Microsoft shareholders to vote for Proposal 4 during their annual meeting scheduled for December 8.

In an SEC filing, the proposal asks Microsoft to disclose additional information illustrating how it will manage climate commitments. This disclosure should go beyond existing disclosures, at reasonable cost, omitting proprietary information, and be made annually.

The proposal notes that when Microsoft first announced its carbon negative goal, it said progress required "not just a bold goal but a detailed plan," and that transparency was one of the guiding principles for this climate plan.

It states that emissions are now 62 percent above the 2020 baseline, and simply asks Microsoft to apply the principles it articulated in 2020; show the plan, be candid about the math, and explain how it will adapt.

In the filing, Trillium warns that falling short of its climate targets may create risk to Microsoft’s credibility, which can influence investor trust. If Microsoft is in danger of failing to meet its 2030 commitments, it could suffer reputational harm, and the filing claims it is already the subject of legal action by investors alleging insufficient disclosure of its AI and cloud spending.

On the flip side, it says that disclosure of a climate transition plan will likely prove valuable to large institutional investors who view climate change as a systemic risk to future economic growth.

We asked Microsoft for comment, but it already recommended in another SEC filing that shareholders vote against the proposal, arguing it fails to show that Microsoft’s existing disclosures are insufficient for investors to assess its climate-related strategy and performance.

Instead, the firm says that the proposal requests a collection of new disclosures that go beyond not just legal and regulatory requirements, but also established voluntary climate-reporting frameworks.

The proposal seeks hypothetical scenarios, contingency plans and other forward-looking information that is inherently uncertain and subject to change, Microsoft states, saying it will remain focused on its Sustainability Report and other environmental reporting while meeting any new disclosure mandates that may arise globally. ®

c11769620a3fa457: Security is the dominant feature of the EU's new Arctic strategy. dotshock / ShutterstockThe EU recently presented its latest Arctic strategy. It is the bloc’s fifth such strategy since 2008 and the first to be published since 2021, a few months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. This conflict has disrupted Arctic governance. The work of the Arctic Council, which includes Russia as one of its eight member states, was paused shortly after the invasion. The council is the primary forum for cooperation in the region. Since 2022, the Russian security threat in the Arctic has also grown. Russia has engaged in hybrid activities in the region, ranging from disinformation operations and GPS jamming to the targeting of pipelines and undersea cables. The EU’s new strategy has four priorities: strengthening peace, security and resilience in the Arctic, addressing climate change, delivering economic development and ensuring regional and social development for Arctic communities. These priorities are broadly in line with the previous 2021 strategy, in which geopolitical issues were already more present than in earlier years. But there are several major changes. More security and less climate action A word count reveals the profound impact the deteriorating cooperation context has had on the EU’s stance on the region. In the latest update, the word “security” is mentioned 52 times compared with 23 times in 2021. By contrast, “climate change” appears only 14 times in the new strategy compared with 30 times previously. This shift towards security is a general trend in the Arctic since 2022. The creation of an annual Arctic Security Conference in 2024, which discusses security trends in the region, is an example of this. Security also figures prominently in recently published national Arctic strategies, including France, Italy, Germany and Sweden. Climate change is not completely absent from the EU’s latest Arctic strategy, and the bloc reaffirmed its commitment to combat it in the document. But, where previously climate change was the cornerstone of the EU’s Arctic engagement, it is now presented through a security lens. Climate change is identified as “amplifying security risks” and a “defining threat” from which Arctic inhabitants need to be “protected”. Security shapes all four priorities of the new strategy. Arctic communities also get much more attention than in earlier documents. Although the inclusion of Indigenous people also figures more prominently, the conflation between Indigenous and local people has previously been criticised by the Saami Council. The conflation undermines the specific rights and distinct interests of Indigenous groups such as the Sámi. A ‘northern neighbourhood’ Another key change in the EU’s new Arctic strategy is the introduction of the concept of a “northern neighbourhood”. The name suggests similarities with the EU’s European Neighbourhood Policy, which it launched in 2004 to foster closer ties with its eastern and southern neighbours. But it is unclear what exact form the northern neighbourhood will take. The northern neighbourhood is not presented as a new multilateral institution. Instead, it has been put forward as a political framework enabling cooperation projects and integration between the EU and “like-minded” partners such as Greenland, Norway, Iceland, Canada and the UK. By excluding Russia, this new political framework signals a change in the EU’s understanding of the Arctic. The EU’s early engagement in the region came from a will to extend European integration to the east and north in the 2000s. The Arctic was also an area where cooperation with Russia was possible, despite disagreements elsewhere. The concept of a northern neighbourhood reveals a geographical shift in focus towards Greenland and the west and north Atlantic more generally. Yet while the US is still listed among the potential members of the northern neighbourhood, it comes with implicit conditions. According to the new strategy, a partnership with the US needs to be “predictable” and based on “shared interests and values”. This is reminiscent of the language that prevailed for Russia in the previous policies. What kind of power is the EU? Perhaps the biggest change in the new strategy lies in the document’s affirmation that multilateral cooperation “can no longer be the sole foundation of the EU’s Arctic approach”. This means two things. First, that multilateralism is no longer the prominent form of cooperation in the Arctic. And second, that the EU’s geopolitical stance in general is changing from being the champion and embodiment of multilateralism to another form of power. This is also visible in the emphasis the new strategy puts on the EU’s material capabilities and infrastructures as conditions for security. It includes mention of, among other things, developing Europe’s capacity to build icebreaker vessels. The EU’s new Arctic strategy signals a broad shift in the European geopolitical mindset. Climate change and multilateralism have been overshadowed by security concerns due to the fractured Arctic geopolitical landscape. However, ultimately, climate change and social concerns will remain key priorities of Arctic inhabitants and the EU should not lose sight of this. ca0f5a1a0dc47e76: The rapid decline of Antarctic sea ice since 2016 has triggered a dramatic shift in a crucial part of Earth’s climate system, scientists say.

In a paper published Wednesday, researchers documented a sharp salinity increase in a vast layer of the Southern Ocean, extending from 2,300 to 4,000 feet deep and encircling Antarctica. The shift reverses decades of freshening and echoes ocean changes usually associated with major global climate shifts over millennia but is now happening in just a few years.

The switch from a decades-long trend of freshening water to increasing salinity has implications that could extend beyond Antarctica. The layer, known as Antarctic Intermediate Water, spreads northward into the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic oceans, transporting heat, carbon, oxygen, and nutrients toward the tropics, and even across the equator, said co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen, a researcher and professor at the University of Melbourne and at the Centre for Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences in Bengaluru, India.

04fb6dfd792e2f58: WESLACO (Texas), Oct 28 — Formerly a Democratic stronghold, the predominantly Hispanic region of southern Texas has swung rightward in recent years, helping Republicans to a narrow majority in Congress and highlighting a broader shift in Latino voter sentiment.
Now, with control of Congress up for grabs in the November 3 midterm elections, Democrats are hoping a star singer running for office will woo voters back.

Latin Grammy-winner Bobby Pulido, known as the “Golden Boy” of Tejano music, is vying to flip Texas’s 15th congressional district, which stretches from the outskirts of San Antonio south to the Mexico border.
With a population that is over 80 per cent Latino, the district has been represented since 2023 by Republican Monica De La Cruz.
She, like Pulido, grew up in the border area known as the Rio Grande Valley — but her father was not a Tejano music pioneer.

Now 53, Pulido has mostly turned his focus from music to politics during the campaign, but he took to the stage at a rally Sunday in the city of Weslasco alongside the band Los Tigres del Norte, performing their hit song La Puerta Negra (The Black Door).

De La Cruz has hit Pulido for his lack of experience, arguing the election was not about choosing a singer for a quinceanera coming-of-age party, but whom voters should trust with their family’s future.
Pulido took the dig in stride, offering to perform under the banner “Make Quinceaneras Great Again,” a parody of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
People sing along Los Tigres del Norte and Bobby Pulido during a joint campaign event in Weslaco, Texas October 25, 2026.
‘We are good people’

Pulido has tied or taken a slight lead over De La Cruz in polls, as high gas prices caused by Trump’s war with Iran and heavy-handed immigration raids push Latino voters away from supporting Republicans.
“Let’s break a record and send a message that they can’t mess with us anymore. We are good people in the Rio Grande Valley,” Pulido told the crowd of thousands at Sunday’s rally.

In today’s polarised US politics, Pulido has aimed to bring people together across the aisle for support, sporting a campaign slogan that says: “I’m not team Red or team Blue. South Texas, I’m team You.”
“Families stopped talking right now because somebody voted for Trump and somebody didn’t,” he said. “I don’t care what happened in the past. We need to look at the future.”
One of the big focus points of his campaign has been dealing with migration along the US-Mexico border.
“I believe we can secure the border without destroying families and our local economy in the process,” Pulido said in a campaign video.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Latin Grammy winner and Democratic candidate for US House Bobby Pulido speaks during the Voto Latino’s ‘Ready. Go. Vote.’ campaign rally outside of the Mustang Lounge Night Club in Weslaco, Texas October 25, 2026. — Brandon Bell/Getty Images/AFP pic
‘He’s from here’
Rally attendee Joe Jimenez, 44, told AFP he had previously voted for De La Cruz but now supports Pulido.

“He’s going to do a good job not because he’s a singer, it’s because he’s from here and he not only represents us but has gone through a lot of things that we have done,” Jimenez said, adding that he felt De La Cruz “let us down.”

A 2016 video of Pulido has generated controversy, in which he pretends to urinate on Trump’s star along the Hollywood Walk of Fame. The candidate has said the gesture was a joke performed with a water bottle.
Margarita Ramirez, a 49-year-old from Pulido’s hometown of Edinburg, said she was supporting the singer.
“He has been very honest in his work as a musician, and so why would he not be honest in his work as a politician? He’s not someone seeking to cause scandals. He’s a family man,” she told AFP. — AFP
ba826d6283a7d219: PARIS, Oct 28 — Climate change must be declared a “global health emergency” to shape governments’ policies after heat caused three million deaths between 2016 and 2023, a report in The Lancet said today.

Published by the British medical journal ahead of the COP 31 climate summit in November, the 10th edition of the report brought together 146 researchers from 30 countries to assess the impact of climate change on the health of the world’s population.
It said there were a record 710,000 heat-related deaths in 2023 with more than 70 per cent of that toll linked to human-caused climate change.

Marina Romanello, the executive director of the health and climate research project Lancet Countdown, said there were “three million heat-related deaths globally in an eight-year span since the Paris Agreement” of 2015.
“That’s roughly equivalent to the entire population of Wales being wiped out in the space of eight years due to heat,” she told a news conference.
And “68 per cent of those deaths are directly attributable to climate change.”
The legally binding international climate treaty adopted in the French capital aimed to limit global warming to well below 2C and pursue efforts to keep it to 1.5C compared to pre-industrial levels.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

An aerial view shows villagers swimming above coral reefs off Nadir Beach, approximately 52 kilometres from Nadi October 5, 2026. Almost all shallow-water coral reefs around the world are at ‘extremely high risk’ of disappearing by 2075 due to climate change, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned on October 22, 2026. — AFP pic
Climate change impact
Romanello said the global health emergency due to climate change should have “an integrated approach so that we’re not responding to emergency after emergency”.
Instead, she called for “a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities, and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies moving forward”.

To determine the share of deaths attributable to warming caused by human activity, the researchers compiled the number of heat-related deaths recorded by states, then subtracted those that would have occurred in the absence of climate change, said Professor Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney.

Jay said the intensity and frequency of periods of intense heat were amplified by climate change, pointing out that last year an extreme drought affected more than half of the world’s land surface for at least one month.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photograph taken on September 9, 2026 shows dead coral lying along a beach at Kariyachalli Island, off the coast of Thoothukudi in India’s Tamil Nadu state. — AFP pic
Economic cost
By reducing worker productivity, warming has cost the global economy more than one trillion dollars per year over the past three years, the researchers said.

South-east Asia and Africa, the hardest-hit regions, are estimated to have lost the equivalent of 3.9 per cent and 3.2 per cent of their GDP, compared with 0.2 per cent for Europe and 1.5 per cent for the Americas.
However there has been concrete progress in some areas.
Since 2016, 56 of the WHO’s 194 member states have adapted their health and early-warning systems to anticipate extreme events.
Investment in clean energy reached US$2.1 trillion (RM8.5 trillion) in 2025 — double that of the amount invested in fossil fuels, which cause climate change.
However fossil fuels still account for 80 per cent of global energy, causing air pollution that results in 2.73 million deaths per year, the study said.
Meanwhile, roughly 323,000 deaths have been avoided in “at least” 77 countries where air pollution from fossil fuels has fallen since 2016, according to the report.

Although funding for climate-related medical research has increased sevenfold to reach US$316 million in 2024, 84 per cent of these funds go to researchers in wealthy countries, even though the least developed nations are the most affected by the growing climate-related health threats.

Romanello said this year for the first time the researchers’ work was complicated by the disappearance of certain data sources, particularly from the United States, such as fossil fuel subsidies, which have not been made public by the US authorities.

And for the past two years, global geopolitical instability has pushed global warming and its health impact into the background, she said, stressing that inaction was exacerbating the situation. — AFP
6abf7f884bc3da1e: HAVANA, Oct 28 — Kevin Martinez has come up with a creative new way to avoid shutting his restaurant when water runs low in Cuba, a common source of frustration for the business owner.

His business is located in the Matanzas province, 100 kilometres east of Havana and one of the regions particularly affected by the shortages.

“On several occasions we had to close the establishment because we didn’t have any water...and that’s what brought us to the point of having to dig the well,” Martinez told AFP.
“I never imagined I’d have to be digging a well, just as I never imagined I’d have to be cooking with coal or installing solar panels,” he said.
The decision to drill, although “a bit expensive,” sets him free from paying for water deliveries three times a week.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Cars drive along a street in Havana October 26, 2026. Water does not reach the homes of 2.7 million Cubans, Yunior Gonzalez, a senior official at the national water company, told AFP. — AFP pic
‘Daily struggle’
Water does not reach the homes of 2.7 million Cubans, Yunior Gonzalez, a senior official at the national water company, told AFP.
“Between 80 and 85 per cent of the water” supplied has to be pumped to get to these households, he said, adding that equipment breakdowns, leaks and drought have exacerbated the problem.
Water difficulties are forcing many Cubans to haul the precious resource for long distances, transporting it via wheelbarrows, bicycles, car trunks and even horse-drawn carts.
Maykel Aguilar, 30, patiently filled a 200-liter tank and several buckets at a pipe connected to a spring on a street in the capital’s old town.
He then must use a wheelbarrow to get it to his home before heaving it up a flight of stairs.
“One little trip like that is enough for a load of laundry, cleaning the house, and cooking, and just like that you’re out of water,” Aguilar said.
Neighbours line up in the same spot, marking their place with tanks, buckets and jerrycans.
“The power outages here happen every day and we have to keep hauling water,” said 40-year-old mother of two Yusimy Guerra.
“It’s a daily struggle,” she sighed.
Water scarcity adds to Cuba’s runaway inflation, while food and medicine also run low amid mounting social unrest.
Municipalities in Havana have recorded several women-led protests over water shortages in recent months.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Residents collect potable water from a public supply point in Havana October 5, 2026. Water scarcity adds to Cuba’s runaway inflation, while food and medicine also run low amid mounting social unrest. — AFP pic
‘Thieves’

More and more Cubans are drilling wells on their properties, building cisterns in their yards, installing tanks and even resorting to so-called “water thieves” — pumps that suck the trickle of water from the mains and force it into their homes.
Several of these installations in the same neighbourhood can reduce the pressure in the network and make it even harder for other households to access water.
Well digger Elizardo Cardoso, who found water 10 meters below the ground at Martinez’s restaurant, says his trade is in high demand.
Water agent Gonzalez meanwhile said the government is moving forward with transforming the sector’s energy mix as a way to reduce dependence on the faulty national power grid.
More than 870 solar-powered water pumps have already been installed out of the 1,300 planned, benefiting half a million Cubans across the country, he said.
The Albear Aqueduct, one of Havana’s main sources of water supply, recently gained two brand-new, gigantic backup generators that run on diesel.
But “they are very expensive programmes,” Gonzalez cautioned. — AFP
14c5b8fc8ba1de0e: MONTREAL, Oct 28 — Young Canadians testified yesterday to a “sense of despair” during a landmark climate trial over the federal government’s alleged climate policy failures and the “scary” consequences of global warming.

The latest testimony from the 15 plaintiffs who brought the suit, all aged 17 to 25, is part of a growing global movement among environmental activists seeking to use courts to force government accountability on climate change.
“I want the court to know that we are doing this for our future,” Sadie Vipond said on the stand.
The 20-year-old student hails from Calgary, in western Canada, where she described thick smoke and overwhelming heat that descends year after year on her hometown.
Wildfires are “something we had to be more and more aware of,” Vipond said, adding that she had to evacuate her home in 2013 because of flooding.
“It again brought this sense of despair” in 2022 when the floods returned.

Members of the legal team and some of the 15 plaintiffs of the first youth climate trial in Canada pose at Federal court in Vancouver on the first day in the La Rose v. His Majesty the King trial October 26, 2026. — AFP pic
Sophia Sidarous, a 25-year-old member of First Nation, gave emotional testimony about the threat climate change poses to her community’s traditional activities.
“Someone actually died from the heat during a powwow,” she said, describing a traditional Indigenous gathering where she lives in Nova Scotia, in eastern Canada.
She described the frustration of belonging to a community of hunters while “we have moose and salmon and various other species that are declining.”

Climate science professor Kirsten Zickfeld, of Simon Fraser University in Vancouver, also testified for nearly three hours to explain to the court the “increase in the intensity and frequency of extreme heat events, of droughts, of heavy rainfall events and also of rapid sea level rise.”
“Canada’s carbon budget is essentially zero or negative,” Zickfeld added, noting that such a burden “will be passed on to future generations.”
Supporters of the first federal youth climate trial in Canadian history hold up signs during a rally outside the Vancouver Art Gallery in Vancouver October 26, 2026. — AFP pic
Overall, the plaintiffs aim to prove that successive governments have violated their constitutional rights to life and security by failing to protect them from the threats posed by climate change.

Canadian targets currently call for a 40-45 per cent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared with 2005 levels, but Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has already indicated those benchmarks may be missed.
The lawsuit, first filed in 2019, was initially dismissed. In 2023, a federal appeals court ruled the youths were entitled to a trial. — AFP

3d1314c4ccbf14f4: Intel has become the latest target for Good Jobs First, which questions why the chipmaker continues to receive tax breaks from key states, long after setting up shop there, and laying off thousands of workers in those regions.

The non-profit organization, which promotes accountability in economic development, says the chipmaker promised billions of dollars in investment and thousands of high-tech jobs for the areas surrounding its manufacturing plants in Hillsboro, Oregon, and Rio Rancho, New Mexico.

Its report, The Bleeding Edge: How the Public Pays the Costs of Intel’s Semiconductor Manufacturing, claims that Intel's property tax breaks cost these communities more than $1.2 billion in lost revenue since 2015, and the brunt of the shortfall has largely fallen on schools funded by those local governments.

For Oregon, Good Jobs First says that property tax abatements from Intel's use of the Strategic Investment Program (SIP) exempted it from at least $1.14 billion, while Hillsboro schools lost $891 million in revenue from 2017 through 2025.
During the same timeframe, Intel paid Oregon $552.4 million in fees, or less than a third of the value of its tax breaks.

In New Mexico, the figures are lower, but still significant. The report puts Chipzilla's property tax exemptions from Industrial Revenue Bonds (IRBs) at $99.6 million in foregone revenue since 2017, while Rio Rancho’s Public Schools lost an estimated $43.4 million over the same nine-year period. Here, the company paid $41.6 million in required payments in lieu of taxes from 2017 through 2025, shared among affected local governments.
Good Jobs First also notes that despite these subsidies, Intel was awarded billions under the CHIPS Act funding from the US federal government.
However, the situation with that is somewhat complex, as the company secured an initial $7.86 billion under the Biden administration, of which $2.2 billion is believed to have been paid out.

The incoming Trump administration, however, decided to rethink the scheme, and ended up making an $8.9 billion deal for 10 percent of Intel’s common stock, made up of the remaining $5.7 billion of the CHIPS Act cash plus an additional $3.2 billion under the Secure Enclave program to make semiconductors for the military.

At the same time, the chipmaker is estimated by Good Jobs First to have laid off more than 4,700 workers at its facilities in Oregon and New Mexico over the past three years, as the company wrestled with restructuring efforts and dramatic losses.
(These are just a fraction of Intel’s total layoffs during the period.)

The issue, according to the non-profit, is that these sites are established Intel facilities which the company has operated for decades. They already have the facilities, infrastructure, skilled workers, and other necessities that a new site might require investment for. Are continued tax breaks truly necessary, Good Jobs First asks, or are they just subsidizing business decisions Intel would make anyway?

It says Intel’s track record in Oregon and New Mexico should be taken as important lessons for other communities considering becoming a home to semiconductor manufacturing, and recommends questioning whether state and local tax breaks are even necessary.

"Tax incentives are supposed to encourage investment, not provide companies with an ongoing stream of public support for decades," said Good Jobs First Research Analyst and report author Kristan Wong Karinen.

"Intel has received tax breaks at these campuses for generations, and local leaders should be asking hard questions about why those subsidies are still necessary, especially with the billions of dollars in federal grants and tax credits they receive from the CHIPS Act."

We asked Intel for a statement regarding these claims by Good Jobs First, and in response it told us: "Intel works closely with governments in the regions where we operate to leverage incentives that support leading-edge semiconductor R&D and manufacturing. We are not providing additional details beyond what's available in our annual reports."

Recent targets for the non-profit have been datacenters, and the states offering tax incentives for developers and operators to build within their jurisdiction. Some states were losing billions in lost revenue to server farm projects, while others were failing to disclose their tax shortfall. ®

b5e79c3f135e3bc3: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 28 — The Court of Appeal today sentenced a headmaster to 20 years in jail and 11 strokes of the cane for making pornography and committing physical sexual assault against a standard six student five years ago.

A three-judge panel, chaired by Justice Datuk Noorin Badaruddin alongside Justices Datuk Mohd Radzi Abdul Hamid and Datuk Meor Hashimi Abdul Hamid, dismissed Anuar Kintan’s appeal against his conviction and sentence of nine years and eight strokes of the cane imposed by the High Court for the charge of making pornography.

The panel, however, allowed the prosecution’s appeal to overturn the lower court’s decisions to acquit and discharge Anuar on the second charge of physical sexual assault against the victim, who was 12 years old at the time.
The court subsequently convicted him of the charge, sentencing him to 11 years with three strokes of the cane.

Justice Noorin, who delivered the unanimous decision, ordered the sentences to be served consecutively. She also issued a warrant of committal for Anuar, 59, to begin his sentence today. He had previously obtained a stay of execution of the sentence and was released on bail of RM14,000 with one surety pending disposal of his appeal.

The court, meanwhile, upheld the lower court’s decision to acquit and discharge Anuar on the third and fourth charges, which involved physical sexual assault on the girl and uttering words intended to be heard by the victim for sexual purposes.

Justice Noorin said the victim had given direct testimony identifying the accused as the person who took the photographs, and that her testimony had been considered by the Sessions Court judge who accepted it.
She said the existence of the photographs was not an isolated circumstance, but was supported by forensic examination that identified the images in Anuar’s Realme mobile phone.
On the second charge, Justice Noorin said the court disagreed that the alibi evidence presented by Anuar had raised reasonable doubt.
The defence had put forward an alibi in which Anuar’s wife testified that he was at home with her, and not at the school, when the incident occurred.

Justice Noorin said the testimony of the victim’s friend provided material support for the prosecution’s case regarding the accused’s presence at the school on April 3, 2021, and his movements with the victim. Therefore, the alibi evidence presented by the accused did not raise reasonable doubt.

On April 19, 2024, the Sessions Court found Anuar guilty of the first offence for making pornography by taking photos of the victim and sentenced him to three years in jail and two strokes of the cane.

The Sessions Court also sentenced him to an additional one year’s imprisonment and two strokes of the cane under Section 16 (1) of the Sexual Offences Against Children Act 2017. The section provides for punishment if an offender commits a sexual crime while holding a position of trust over a child. The sentences were to run consecutively.
The Sessions Court, however, acquitted him of the second, third and fourth charges.
The High Court on Aug 15 last year increased the prison sentence for the first charge to nine years’ imprisonment and eight strokes of the cane and upheld his acquittal for the other three charges.
The offences were committed at a school in Perak in the middle of March 2021 and on April 3, 2021.
At the proceedings today, Anuar was represented by lawyer Amir Khusyairi Mohamad Tanusi while Deputy Public Prosecutors Azlina Mahmod and P. Sarulatha appeared for the prosecution. — Bernama
e8c6c1e72f34fb01: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 28 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has stressed that Budget 2027 was formulated to continue promoting Islam, including through specific measures to strengthen pondok religious schools nationwide.

Anwar, who is also Finance Minister, said the government had sought the views of Islamic scholars and religious teachers in drawing up the budget to ensure that the development needs of Islam received due attention.
He therefore criticised certain quarters for labelling the leader behind the Madani Government’s Budget 2027 as a “hypocrite”.

“When formulating Budget 2027, we asked what more could be done for Islam and what else could be added. In the past, we neglected pondok institutions and pesantren (Islamic boarding schools), but now we are rebuilding them.

“In the past, we sidelined the syeikhs, religious teachers and tuan-tuan guru (respected religious scholars), but now we invite them and seek their views,” he said when speaking at the Majlis Ilmu MADANI programme at Kompleks Seri Perdana here today, which featured renowned Indonesian preacher Ustaz Dr Abdul Somad Batubara as a guest.

Also present were the Prime Minister’s wife, Datuk Seri Dr Wan Azizah Wan Ismail; Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Religious Affairs) Dr Zulkifli Hasan; and Weststar Group founder and managing director Tan Sri Dr Syed Azman Syed Ibrahim.
Anwar admitted that he was somewhat angered by the matter but said he remained patient, describing it as a systemic problem.

“When the matter was debated in Parliament, he called the leader a hypocrite and the budget hypocritical. If I were to ask Ustaz Abdul Somad, he would say, ‘Be patient, Pak.’ My heart was boiling, but I remained patient and did not respond.

“I just want to say that this is merely symptomatic of the real problem … those who profess Islam do not help or set a good example in terms of morals, personal conduct, moderation and tolerance,” he said.
Previously, Dewan Rakyat Speaker Tan Sri Johari Abdul had directed Datuk Seri Takiyuddin Hassan (PN-Kota Bharu) to withdraw the word “hypocrite” that he had used during the debate.

The Prime Minister also expressed his appreciation to Abdul Somad for sharing his knowledge at the programme, adding that the preacher’s advice was always taken seriously in efforts to make Malaysia a better country.
“Ustaz Abdul Somad is now a prominent figure, but he is also controversial in some respects because he is bold in his criticism, which can sometimes be sharp.

“His criticism reaches all those in power, including in Malaysia. However, based on our experience in matters of governance and procedures, we welcome such criticism and try to make improvements,” he said.
ba7f5ac2b22a607f: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — The High Court here today dismissed the appeal by former Axis Incorporation Bhd board adviser Lee Koon Huat against his conviction and sentence on four charges of abetting the furnishing of false financial statements to Bursa Malaysia.

In a statement today, the Securities Commission (SC) said Judge Noor Ruwena Md Nurdin held that the prosecution had proven the charges against Lee beyond reasonable doubt at trial and there were no grounds to interfere with the Sessions Court’s decision.
“The High Court further agreed with the SC’s submission that the sentence imposed against Lee was appropriate in view of Lee’s role in the commission of the offences.

“As such, the court dismissed Lee’s appeal against sentence and upheld the sentence imposed by the Sessions Court, being six months’ imprisonment and a fine of RM200,000 for each charge or in default, six months’ imprisonment,” it said.
The statement said, the court allowed Lee’s application for stay of execution in respect of the sentence of imprisonment, but declined to grant a stay in respect of the fine.
“Lee will have to pay a total fine of RM800,000 by today, failing which he will be imprisoned in default of the payment,” said the statement.

The SC said Lee was initially charged at the Sessions Court on 23 March 2013 with four charges under Section 122C(c) read together with Section 122B(a)(bb) of the Securities Industry Act 1983 (SIA) for abetting Axis in the furnishing of false financial statements relating to the revenue of Axis for the financial year 2007.
“Evidence adduced during the trial established that Lee had instructed the inflation of Axis’ reported revenue in its four unaudited quarterly results for the financial year 2007,” it said.

The SC had also previously charged three former Axis executive directors, Lee Han Boon, Saipuddin Lim Abdullah and Koh Tee Jin, with offences relating to the furnishing of false financial statements for the 2007 and 2008 financial years.
All three pleaded guilty and were sentenced to imprisonment terms ranging from one day to 12 months, while Lee Han Boon and Koh were also sentenced to fine of RM200,000 respectively.

Deputy Public Prosecutor Shoba Venu Gobal and prosecuting officers Low Wen Zhen, Eunice Ong, and Amina Qistina Mohd Idris appeared for the SC while Lee was represented by counsel Jason Ng Kau and Caroline Lee. — Bernama
ad8a7bfc37201941: Patients who think they're getting an annual checkup often end up with an unexpected bill. The Good Brigade/DigitalVision Collection via Getty ImagesI was teaching health economics when a student raised his hand. We were discussing the Affordable Care Act, or ACA, which requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services at no additional cost to patients. I explained that preventive care could cost nothing. The student had expected that, too. Instead, he said, he received a bill for more than US$500 after his checkup. He was so frustrated that he said he would never go back for another annual checkup. I suggested he contact his insurer to find out why he had been charged and whether his visit had been billed as preventive care. Then another student spoke up. Her husband had paid several hundred dollars for what he thought would be a free checkup too. The very next day, I received a $78 bill for my own Pap smear. I expected my insurance to cover this cervical cancer screening without cost-sharing because it is among the preventive services recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and generally covered under the ACA. When I called my insurer, I learned that the visit had been billed as a regular outpatient office visit, with no mention of the Pap smear. I then called my primary care provider’s office. The clinic acknowledged a coding error and corrected it. My bill dropped to zero. As an assistant professor of health policy and addiction studies at Penn State Harrisburg, I know whom to call and what questions to ask when I receive an unexpected medical bill. Many of my graduate students worked full time and took evening classes. Would they know how to dispute a bill, or have time? Those experiences led me to investigate how often patients pay out of pocket for annual checkups. I teamed up with fellow researchers Erin Duffy and Max Crowley to examine this question. In our analysis of a Pennsylvania survey, nearly 1 in 4 insured respondents reported paying for their most recent checkup. Why a preventive visit may come with a bill Many health care services covered by insurance are subject to copayments or deductibles. A copayment is a fixed amount patients pay for a covered service, while a deductible is the amount they generally must pay for covered care before insurance starts paying. The ACA, however, requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services, including screenings for high blood pressure and certain cancers, vaccinations and counseling to help people quit smoking. These should come at no cost to patients. Generally, this applies when patients see providers who are in their insurance plan’s network. But that doesn’t mean every annual checkup is free. If a patient discusses a new symptom or asks the clinician to manage an existing condition during their annual checkup, it can result in a separate office-visit charge. A test may be billed as diagnostic rather than preventive, and coverage varies by plan and provider. Sometimes, as in my case, a coding error is responsible. Not every charge is inappropriate. The challenge is that patients often cannot tell which services should be covered, why they were billed, or whether a mistake occurred. What our survey found Previous studies have found, using insurance claims, that patients sometimes face out-of-pocket costs during preventive visits. But these records show how visits were billed, not necessarily what patients believed they were receiving. We wanted to know whether people who thought they were getting annual checkups also reported paying out of pocket. Our study, published in August 2026 in the peer-reviewed journal Prevention Science, used the 2024 Penn State Lion Poll, an online survey of Pennsylvania adults. We analyzed responses from 912 insured adults who reported an annual checkup within the preceding 10 years. Most had one in the past year. Of those respondents, 23.5% reported paying out of pocket for their most recent checkup. Among those who paid, the average reported out-of-pocket amount was $68.50. After accounting for other characteristics such as age, gender, insurance type, income and education, we found that respondents who were not familiar with ACA preventive-care protections were about 12 percentage points more likely to report paying than those who were familiar with the protections. That difference is equivalent to roughly 12 more people paying out of every 100. Those who considered healthcare unaffordable were about 13 percentage points more likely to pay than those who found it affordable. Because our survey relied on patients’ reports rather than billing records, we could not determine why individual charges occurred, or whether they were appropriate. The findings show associations, not causation, and our nonrandom sample cannot provide a precise statewide estimate. How doctor visits are billed doesn’t always match what service patients think they are receiving. adamkaz/E+ Collection via Getty Images Why these bills matter I kept thinking about the student who said he would never return for another checkup. Research has shown that even modest out-of-pocket costs can discourage people from getting recommended screenings. Delaying preventive care could mean missing opportunities to detect health problems early, when treatment may be more effective. Our survey did not find a statistically significant association between paying for a previous checkup and planning another one. However, respondents who were unfamiliar with ACA protections or considered healthcare unaffordable were less likely to plan a checkup. These findings suggest that uncertainty about costs may discourage people from seeking preventive care. What patients can do Before a visit, ask your insurer which preventive services are covered without cost-sharing and confirm that your provider is in-network. Ask the clinic whether discussing other health concerns or receiving additional tests could trigger a charge. If a bill arrives, compare it with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, which you can typically find in your online insurance account or receive by mail. Ask the provider’s billing office which services and codes were submitted and request a correction if something appears wrong. You can also contact your insurer to question or appeal a coverage decision. A colleague told me she challenged a $20 or $30 copayment requested at check-in for an annual visit after remembering our conversations. The charge was removed. Patients should not have to become experts in insurance billing to receive preventive care. Clearer coverage information and more transparent billing could help people seek care without fearing unexpected costs. Read more of our stories about Philadelphia and Pennsylvania, or sign up for our Philadelphia newsletter on Substack. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the views of SSRI or Penn State.
1084f4473e021767: Paying for childcare remains one of the biggest costs for households, often costing as much as housing. AP Photo/Craig MitchelldyerWhile affordability pressures are hitting Americans in many facets of their lives, from groceries to gas prices to housing costs, one important expense often gets less attention – childcare. After a huge infusion of federal funds into childcare dried up at the end of the Biden administration, experts warned that this sharp cutoff, sometimes dubbed the “childcare cliff,” would force parents to either scale back work to handle the extra caretaking or pay steep costs out of pocket. The potential effects of the federal cuts are hard to estimate, in part because states took different approaches in the aftermath. In some cases, they offset the sharp cuts in part by redirecting other funds to childcare. But several states, including Vermont, New Mexico and Kentucky, have gone further and innovated on their own to shore up support for working parents and their young children. Meanwhile, New York City is expanding free toddler slots for lower-income families, following Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s announcement to build a universal early childcare system. Taken together, these experiments point to bipartisan ways to support working parents, especially if the results of the November 2026 midterms signal a new willingness to tackle one of the biggest cost burdens for families. As researchers of sociology and childcare policy with six children from 1 to 16 years old between us, we have also gained insights from our own data gathered over 75 interviews with parents in St. Louis, Missouri, over the past few years. We see them struggling with a fragmented childcare system that’s in need of a deep strategic investment. These families face limited choices and soaring costs for an essential good that allows a parent to go to work. Out-of-pocket expenses for parents using center-based care in childcare centers and private preschool programs have more than doubled since 2019. In 2024, the national average price of childcare was US$13,128 annually, which rivals housing as the most expensive item in family budgets. States go their own way The disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic laid bare the critical role that reliable, high-quality childcare plays for working families. But we believe it also presented an opportunity for innovative investments in the nation’s fractured childcare landscape. Pandemic relief legislation in 2021 directed nearly $40 billion to shore up the supply and quality of childcare. This funding increase, which was a fourfold jump over previous levels, supported childcare staff with higher wages and allowed for other investments to improve the quality of care. The reach was vast, with stabilization funds flowing to 220,000 providers serving 9.6 million children. Many states also provided grants to create new slots and improve how providers got paid. As those funds began drying up in September 2023, some states started to address these shortfalls on their own. In some cases, they took significant steps at a policy level to channel more support to working parents. We believe these investments could serve as examples for the rest of the country. One is Vermont, which in 2023 became the first state to pass a law establishing a childcare entitlement. Following more than a decade of advocacy and bipartisan support, the law established a near-universal public childcare system, funded partially through a payroll tax of 0.44% split between employers and employees. Through an expansion of subsidies along income tiers, the number of families covered rose by 55% from July 2022 to May 2025, while flexible grants increased the number of providers and focused on improving the quality of care. About 12,000 children are now covered under this program. New Mexico went even further. In November 2025, the state became the first in the nation to offer universal childcare. Based on an older program that provided free childcare to low-income families, the initiative expanded support to all working parents regardless of income. Children draw at a daycare center in Albuquerque, N.M., which has gone further than any other state in expanding subsidies for working parents. AP Photo/Susan Montoya Bryan Before the expansion, 32,000 children were covered, a number the state aims to double by 2028. On average, the state estimates that the program will save families $12,000 a year. Meanwhile, the Kentucky legislature in April 2026 passed a measure with strong bipartisan support to make major investments in the state’s childcare infrastructure. Key provisions include free childcare for the children of childcare center employees, increased state-subsidized reimbursement rates, and required training to support very young special needs children. The Kentucky measure also loosened regulations that had made it tough for employers to share costs for care, such as renting facilities, while pitching a pilot program to open one-room “microcenters” in communities that lacked sufficient childcare options. In addition, Gov. Andy Beshear launched a complementary Pre-K for All pilot program in several counties. Another example is New York City, where Mamdani has announced an expansion for toddlers as young as 2 years old in all five of the city’s boroughs, building on the city’s programs for free childcare for 3-K and pre-K. To date, this effort has increased some slots, although the rollout in September hit bumps. The childcare crunch by the numbers Given the skyrocketing costs, over 70% of families who sought care say it’s difficult to find childcare – and that doesn’t count the 11% who fail to find any at all, according to a 2023 government survey. That report found that families with Black or Hispanic children or infants, and those living in the South and West, are more likely to run into cost as a barrier. On the supply side, three-quarters of providers say they have to turn many families away or put them on waiting lists. Center-based care for an infant costs more than in-state college tuition at a public university in 32 states, yet childcare workers, who are overwhelmingly women of color, earn the same as parking lot attendants and dog walkers. That makes them some of the lowest-paid workers in the entire economy. Amid soaring costs and scarce supply, roughly half of all U.S. families live in so-called childcare deserts – areas where there are three children under 5 for every licensed-care slot. The answer for many families in these cases is to rely on ad hoc and irregular informal care. Some parents told us they’re turning to relatives and neighbors for help. Others resorted to using unlicensed, and potentially unsafe, childcare providers because they found no other viable options. And for some remote workers, the daunting solution is to care for their kids themselves while working. The problem with such makeshift arrangements is that they tend, on average, to offer fewer of the learning opportunities linked to children’s long-term development and social mobility. And even these arrangements can be tough to afford: One single mother we interviewed told us she paid for a week’s childcare in kind with her own breast milk, which went to feed the care provider’s grandchildren. We also spoke to parents who reported choosing between childcare bills and heat, electricity or rent. Another mom told us about a more unconventional solution. She and her husband work full time but can’t afford the childcare options in their community, so she decided to join a gym that provides free childcare while its members exercise. She brings her laptop and works, rather than working out, while her toddler plays. These parents are scraping by in the absence of the affordable, subsidized childcare options commonplace in other countries. But this crunch is also a lose-lose proposition for the economy. The U.S. could lose as much as $290 billion per year by 2030 in forgone economic activity due to women not working or not working as much due to childcare pressures, according to the consultancy BCG. A path forward The Trump administration has laid out its own vision. Vice President JD Vance announced in September 2026 a preliminary proposal to repurpose existing funds for childcare subsidies as a cash transfer to married parents, provided that one spouse stays home. We believe, however, this approach fails to reflect the real needs of the millions of U.S. parents who can’t pay their bills if they only get one paycheck. In fact, under the subsidy program that Vance cited, only 16% of eligible children are reached today anyway. We believe, based on our research, that any comprehensive overhaul has four important components. First is a robust national policy for paid family leave, which would let families make the best care decisions for newborns, infants and parents themselves rather than sprinting back to work. Paid family leave would also ease demand for scarce infant care in the market. Second is an expansion of early childhood care and education programs. By publicly subsidizing childcare, particularly for low-income families and special needs kids, policymakers can help close the affordability gap for high-quality care. Third is a greater investment in childcare workers. Qualified caregivers are the cornerstone of high-quality childcare. If their wages and working conditions improve, it means fewer will have to take side hustles or quit for better jobs. Finally, providers will need more incentives to open in underserved areas. Childcare is expensive to provide and runs on thin margins. In low-income and rural areas, many families can’t pay prices that cover the true cost of care, and subsidy payments are often set below that cost. So opening a center there doesn’t make much financial sense. Startup grants, higher subsidy rates and operating support help close that gap, which makes it possible to open and stay open where need is greatest.
