04f101fb6f68cf59: If you're going with a lower-cost health insurance plan, make sure to read the fine print. Pla2na/iStock via Getty Images PlusHealthcare costs are a major concern for Americans, and health insurance premiums are a primary fuel for that anxiety. Shrinking federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans led to large premium increases for millions of Americans in 2025, causing many people to drop coverage. With premiums expected to rise further and Medicaid work requirements set to begin in January 2027, many Americans are left scrambling for affordable options. We are health economists who study public policies aimed at expanding health insurance coverage. When it comes to our own health insurance, we are fortunate: We are among the roughly 160 million Americans who receive coverage through their employers. But if you don’t work for a large employer that provides health benefits, finding coverage for your family can be confusing and, increasingly, expensive. People looking for low-cost alternatives have no doubt encountered several options. They may look appealing and, in some cases, may be appropriate, but they can also carry real risks. Navigating trade-offs Historically, people who didn’t have access to employer-sponsored coverage had limited health insurance options. Before the Affordable Care Act went into effect in 2014, insurers could charge you a higher premium based on your health status, exclude coverage for preexisting medical conditions, or deny you coverage altogether. The ACA eliminated this kind of discrimination, established a minimum standard of 10 essential benefits that health insurance plans had to cover, and required plans to fully cover the cost of preventive care. It also introduced income-based subsidies that could be used to purchase coverage in newly established online marketplaces. Americans who are not insured through an employer-sponsored plan must find coverage through sources like the ACA marketplaces. mixetto/E+ via Getty Images Low-cost plans that aren’t available through ACA marketplaces are essentially vestiges of the pre-ACA health insurance landscape. Regardless of where you get coverage, choosing health insurance involves trade-offs. The more you pay in premiums, the more comprehensive your coverage will be in terms of how much you must pay when you need care and the breadth of the network of covered providers. Some trade-offs are clear when you choose a plan, but some lower-cost options may have limitations that are not immediately obvious. Less costly short-term plans As their name suggests, short-term, limited-duration plans are designed for people with temporary gaps in coverage, such as those who are between jobs or months away from qualifying for Medicare. These plans, which can be purchased for periods of up to six months, tend to be cheaper than marketplace coverage for two reasons. First, because they are not subject to ACA rules, they may not provide the full range of essential health benefits. Short-term, limited-duration plans often do not cover maternity care and commonly don’t have an annual limit on out-of-pocket costs. In fact, these plans may cap how much they will pay in a year, leaving policyholders stuck with large, unexpected expenses. Second, unlike plans offered through the ACA marketplaces, short-term, limited-duration plans are allowed to deny coverage based on your health status. Screening out higher-cost consumers reduces premiums, but if you are not in perfect health, you may not be able to find an insurer that will sell you one of these more limited plans. Because of a concern that they destabilize the market by siphoning off healthy consumers, short-term, limited-duration plans are banned in five states. Alternatives that look like insurance Another seemingly affordable option is healthcare sharing ministries, arrangements through which consumers with common religious beliefs agree to share medical expenses. Their websites resemble those of health insurance companies – for example, they often present different plan options offering different levels of benefits – but they avoid using standard insurance terms like “premium” or “deductible” because these offerings are not insurance. Because they are not regulated as insurance companies, healthcare sharing ministries are not subject to consumer protections or other state or federal requirements. There is also no guarantee that the ministry will cover your medical expenses when you submit a claim. Like short-term, limited-duration plans, healthcare sharing ministries may deny coverage based on your health history, exclude coverage for preexisting conditions and put a limit on the dollar amount they will pay in benefits. Another lower-cost option available in 14 states is health coverage offered by a farm bureau. These plans are similar to healthcare sharing ministries in that they are limited to a certain group of people – to enroll, you must be a member of the state’s farm bureau, though that does not mean you necessarily have to work in agriculture. These plans are also not subject to federal or state insurance regulations. This means that, like short-term, limited-duration plans, they can offer lower prices by not offering certain benefits required by the ACA and by screening out high-cost consumers. Unlike short-term, limited-duration plans, there is no limit on how long you can hold farm bureau coverage. Choosing a health insurance plan often requires fighting through a thicket of jargon. What should you do? Although the cost of marketplace coverage has increased dramatically since 2025, for many consumers who need coverage for more than six months, it remains the best option. If you are single with an annual income below US$64,000, a couple with an annual income below $87,000, or a family of four with an annual income less than $132,000, you should still be eligible for a premium subsidy. And you will know that the plan you are purchasing is real insurance that covers a standard set of benefits and is subject to robust consumer protections. If you are considering an alternative to marketplace coverage, there are a few things you should do to protect yourself: Make sure you ask for a summary of benefits and coverage. This is a plain language summary of a health plan’s benefits and coverage with examples of how much the plan would cover for two specific conditions – diabetes and childbirth. Insurers and employers who offer coverage are required to provide this document to anyone applying for coverage. If they cannot provide one, what they are selling may not actually be insurance. If they do provide a summary of benefits and coverage, read it carefully. As we noted earlier, one reason some options might be less expensive than a marketplace plan is that they provide much less coverage. Don’t assume that they cover all the benefits you would expect from a health insurance plan, or that they will cover the full cost of the care you receive. Finally, never enter your phone number into a “do you need insurance” website. This area is rife with fraud, including multiple cases in which telemarketers misled consumers into paying hundreds of dollars per month to purchase sham health insurance. Health insurance is expensive because healthcare is expensive – which means that consumers have to make difficult trade-offs. There is no easy answer, but beware of options that look too good to be true. They very well might be. Thomas Buchmueller is a Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. 119cf39f6711bef0: Many of the stores where people use SNAP benefits are small. O2O Creative/E+ via Getty ImagesAfter 10 states began to add new restrictions to what people could buy with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits in early 2026, the number of convenience stores authorized to accept those benefits was 1.4% lower than would be expected based on trends in states without the policy change. That’s what we found in our study, published in October 2026 in Health Affairs Scholar – a peer-reviewed journal. SNAP, a federally funded program administered by the states, helps about 36 million low-income Americans afford groceries with government benefits that can be used at more than 250,000 stores to buy fresh fruit, ground beef, canned beans and other groceries. Using the benefits for many items, including hot food, alcohol, toiletries and pet food, has long been prohibited. States can now obtain federal waivers to prohibit SNAP benefits from being used to buy other products. The 10 states with waivers that we studied had a mix of rules. Some only barred the sale of soda and other sugary drinks. Other prohibitions applied to energy drinks, candy, cake and other prepared desserts. In states like Oklahoma and Florida that have adopted these new SNAP restrictions to discourage unhealthy diets, the number of convenience stores participating in the program has fallen relative to other states that haven’t made these changes. That was especially notable in areas with high numbers of low-income people where a large share of the population gets SNAP benefits. We analyzed the number of stores participating in SNAP from January 2025 through June 2026 for the 10 states. We compared changes to that number before and after the waivers took effect with what happened in the rest of the country. We found no clear evidence that the number of supermarkets or superstores was declining in waiver states. Although it’s slightly lower than otherwise expected, this effect is not statistically significant. Because the restrictions vary, we also investigated whether the type mattered: sugary drinks only, or sugary drinks plus other products that state officials wanted to discourage. We found the largest declines in the number of SNAP-authorized convenience stores in states restricting both drinks and candy: an average of 2.2%. Why it matters Stores in waiver states may need to update their checkout systems and train employees to prevent purchases that are no longer allowed with SNAP benefits – potentially a time-consuming burden for some retailers. That may help explain why the number of SNAP-authorized convenience stores is declining. Although most people use SNAP benefits to buy food at big stores, they also purchase some groceries at convenience stores, especially in neighborhoods where there are few supermarkets. Other federal policies are also changing how SNAP works due to provisions in the big tax and policy legislation that Congress passed in July 2025. It changed some eligibility rules and how much states pay to administer the program. Even before all those changes take effect, many people who are likely eligible for SNAP benefits are having a harder time getting them, due to the steps states are taking to prepare for the new rules. The number of Americans enrolled in the program is falling fast despite no sign that their needs are shrinking. What still isn’t known We focused on changes to the number of stores authorized to accept SNAP in states with waivers. We didn’t study whether stores closed, or exactly why stores left the program. We also don’t know what role court rulings will play. On June 22, near the end of our study, a federal court invalidated SNAP food restrictions in five states: Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee and West Virginia. Waiver programs in other states – Indiana, Utah, Idaho, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Texas and Florida – were allowed to continue. Four states had similar restrictions in the works: South Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio and Virginia. Those plans are on hold. Beginning in November 2026, most U.S. stores will also have to meet new requirements of a different kind to participate in SNAP. They’ll need to stock a wider variety of staple foods, such as grains, dairy products and produce. These requirements could pose additional challenges for convenience stores. Further research is needed to see if the effects we found change over time, including in states that introduce these restrictions after the period we studied. a94cb7158a379b67: Amber Titus, 38, holds a take-home dose of methadone on Sept. 18 in Bisbee Junction, Ariz. Daniela Dawson, CC BY-NDThree times a week, Amber Titus wakes up at 5 a.m. to get ready for the 45-minute drive to the methadone clinic. Titus, 38, and her husband live with their two young children in Bisbee Junction, Arizona, a rural community near the U.S.-Mexico border. The couple started taking methadone, a medication that treats opioid addiction, in early 2025. “It’s been a godsend,” she said. But accessing methadone is not easy. The closest place they can receive treatment is a clinic in Sierra Vista, about 30 miles from their home. The clinic opens on weekdays at 4:30 a.m. but closes before midday. Titus has to get her methadone dose and arrive at work in Bisbee before her shift starts at 9 a.m. Arriving just 10 to 15 minutes late for an appointment can mean missing a dose because rules are so strict, she said, even when the clinic is still open. Like many people with opioid use disorder, Amber Titus struggles to access methadone treatment. Three times a week, she drives 45 minutes each way with her 1-year-old son in his car seat to get the medication. Here’s her story. That’s the routine when they have their own transportation. In August, their car was totaled in a crash. Until they got another one, Titus called Medicaid, her insurance provider, to schedule rides to the clinic. “They said they’d be at my house at 6 o'clock in the morning,” Titus told The Conversation. The driver was late every day. “I missed my methadone dose for the whole week,” she said. Nationwide, more than 120 people a day died from opioid overdoses in 2025, according to federal estimates. Methadone is one of the most effective medications for opioid use disorder, cutting the risk of fatal overdose by roughly half. Yet only 22% of people with the disorder ever receive it. For more than five decades, only specialized, government-approved clinics, known as opioid treatment programs, have dispensed methadone, not regular doctors or pharmacies. Many clinics require patients to show up in person every single day, with average one-way drive times approaching 50 minutes in rural communities. Today, private equity firms have acquired large shares of the market for methadone clinics, telling lawmakers their capital has expanded treatment and modernized care. I am a healthcare economist at Brown University who studies how private equity is reshaping American medicine. My recent research on private equity’s growing footprint in addiction treatment, co-authored with researchers from the University of Pittsburgh and RAND, found that despite acquiring over one-third of methadone clinics in the U.S., private equity investments have not expanded methadone availability or the construction of new facilities. This research has informed federal investigations into the role of private equity in expanding access to medications for addiction treatment. Currently, U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., has an investigation into three of the country’s largest methadone clinic operators, citing concerns that they oppose expanding treatment access for financial reasons rather than patient safety. Why methadone fits the private equity model Because methadone is so tightly regulated, opioid treatment programs are, in effect, a government-created monopoly. In most of the country, if you want methadone, there’s a short list of clinics licensed to give it to you and no other way to get it. Moreover, people with opioid use disorder generally must travel to opioid treatment programs every day, where staff must observe them taking methadone, with strict limits on how much methadone patients can take home and when they can do so. Take-home methadone varies based on the state, time in treatment and clinician discretion. Only 19% of people who received take-home methadone received three or more days’ supply. That kind of guaranteed, captive demand is exactly the sort of investment that can be profitable for private equity investors. Whoever controls the clinics in a region controls access to the medication and can set the terms for patients in most need of medication. Private equity firms have invested more than US$1 trillion in U.S. healthcare over the past two decades, touching everything from fertility clinics to hospice care. Many Americans have never heard the term private equity, but these firms now own more than 400 U.S. hospitals and oversee doctors in more than a quarter of the country’s emergency rooms. In opioid treatment specifically, firms have used a platform and add-on strategy: buying one large clinic, then steadily acquiring smaller nearby ones, similar to a company quietly buying up every gas station in a county until, years later, one owner controls them all. Individually, each deal looks too small to matter. Collectively, a single firm can end up controlling an entire region’s methadone supply. To be clear, private investment isn’t inherently harmful. Research shows that in markets where quality is easy to see, competition is robust and there’s no government subsidy – restaurants, for instance – private equity can have neutral or even positive effects. Healthcare has none of those features. Patients often can’t judge provider quality, they rarely pay for care directly, and government programs act as both payer and regulator. Market share grew, methadone supply didn’t My research has quantified what actually happened after private equity acquisitions of opioid treatment programs. Previous research I have done, which my ongoing work builds upon, examined acquisitions from 2011 to 2019 and found that within two years of a private equity firm moving into a county, it typically controlled 67% of the local methadone treatment market – and in more than a quarter of counties, a single firm controlled all of it. Despite acquiring that much market power, these acquisitions generally do not result in the construction of new methadone clinics or an increase in methadone treatment. Additionally, the data shows that methadone shipments, or what clinics have to dispense to patients, and opioid-related deaths were unchanged during the study period. In plain terms: Private equity firms haven’t been building new capacity – they’ve been buying up the capacity that already existed. As of October 2026, there are 1,572 methadone clinics registered with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Nationally, 35% of opioid treatment providers are affiliated with private equity firms, and in 19 states and the District of Columbia more than half have private equity owners. Montana has four clinics, all owned by Community Medical Services, more commonly known as CMS. The company was operating there before it was acquired by private equity. In North Dakota, CMS owns three of the state’s four methadone clinics. In Arizona, CMS owns the Sierra Vista clinic where Titus gets her methadone. Amber Titus, 38, leaves her appointment at Community Medical Services’ methadone clinic in Sierra Vista, Ariz., on Sept. 18. Daniela Dawson, CC BY-ND In 2018, a prospective investor advised shutting down CMS’ Montana and North Dakota clinics as unprofitable. Nick Stavros, CEO of CMS, opted to partner with a different private equity firm to keep the clinics open. Before private equity investment, CMS had 14 clinics in four states. It now has 79 clinics in 14 states, according to Stavros. The total includes five clinics in prisons and three mobile units. Unlike the typical private equity investment strategy of acquisitions, a majority of the company’s recent growth – 49 clinics – has come from new sites, he said. No expansion has taken place in Montana. Building a new clinic costs about $2.5 million, more than many rural areas can support, Stavros said. Proponents of private equity ownership argue it can help fill gaps left by inadequate public funding for addiction treatment. The strongest evidence in their favor: One study found clinics became significantly more likely to accept Medicare and Medicaid after acquisition, likely because large chains can afford administrative infrastructure that small, independent clinics cannot. That’s a real benefit worth acknowledging. But look past insurance acceptance and ask whether more people are actually getting – and staying on – treatment, and the picture darkens. For buprenorphine, a related medication that can be prescribed more broadly than methadone, one study found patient volume at private equity-acquired facilities rose about 22% after acquisition. Similar data for methadone was not available. But the same study found the share of patients who stayed continuously on buprenorphine for 180 days – the national quality benchmark – fell by nearly 8 percentage points. Early discontinuation is one of the strongest predictors of relapse and overdose. A proposal to expand methadone access These findings matter beyond academic journals, because they are at the heart of an active policy debate. Congress is weighing the Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act 2.0, which would let regular doctors prescribe methadone and let pharmacies dispense it, breaking the decades-old rule that methadone can be dispensed only at opioid treatment programs. The Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act was introduced in 2023. After facing opposition, it did not reach a House or Senate vote before the end of the congressional term. Lawmakers later reintroduced the bill with changes as Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act 2.0, which is currently in consideration by the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees. The committees have not yet scheduled the next step, a markup of the bill, and the current congressional term ends in January 2027. In an email, U.S. Rep. Donald Norcross, D-N.J., one of the bill’s sponsors, recalled a snowstorm years earlier when he noticed a single track of footprints crossing an otherwise empty street to a methadone clinic. “I realized that no matter what else is happening in the world,” Norcross said, “some of our neighbors’ lives literally revolve around getting to that building every single day.” Methadone for opioid use disorder is typically taken orally, most often as a liquid. Daniela Dawson, CC BY-ND The bill has widespread support from patient advocacy organizations and medical societies. At the same time, a STAT investigation found that the main opposition to the legislation comes from the American Association for the Treatment of Opioid Dependence, AATOD, a major trade group representing methadone clinics. This coalition argues that expanded prescribing and pharmacy dispensing of methadone would increase diversion and overdose risk. The evidence so far does not support that claim. Moreover, firms that control large shares of their local markets may have a financial incentive to keep new competitors, including doctors and pharmacies, out. Mark Parrino, AATOD’s president, told The Conversation the trade group opposes the bill for two reasons. First, the bill would let the Health and Human Services secretary determine which additional practitioners are qualified to prescribe methadone for opioid use disorder. Second, it would allow methadone to be dispensed in dispersible tablet as well as liquid form. Tablets “were definitely” involved in a rise in methadone-related deaths that began around 1999, Parrino said. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and a Food and Drug Administration advisory tied those deaths to methadone prescribed for pain, not addiction treatment. Stavros, who is AATOD’s Arizona representative, said he did not see the bill as a threat to CMS’ business model, but he cited concerns that removing all regulation too quickly could allow a few bad providers to drive up methadone overdoses and increase stigma against the drug. “We need to find ways to increase access,” he said. “If somebody would come up with … a slow, gradual transition that led to pharmacy prescribing,” Stavros said he would support it. Dr. Melody Glenn, associate professor of addiction and emergency medicine at the University of Arizona, previously worked at a methadone clinic in Tucson and supports MOTAA 2.0, though she said the legislation should go further. “It’s time to remove the regulatory barriers to these lifesaving medications,” Glenn told The Conversation in an email. The bill would allow doctors specializing in addiction medicine, like her, to prescribe methadone. Glenn said it’s frustrating that such an effective treatment for opioid use disorder exists, yet many people who could benefit never receive it. “They don’t have to die,” she said. Bringing private equity deals into view Two other policy responses are gaining traction. The first is ownership transparency. Regulators, researchers and patients cannot scrutinize what they cannot see, yet private equity is exempt from the disclosure rules that apply to publicly traded companies. Indiana, California and Maine have enacted or proposed reform to disclose private equity and management company ownership as a condition of being able to bill Medicare or Medicaid. Vermont passed similar legislation this year, on which I was invited to provide expert testimony. The second is lowering the reporting threshold for acquiring a healthcare company to make them more visible to agencies enforcing U.S. antitrust laws, which are intended to promote competition and prevent monopolies. The U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission consider ownership of 30% or more of a local market for a product or service a red flag for anticompetitive behavior. Yet, as my research shows, private equity chains typically control at least 67% of a local methadone market within two years of their first clinic purchase in a county. The reason most never trigger the federal reporting requirement is because these acquisitions happen through a series of smaller, piecemeal deals rather than one large merger. The reporting requirement applies only to deals worth more than about $134 million. Some states have introduced proposals to lower thresholds to around $10 million specifically for healthcare deals, so the vast majority become visible to enforcement agencies before they close. Structural barriers to getting treatment The U.S. is experiencing an ongoing and severe opioid crisis. In 2023, approximately 80% of the more than 100,000 drug overdose deaths involved an opioid. In 2024, federal data shows the number of people who died from drug overdoses declined to nearly 80,000, and more than 54,000 of those deaths involved opioids. We already have medications that work. The barriers preventing people from accessing them are not primarily clinical. They are structural – and, in this case, actively maintained by financial investors who profit from the status quo. Titus visits a resident during an outreach stop for Cochise Harm Reduction on Sept. 18. Daniela Dawson, CC BY-ND “Addiction isn’t a choice,” Titus told The Conversation. She and her husband work for Cochise Harm Reduction, a grassroots nonprofit organization based in rural southeast Arizona that works to make life better for people who use drugs. “It’s a learning curve and eventually … you get tired of it and you want help.” Aleka Kroitzsh, researcher, and Kristi Tanner, senior accountability editor, contributed reporting. 51fadb1c082d08d3: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 28 — Malaysia has opted for diplomacy in dealing with the refugee issue involving Myanmar, despite facing international criticism over the government’s approach to resolving the matter, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said.
He said the approach was necessary to seek a solution after years of criticism and condemnation directed at Myanmar had failed to bring about any significant change in the country’s policies.

“When I invited Myanmar President (Min Aung Hlaing), what was the objective? In my two previous meetings with him, I urged him to moderate his stance. We have been expressing anger and criticising them for 20 or 30 years, but it has had no effect. There has been no change in policy.

“The people in Rakhine, the Rohingya, continue to suffer. Some 200,000 have fled here, placing a burden on us as well. The people, including the Malay community, are becoming increasingly upset over the situation
Anwar was speaking at the ‘Majlis Ilmu Madani’ programme at Kompleks Seri Perdana here today, featuring prominent Indonesian preacher Ustaz Dr Abdul Somad Batubara as a guest.
He was explaining Malaysia’s position on refugees from Myanmar, including the Rohingya, and efforts to facilitate their return to their country of origin. — Bernama
7f9e54d5ff79b396: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models

When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup, he didn’t think its data was worth much. But he’s since turned the company’s digital archives into tens of thousands of dollars, selling its codebase and workspace data.

He’s part of a growing market in which companies that help shut down startups sell their data to AI labs. Demand has grown as training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets, with buyers seeking real-world records to help train AI agents. But the sales raise legal and ethical questions.
Read the full story on the AI labs buying up the remains of failed startups.
—Matthew King
Are we there yet? Interspecies communication
Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us.

Decoding how animals communicate with one another could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world. A growing arsenal of devices and advances in AI have made it easier to study their howls, squeaks, and clicks, but making sense of it all remains complex.
Find out how close we are to interspecies communication.
—Cassandra Willyard

MIT Technology Review Narrated: what it would take to build a city on the moon
The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.

A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.
That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.

Anwar, who is also Finance Minister, said technological advancement was essential to ensuring the country kept pace with global developments, but must be anchored in religious faith, moral values, culture and literature.
“If we fail to master technology, others will overwhelm us. That is the principle. In the past, we fell behind because others mastered technology while we did not.

The Majlis Ilmu Madani programme, held at the Prime Minister’s official residence, is part of efforts to foster a society that values knowledge and appreciates the importance of proper conduct and good character.

9f576285187c230f: Cisco has open sourced a behavior detection engine that watches AI agents, to help security teams prevent rogue agents from going off the rails like they did with the Hugging Face hack – or worse.

It’s called Project Quarry, and it aims to provide a “shared language” for evaluating agent behavior, along the lines of what Snort, which Cisco also maintains, did for detecting malicious network traffic and what YARA did for rule-based malware identification.
Most detection tools rely on specific interactions with an AI model or agent. Did it attempt prompt injection? Or did the agent call an attack tool?
“But what is missing is the entire context under which something may occur,” Amy Chang, head of AI threat and security research at Cisco, said in an exclusive interview with The Register.

She likened this to credit card fraud detection. Without context, individual transactions such as a small test charge or a single purchase in a location far away from a card-holder's usual location may not raise any flags.
“And then you try again,” making another fraudulent purchase, “and that went through, too. So now I’m gonna buy the PS5,” Chang said.

“Those are the things that Quarry addresses by taking into consideration the entire agent session,” she explained. “One tool call may seem in-scope until you realize that that next step is taking that information and sending it to an attacker-controlled inbox or server.”

Even data theft is a sequence and not a single agentic action. Agentic AI security firm Invariant Labs demonstrated this with a proof-of-concept attack against GitHub's MCP server that hijacked a user's agent via a malicious GitHub Issue, and coerced it into leaking data from private repositories.

Simply reading a configuration file, or sending a request to an external endpoint may be legitimate agentic actions. However, combining the two can lead to data exfiltration – and shows “why action relationships matter,” wrote Chang and fellow Cisco researchers Adam Swanda, Ravikumar Balakrishnan, and Konstantin Berlin in a blog post about Quarry shared with The Register ahead of publication

“A policy can produce a finding when the trace shows a sensitive file read followed within a defined window by an external send,” they wrote. “The risk comes from the relationship between the two actions, so the finding should preserve evidence from both."
Quarry covers single- and multi-turn large language model conversations, agents, tool use, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, and multimodal inputs.

In addition to the open source code itself, the project’s GitHub repository includes installation instructions, supported Python versions, plugins for Claude Code, Codex and other MCP-compatible agents, configuration examples, rule-writing guidance, and a rule starter pack.
For instance, with the rule pack, “If a base-64 encoded malware is somewhere in the tool call, that would result in a block,” Chang said.

The rule format looks similar to a YARA or Snort rule, with a header that details the traffic to examine, content to match, and metadata for tracking the rule. Here’s a Quarry rule that flags an agent that reads a credentials file:

While the Cisco Ai researchers have not run Quarry against data describing the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, they suggest that if the intrusion had been read as a complete, step-by-step record of a single session, there were several points where the AI agents’ steps would have given a Quarry rule something to act on and flag for humans.
For example, Quarry would probably have flagged internet access from a sandbox.
“The rule can flag specific tool calls that reach an external server asset that wasn’t in the task’s allow list,” Chang said.
“Another one would be credentials found and used somewhere else.”

According to OpenAI’s technical report about the Hugging Face intrusion, this is exactly what happened on July 10, when an agent validated 14 exposed Hugging Face tokens with write access and shared them.

“The rule would flag that there was a credential in the tool result that then called an outside service, which is likely not within the parameters of what you would want to do in this case,” Chang said. “We don't want you to go and search for credentials that may have been leaked or inadvertently exposed and then utilize them to conduct a task.”

The Cisco team is quick to say that rules along are not a substitute for chain-of-thought monitors, or other forms of human oversight – but they do help record a pattern that other teams can then “review, test, and apply to their own agents,” they wrote.
Herein also lies the benefit of open source, and a collective approach to defending against adversarial use of AI, Chang said.
“Do we have all the answers? No,” Chang said. “We all see slices of the problem, and it’s important for us to share what we see.”®

a7f329bb1936cd9a: UK domain registrar 123 Reg (no relation – Ed) says it was the victim of an “AI-driven cyberattack” that exposed customer data.

Customers began receiving their notification emails this week, informing them that their contact information, "related customer relationship data," company VAT numbers, and "product information from an application programming interface (API)" were compromised.

A company spokesperson elaborated, saying this means that names, phone numbers, countries, language and currency preferences, account creation dates, the products on the account, and marketing preferences were affected.
123 Reg described the September 18 intrusion as "the first known AI-driven cyberattack against our company," and told The Register that early signs point toward a China-nexus attacker.

"Our investigation identified IP addresses that we assessed to be the core attacker infrastructure, which were hosted in China and Singapore, indicating a strong Chinese nexus," the spokesperson said.

"Our investigation further identified AI cyberattack 'skills' hosted on Chinese infrastructure, including copies of skills open sourced by Anthropic and several other AI exploitation frameworks and scripts."

They went on to say that many of the artefacts left behind led 123 Reg to suspect that a Chinese state-sponsored group, known for abusing Claude Code in attacks against at least 30 organizations, could be behind the break-in.
There is also a suspicion that the same group that hit a number of South Korea’s financial institutions using open-source Chinese AI tool ARTEX, was behind the attack on 123 Reg too.

"The TA's mirror of 'anthropic_skills,' and the account naming conventions found on the Chinese servers are consistent with preparation of this class of AI-augmented operation," the spokesperson told us.

"In addition, on October 7, 2026, CrowdStrike published CSA-261162, describing an unknown, likely Chinese-speaking actor that targeted several South Korean financial organizations starting in late September 2026, which is the same period during which we were attacked.
"That actor used ARTEX, an open-source Chinese-developed agentic penetration-testing tool released in July 2026, which was also observed to be used in the attack that targeted us."

The GoDaddy-owned registrar reported the attack to law enforcement agencies, brought in outside cybersecurity support, and notified the FTC, as well as the data protection authorities in the UK and EU.

The company spokesperson added that it worked with Singapore-based ISPs to shut down the attacker's servers in the region, which helped disrupt the attack, in addition to "other actions by us and industry partners."

123 Reg's email to customers stated the attacker's activity "was limited to reading" customer data, although the spokesperson told us "it's possible they created copies of the information," and that this is what prompted the notification.
The registrar urged customers to stay alert to the potential misuse of their data, and to treat communications appearing to come from the company with caution.

"If you receive a message or call and aren't sure it's from 123 Reg, go directly to our website and log in," the email said. "We will never contact you to request your password, payment details, or verification codes by email, text, or phone.

"We also strongly recommend turning on two-step verification (2SV), which helps keep your account protected even if someone tricks you into sharing your password. You can find instructions for setting up 2SV in your 123 Reg account.
"We apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused." ®
417246b2ff463a16: BANGKOK, Oct 28 — Thai authorities have vowed to seize more than US$1 billion (RM4.08 billion) in assets from a group accused of laundering proceeds from South-east Asia-based scam syndicates.
A criminal court issued arrest warrants yesterday for the alleged ring leader, South African Ben Smith, his Thai wife Cattaliya Beevor, Cambodian businessman Yim Leak and four others, police said.
Senior police investigator Ratthachin Jermsap told AFP that Smith and Yim Leak were believed to have left Thailand.

Media reports have previously linked Smith, also known as Benjamin Mauerberger, to transnational scam operations in Cambodia, part of a multibillion-dollar illicit industry that has ballooned in the region.
Yim Leak belongs to an elite political family and is the brother of a senior Cambodian police official.

Thai anti-money laundering officials and securities regulators told reporters Tuesday that illicit proceeds from criminal enterprises were moved by the group through overseas financial firms before being traded for stocks on the Thai stock exchange.

The Anti-Money Laundering Office (AMLO) will seize assets, including shares worth more than 14 billion baht, and real estate, cash and vehicles valued at 21 billion baht, totalling more than US$1 billion, police said in a statement.
The seizures included shares in major Thai firms, including Bangchak, one of the country’s biggest oil refiners, according to AMLO deputy head Kamonsit Wongbutnoi.
Bangchak said in a statement that the asset seizures concerned individual investors and business operations were unaffected.
Confiscated assets would go towards compensating victims of online scams, Kamonsit told reporters.
The group of seven were charged with conspiracy to launder money and acting as a criminal organisation, police said.
A representative for Yim Leak did not respond to questions about the charges on Wednesday but referred AFP to an October 8 statement issued by his lawyers.
It accused Thai officials of conducting a trial by media against Yim Leak before he was charged. It said Thailand froze more than US$600 million in assets, including his family’s, without a hearing.
A lawyer for Smith, Witoon Kengngan, declined to comment.
In February, Thai authorities ordered the seizure of assets worth more than US$410 million from Smith and other individuals accused of fraud.

Thai opposition lawmaker Rangsiman Rome, who is being sued by Smith for defamation over comments he made about scams, told AFP on Wednesday the fresh seizures and arrest warrants were “a positive development... even if it’s taken a while”. — AFP
ae807c1ff0265133: MUMBAI: Shares in India's Jio Platforms surged nearly 27% on its market debut Wednesday, after raising more than US$3 billion in the country's biggest initial public offering.

The company, home to India's biggest wireless operator and which is the digital services arm of billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries, ended the first day of trading at 1,417.5 rupees on the National Stock Exchange -- well up from its 1,119-rupee issue price.
Wednesday's rally gave Jio a valuation of about US$137 billion, turning it into India's second-most valuable listed firm after its parent.
Launched a decade ago, Jio's wireless service disrupted the market with steep discounts that helped it rapidly win customers from rival telecom firms Bharti Airtel and Vodafone.

With more than 530 million subscribers, the firm currently makes most of its money from telecoms, but has expanded in recent years into newer areas including digital services and artificial intelligence.
The listing, one of the most anticipated this year, attracted robust demand last week with the IPO being 22 times oversubscribed.

"In our first 10 years, we democratised data... In our next 10, we want to democratise every technology that can transform Indian lives," Akash Ambani, managing director of Jio Platforms and Mukesh's eldest son, said at the listing ceremony in financial capital Mumbai.
"AI, cloud, connected devices, connectivity even from space and digital services not yet imagined."
The ceremony, which was attended by several members of the Ambani family, saw the billionaire patriarch fight back tears during the speeches delivered by his children.
Analysts at Nomura, who initiated coverage on the stock on Wednesday, said the company's focus for Jio had shifted "from adding users to earning more from each customer".
"We believe the heavy 5G investment cycle is largely behind for Jio... freeing up significant cash flow," they said.
Experts say Jio is key to Reliance's strategy to evolve beyond its traditional oil business and the touchstone of its future tech ambitions.

Local media have reported that it is considering a low-orbit satellite constellation to provide internet services from space -- a venture that would see it compete with Elon Musk's Starlink, which has been trying for years to launch in India.

The world's richest man accused unnamed Indian "oligarchs" this month of preventing Starlink's rollout in the country, and referred to the Reliance chairman as "Prime Minister Ambani" and the "real boss of India".
Reliance responded by noting that it had never "feared competition" and welcomed offerings from rivals in satellite communications, including Starlink.
While Jio has expanded beyond its telecom roots, experts have cautioned investors that it will take time for its efforts to bear fruit.
Monetisation of newer digital services are "still to be demonstrated at scale", analysts at financial services firm Motilal Oswal noted earlier this month.
b15ba52ca83510b1: LOS ANGELES: Apple is expected to unveil its first touchscreen MacBooks on Wednesday, abandoning a long-held aversion to the technology as it caps a burst of product launches ahead of the crucial holiday shopping season.
Apple is holding an event in Los Angeles after launching a folding iPhone, Duo, at its Silicon Valley headquarters in September and a smart home hub in New York earlier this month.

While those products will test new markets for Apple, the Los Angeles event could rekindle an old question: should Apple put the touchscreens that it made mainstream in iPhones and iPads in its oldest product line?

Apple executives long resisted the idea, with Steve Jobs saying in 2010 that touchscreens on laptops were "ergonomically terrible" and then-CEO Tim Cook saying in 2012 that such devices would be as pleasing to users as converging a toaster and a refrigerator.
Before becoming Apple's current CEO, John Ternus argued that Apple already made a touchscreen computer with its iPad lineup.

However, touchscreens have been widely available for more than a decade on Windows devices, and with the iPhone nearing its two-decade anniversary, a new generation of buyers expects screens to respond to touch.

"I believe they were always wrong on pushing back on touch, and this is the long arm of reality setting in," said Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. "Some things are purely inevitable," Sag said.

A key question for Apple is how customers will respond. The company has seen an uptick in Mac sales, but much of that growth has been among technology enthusiasts and businesses buying the machines to handle AI tasks on-device.

While Apple this week announced an upgraded base model of its MacBook Pro with a new M6 chip, Bloomberg News has reported that it plans to ship touchscreen models with its existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips that already come in MacBook Pro models, meaning the new machines would not gain a significant performance boost over existing ones.
"The only thing people want is more memory and better processors for local models!" prominent tech commentator Jason Calacanis, the host of the All-In Podcast, wrote on X.

085f662b6c506ab0: The question of who controls satellite-based connectivity came into sharp focus in recent weeks after Ukraine's service was throttled and then restored.

Wherever Reg readers stand on those activities involving SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield, reliance on a foreign power that may not stay friendly is now under intense scrutiny. Alternatives exist, including Eutelsat OneWeb's constellation, and more are in the works. The Register toured the Harwell facility of another contender – Open Cosmos.

The business is just over a decade old and operates from multiple locations, including the UK, Greece, and Portugal. It has launched dozens of missions over the years, including its OpenConstellation service, which organizations use to share data from Earth observation satellites.

When it launched OpenConstellation in 2022, the aim was to have 25 satellites offering a mix of spatial and spectral resolution. While other services, such as the European Commission's Copernicus, provide similar data, OpenConstellation lets customers assign satellites specific tasks for specific data collection.

However, it is ConnectedCosmos that will interest users concerned about putting all their connectivity eggs in a basket that might be abruptly snatched away. The first two satellites in the constellation are now in orbit; they were launched by Rocket Lab in January 2026. The business plans to operate more than 96 satellites by the end of 2028 and to achieve full coverage by 2030. The core connectivity backbone will consist of 192 satellites, which founder and CEO Rafel Jordà Siquier described as "the foundation, not the ceiling."

The company reckons it can churn out one satellite per day, and judging by what we saw in Harwell, that figure seems realistic, though it's a far cry from the approximately 70 Starlinks per week SpaceX claimed in its IPO filing.
Because ConnectedCosmos operates from an altitude above 1,000 km, it needs far fewer satellites, though at the cost of latency increases.

Jordi Barrera Ars, co-founder and CTO, told us that latency was "anything between 30 and 80 milliseconds." This is OK for most applications, but not great for some. Direct to smartphone is, for example, not currently on the cards. Open Cosmos's VP of Commercial Satcom, Danielle Edwards, said, "We're very much in the direct device business. Direct to smartphone is not an area that we have an interest in right now."
"Never say never…" she added, "and who knows what might come along next Tuesday. But for right now, the direct device play really is on the IoT side."

During the tour, Open Cosmos showed off its assembly and testing facilities (including temperature and pressure testing), as well as a shaker table that simulates launch conditions. The satellites themselves consist of a common bus, onto which solar panels and the payload are fitted. Then they are stored, ready for launch, in what one company representative called "the satellite nursery".

The approach is interesting: OpenConstellation satellites use the ConnectedCosmos constellation as a connectivity backbone, while the latter also provides point-to-point broadband. According to Open Cosmos:
"The constellation is deliberately designed around the requirements of government, institutional and commercial customers that need secure, resilient connectivity and clear custody of critical data."
It is very much a European alternative to customers who are worried about existing services.

The service on offer from Open Cosmos will not, for example, be suitable for guiding drones traveling at high velocities, that isn't really the point, but it will provide sovereign communication channels that aren't beholden to the whim of a man and a big, red Off switch. Where the Starlink constellation stands at well over 10,000 satellites, the numbers proposed by Open Cosmos are far more modest and less likely to alarm astronomers in quite the same way.

Plus, the company has sector experience through its OpenConstellation platform (as well as custom spacecraft built for individual customers). And, unlike so many in the industry, its satellites and facilities exist beyond PowerPoint presentations. After all, we've seen them. ®
1150023a1ba2270d: URDA (Spain), Oct 28 — A collision between two high-speed trains south of Madrid killed 30 people today and the toll could rise, regional authorities said in Spain’s second such disaster this year.

Images shared by local media showed the wreckage of two trains strewn on the tracks and an embankment as emergency services rushed to the scene, while shocked travellers dragged away their suitcases as they escaped.

The accident in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha comes one month before Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faced heavy criticism for the first disaster, seeks to overturn unfavourable polls in an early general election.
Sources from authorities in Castilla-La Mancha told AFP “at least 30” people had died, raising a previous toll of 10. Authorities have not yet given a toll for any wounded.
Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the government of Castilla-La Mancha, had told local media CMM that “it is possible that the number will increase”.

State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.
A spokesperson for the Spanish emergency services told AFP the trains collided just before 9am (0800 GMT/4pm Malaysian time) in the municipality of Urda, around 130 kilometres south of Madrid.
“All resources are currently being deployed,” the emergency services spokesperson said, including “several fire crews, three helicopters, and two mobile intensive care units”.

Ths still image from video taken and released by Spain’s Civil Guard on October 28, 2026 shows an aerial scene of a train crash between a high speed Renfe AVE train and Iryo train around 150km south of Madrid between Urda and Los Yebenes in the province of Toledo. — Spain’s Civil Guard handout/AFP pic
‘Shocked’

Sanchez, who is seeking to extend his eight-year premiership in the November 29 vote, said on X that he was “shocked” by the accident and sent “my love, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families”.
He cancelled his participation in a summit on obesity in Madrid after the news broke, while his Socialist party suspended all its campaign activities.

Condolences flooded in from across Spain and Europe. The Spanish royal household said on X it was “shocked and concerned” by the accident, conveying its support to the victims, their loved ones and the emergency services.
European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said “Europe mourns” with the victims after the “devastating news”, while French President Emmanuel Macron expressed his country’s “solidarity”.
Spain’s high-speed rail network has received huge investment in recent years, growing to become the world’s second-largest after China and a source of national pride.

But today’s accident comes after another collision between two high-speed trains outside the southern village of Adamuz in January left 46 dead, which raised major questions about safety on the country’s railways.
That crash was Spain’s deadliest train accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela.
Both of this year’s accidents happened on the line linking Madrid to the southern city of Seville.
One of the country’s busiest routes, it was Spain’s first high-speed line when it opened in 1992 to coincide with the Seville universal exposition. — AFP
41f88c5264b6a084: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 28 — More shiny new Apple products are still being rolled out after introducing the new iPad mini with an OLED display yesterday.

iMac 2026 M6 Malaysia pricing and availability
The new iMac M6 is available in two chip configurations, both starting with 16GB of unified memory and 256GB SSD storage.
Here are the official starting prices in Malaysia:
iMac M6 (10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, 16GB RAM, 256GB SSD) – RM6,499
iMac M6 (12-core CPU, 12-core GPU, 16GB RAM, 256GB SSD) – RM7,499
For students or educators, Apple’s Education Pricing for the new iMac starts from RM6,299.
Pre-orders for the new iMac M6 begin in Malaysia on October 29, 2026 at 1:10am MYT, while general availability starts on November 6, 2026.

For users who require more memory or storage, Apple offers several build-to-order upgrades.

For unified memory, upgrading from 16GB to 24GB costs an additional RM900. Meanwhile, upgrading to 32GB costs RM1,800, although this option is only available for the higher-spec M6 model with a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU.

For SSD storage, upgrading from the base 256GB to 512GB costs an additional RM900, while 1TB costs RM2,250. If you need 2TB of storage, it costs an additional RM4,500, but this option is exclusive to the higher-spec M6 configuration.
There’s also an option to add a 2.5Gb Ethernet port for an additional RM100, while adding a nano-textured glass costs an extra RM900.

Both iMac configurations come bundled with a colour-matched Magic Mouse and Magic Keyboard. However, the higher-spec 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU version gets a Magic Keyboard with Touch ID as standard.
With the iMac 2026 options maxed out with higher-spec M6 chip (12-core CPU, 12-core GPU), 32GB RAM, 2TB storage and nano-textured glass, you’re looking at a total cost of RM14,699.
This is inclusive of the default Magic Keyboard and Magic Mouse in matching colour.
What’s new with iMac 2026?
The single biggest upgrade for the 2026 iMac is the new Apple M6 chip, replacing the M4 found in the previous generation.

The base model now features a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, compared to the previous entry-level M4 model’s 8-core CPU and 8-core GPU. Meanwhile, the higher-spec configuration gets a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, up from 10 cores each on the previous generation.

Built on Apple’s 2nm process technology, the M6 offers an updated CPU and GPU architecture with Neural Accelerators to accelerate AI workloads. It also comes with a Dual 16-core Neural Engine and memory bandwidth of up to 170GB/s.

According to Apple, the new iMac delivers up to 1.5 times faster productivity performance and up to twice the graphics performance compared to the M4 model. For AI workloads, Apple claims up to five times faster on-device AI performance.
Besides the new chip, the iMac M6 also gets faster SSD storage, with Apple claiming up to twice the read and write performance compared to the previous generation.
Connectivity has been upgraded to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 thanks to the new Apple N1 chip.

In terms of ports, the new iMac offers up to four Thunderbolt 4 ports, although this is only available on the higher-spec 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU version. It also supports up to two external 6K displays.

The display itself remains unchanged. You still get a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display with 500 nits of brightness, P3 wide colour support and over one billion colours. Apple also offers an optional nano-texture glass finish on the higher-spec model to reduce glare and reflections.

For video calls, the iMac retains its 12MP Center Stage camera, which automatically keeps users in frame. There’s also Desk View, which allows users to show a top-down view of their desk during video calls.

The built-in audio setup remains unchanged with a six-speaker sound system comprising two pairs of force-cancelling woofers and two tweeters. It supports Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, while a studio-quality three-microphone array handles voice calls and recordings.
The new iMac 2026 also retains its colourful design, available in seven colours: blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver.
Out of the box, the new iMac runs on macOS 27 Golden Gate, which introduces further refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass interface and other system features. — SoyaCincau

d936dbc60e23e767: MADRID, Oct 28 — Real Madrid apologised to China today for Kylian Mbappe’s comments poking fun at Mao Zedong, after the star striker’s remarks sparked a social media storm and saw Spanish football yanked off state TV.
Mocking former leader Mao — blamed by historians for millions of deaths — is taboo in China, and Mbappe’s remarks saw him become the latest foreign sports figure to anger Beijing.

In a clip of a video interview with French show The Bridge” — since taken down — Mbappe talked about being amused by an internet meme of his face photoshopped onto “some guy, think he’s a Chinese dictator”, an apparent reference to Mao.
Real Madrid “wishes to express its apologies to the Chinese people for any offence caused by the recent remarks of our player Kylian Mbappe”, the club said in a statement.

“The club joins in the public apology issued by Kylian Mbappe, in which the player himself expressed his regret for his words and reiterated his respect for the Chinese people,” the 15-time European champions said.

The statement came a day after Mbappe issued his own apology, in French, Chinese and English, saying: “My comment was ill-judged and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world.”
Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing today: “We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made.”
La Liga, which saw the broadcast of its matches suspended in China, said yesterday it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappe’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans”.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Chinese state television has suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches following remarks by Real Madrid star Kylian Mbappe about Mao Zedong, state-owned China Media Group announced on October 27, 2026. — AFP pic

Earlier, the state-run Global Times said in an editorial that it was “not difficult to see that the club’s longstanding tolerance of such behaviour has contributed to Mbappe’s latest offensive remarks”.

Chinese beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year’s World Cup ran adverts with AI-generated images of Mbappe, said yesterday it had scrapped its partnership with the player, as did dairy firms Mengniu and Milkground.
CMG, which oversees public broadcaster CCTV, said it had decided to suspend broadcasts of La Liga, the world’s second-richest football league after England’s Premier League.
Mbappe, 27, continued to face a torrent of criticism from Chinese web users today, some of it racist.
“His remarks were hurtful toward China and the Chinese people, so they cannot be translated,” wrote one user on social media platform Weibo.
Mbappe’s original joke about Mao was not reposted — or had been scrubbed — from China’s tightly controlled social media.
Chinese social media app Xiaohongshu had meanwhile frozen Mbappe’s account, where he has over a million followers.
The same was done on the Weibo app, with a notice stating that “the user has been banned from following due to violating laws or the Weibo Community Convention”.
Some Chinese media reports said global brands like Dior and Hublot had removed their Mbappe-related content on Weibo.
An AFP search on Dior and Hublot’s Weibo page with Mbappe’s Chinese name produced no results.
‘Respect history’
Offline too the Mbappe brand appeared to be under threat.
When AFP visited the Adidas flagship store in Beijing’s Sanlitun shopping district, Real Madrid shirts were available for sale, but none bearing the striker’s name.
Chinese state media have previously praised Mbappe as a “footballing sensation” and “talent”.
His face is plastered on billboards, on soft drinks and across social media.
Mbappe is sometimes affectionately referred to as “Guigui”, meaning “turtle” in Chinese, for his resemblance to a character from the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles movie.
Other major overseas sports leagues have previously angered China.
China suspended sponsorship deals with the NBA while the state broadcaster pulled NBA games off Chinese television for a year in October 2019.
This followed Houston Rockets executive Daryl Morey tweeting “Fight for freedom, stand with Hong Kong”, referring to protests Beijing called separatist and seditious.

“Respecting the history, culture, social customs and national sentiments of others is a fundamental principle for cross-border interaction, a standard of conduct widely upheld by the international community,” the official People’s Daily newspaper said in an opinion piece. — AFP

c3dd7b56c8c9e3cf: After suffering more than 10,000 corporate meetings, one executive has decided that the world hasn't endured nearly enough management jargon and built an app capable of generating 270 million variations of it.

Dave Doty, who claims to have spent 35 years collecting buzzwords, clichés, and other verbal atrocities inflicted on office workers, turned his life's work into Executive Eightball, an iPhone and Android app designed to help users sound convincingly corporate while saying nothing.
The idea came about after Doty spent decades recording the nonsense he heard in meetings, presumably while everyone else was busy circling back, touching base, and taking things offline.

"I am an executive who has suffered through over 10,000 meetings during the course of my 30-year career," Doty told The Register. "To keep my sanity, in each of them, I wrote down all of the buzz words and business clichés and have built an enormous database of them."
He described his creation as "sort of what would happen if Dilbert and George Costanza had a love child."

The app, which is now available on Apple's App Store and Google Play, takes Doty's collection of corporate waffle and assembles it into sentences that wouldn't look out of place in a CEO's quarterly update or a particularly painful all-hands meeting.

Among the pearls of wisdom it can produce are "We must dashboard the outputs to enable us to focus on operational directives and break the paradigm" and "Drive to cross-functional synergies so we can reengineer the organization and unleash shareholder value."

Doty claims Executive Eightball can produce approximately 270 million unique sentences in 15 languages, meaning workers across the globe can now contribute to meetings without the tiresome business of having an actual idea.

The app's listing promises to help users "Speak fluent corporate nonsense instantly," with suggested applications including office humor, LinkedIn jokes, presentation icebreakers, and, perhaps most appropriately, "Fake CEO energy."
There's a free version, although you'll have to put up with ads and a limited supply of corporate waffle. For $0.99, you can unlock the lot and talk complete rubbish to your heart's content.

The timing is rather fitting. In March, research covered by The Register suggested that people who enthusiastically embrace corporate buzzwords may actually be worse at their jobs. Now there's an app to help the rest of us catch up.
Doty, meanwhile, appears delighted with his contribution to the corporate world.

"This is truly a paradigm shift for corporate leadership and my greatest lifetime contribution to society," he wrote in his latest email, urging potential customers to subscribe to the paid version to "unleash the value."
After 35 years and 10,000 meetings, at least someone has finally found a productive use for all that wasted time. ®

78745816ceefa119: KUALA LUMPUR: Late buying in selected heavyweight stocks, particularly utility counters, lifted Bursa Malaysia to close marginally higher on Wednesday, in line with regional markets.
At 5pm, the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) rose 2.02 points, or 0.13%, to 1,613.87 from Tuesday’s close of 1,611.85.

Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said regional markets were mostly firmer, tracking overnight gains on Wall Street, with strong semiconductor earnings reinforcing optimism over artificial intelligence demand.
He said investors remained focused on the US Federal Reserve's interest rate decision and upcoming earnings from major technology companies.
“On the domestic front, we maintain our cautiously optimistic view, supported by resilient economic fundamentals and relatively attractive valuations.

“We believe recent corrections offer opportunities for selective accumulation of fundamentally sound blue chip stocks, although subdued liquidity and external uncertainties may limit the recovery. For the remainder of the week, we expect the FBM KLCI to trade within the 1,600-1,630 range, with a mild upward bias,” he told Bernama.
The benchmark index opened 2.64 points higher at 1,614.49 and moved between 1,609.44 and 1,615.87 during the trading session.
The broader market was positive, with gainers outpacing losers 658 to 418, while 524 counters were unchanged, 1,267 untraded, and 104 suspended.
Turnover decreased to 3.16 billion units worth RM2.28 billion from Tuesday’s 3.37 billion units worth RM3.10 billion.

Among the heavyweight stocks, YTL Power International gained 17 sen to RM5.27, while YTL Corporation added 10 sen to RM2.15. Maybank and CIMB were flat at RM9.99 and RM7.11, respectively, while Public Bank slid four sen to RM4.71.

In active trade, Zetrix AI and MAG were flat at 8.5 sen and 15.5 sen, respectively, V.S Industry rose one sen to 35.5 sen, Top Glove added half a sen to 97 sen, while GIIB Holdings eased 2.5 to 71 sen.

Nestle led the top gainers, adding RM3.70 to RM97.98, Malaysian Pacific Industries improved 84 sen to RM42.14, ViTrox rose 24 sen to RM11.06, while Sarawak Oil Palms and Fraser & Neave added 22 sen each to RM5.50 and RM19.90, respectively.

Among the top losers, United Plantations dipped 38 sen to RM29.32, Hong Leong Industries slid 28 sen to RM16.22, Ayer Holdings shed 25 sen to RM7.75, Westports slipped 20 sen to RM6.88, and Dufu Technology erased 16 sen to RM3.01.

On the index board, the FBM Emas Index increased 27.98 points to 12,067.27, the FBM Top 100 Index rose 24.75 points to 11,859.28, the FBM Mid 70 Index garnered 77.90 points to 17,448.02, the FBM Emas Shariah Index gained 31.41 points to 12,081.14, and the FBM ACE Index jumped 63.29 points to 5,481.92.

Sector-wise, the industrial products and services index edged up 2.12 points to 179.03, the energy index climbed 0.63 of a point to 846.37, while the financial services index slipped 21.79 points to 18,579.24, and the plantation index lost 7.43 points to 8,646.83.
The Main Market volume declined to 1.69 billion units worth RM1.99 billion from 1.99 billion units worth RM2.81 billion on Tuesday.
However, warrants turnover expanded to 1.07 billion units worth RM137.84 million against 952.13 million units worth RM113.35 million previously.
The ACE Market volume fell to 405.80 million units valued at RM160.63 million from 433.23 million units valued at RM181.44 million yesterday.

Meanwhile, consumer products and services counters accounted for 245.58 million shares traded on the Main Market, industrial products and services (295.29 million), construction (127.13 million), technology (559.68 million), financial services (46.27 million), property (86.05 million), plantation (23.03 million), real estate investment trusts (10.89 million), closed-end fund (20,000), energy (87.02 million), healthcare (92.82 million), telecommunications and media (27.31 million), transportation and logistics (50.72 million), utilities (33.79 million), and business trusts (521,900).
4edc65ce2580159a: Newly formed Quake AI is a cloud provider that expects its users will be mostly agents rather than humans.

It was created after US-based Rumble Inc acquired German datacenter operator Northern Data in June. The parent then rebranded as RUM Group, a holding company for Quake AI (formerly Northern Data) and the Rumble video platform.
Quake AI is an Nvidia Cloud Partner (NCP) operating a 22,000 GPUs estate, making it a neocloud: a specialized infrastructure provider dedicated to AI workloads.

Yet where other neoclouds are building a full stack of services around their GPU farms, Quake AI wants to make its infrastructure discoverable to AI agents, which may soon be traversing the internet in hordes on behalf of their owners.
RUM Group's chief financial officer Mike Massey told The Register that "Cloud 1.0 - let's call it applications - is like a user interface of how you interact with a machine of some kind."

He added: "Now, if you think about agents, they don't use vision. That's not how they interact with systems. They interact with APIs and with information effectively, and that means they want highly discoverable, highly data-driven platforms..

“So, to us, the things that make GPUs and AI compute easier to consume for humans, things like model-as-a-service, dashboards and one-click settings, are actually orthogonal to, if not detrimental to what agents are going to want, agents are going to want homogeneous compute… to understand and know what your data and your expectations are in terms of performance and uptimes, and then they're going to want to consume that compute as a utility,” he claimed.
In other words, Quake AI believes that, at some point, the customers for its compute services are going to be AI agents rather than people, but carrying out tasks on their behalf.
“I think that is the case, and it's the vision that we are driving towards, and you know ultimately agents are in service of people, right?” Massey said.

In its view of things, agents won't go through an intermediary, they'll go to the compute to retrieve the answers they need. "So all of these tool frameworks and all of these things that we have set up, I think, are a hindrance or an encumbrance to what the agents are going to want to consume, which is a utility," he explained.

"Yes, we're a little crazy in this regard," Massey added. "It's different. But I think our worldview is very grounded in the data and the realities. Like, we're a technical team. We understand the engineering, and at the end of the day, I think that most would validate our hypothesis," he continued.
John Hoffman, CEO of Northern Data and acting CEO of Quake AI, compared this with a solution he had been shown of an AI that was developed to navigate the internet by itself.

"I told it I wanted pizza. It went on to DoorDash's website. Typed pizza in the search box, clicked on the pizza with the highest ranking, went to add to order, knows I like pepperoni, and it clicked through all of this," he said.

"Don't get me wrong, this was a good solution that solves the problem. But the amount of compute that you are using to try to get an AI agent to act like a human that has eyes that can see web links is insanity compared to if DoorDash just created an API that is queryable," Hoffman claimed.

Done that way, the compute usage would be one thousandth of the way that the problem was actually accomplished, Quake AI claims, but it will require that everybody embraces the idea of how agents interact.
"And they don't interact with interfaces or applications. They interact with data and APIs. Just give me the raw data. That's what it wants," Hoffman told us.
"I would imagine DoorDash is developing an API for agents," he added. "It just makes sense, and that’s why we're doing the same exact thing."

Earlier this year, TollBit, an outfit that tracks AI bot traffic, said that agents were gradually taking over the internet. Its State of the Bots report found that by the end of 2025, there was roughly one AI bot visit for every 31 human visits to a site, up from just one for every 200 human visits at the start of the year.

Last year, consultants McKinsey & Company produced a report saying that the neocloud operators had to evolve beyond being just a provider of GPUs-as-a-service and move up the AI stack to sell services on top of bare metal, or risk being commoditized into competing on price.

Analyst firm Gartner was also reading the last rites for much of the neocloud industry recently, forecasting that AI services are unlikely to deliver enough revenue to cover the expected capital expenditure on IT infrastructure between now and 2030, and that consolidation in the provider market was inevitable.

Quake AI's gamble is that AI agents will be a reality, and that by tailoring its APIs to make it easier for these autonomous software bots to access its resources as needed, it will be one of the winners. ®
f7a43038467458ae: THE HAGUE: Dutch brewer Heineken reported a near 5% gain in total volumes sold in the third quarter (Q3), driven by strong growth in its Asia-Pacific market.

The world's second-biggest brewer after AB InBev said its total volumes, including beer, cider, and non-alcoholic drinks, came in at 76 million hectolitres, compared to 71.6 million in the same period last year.
"Asia-Pacific led the growth, with "particularly strong momentum" in Vietnam, China and India driving volumes in that region up by 17.3%," Heineken said.
Its non-alcoholic beer Heineken 0.0 also performed well, with double-digit growth in 26 markets.
New chief executive Rafa Oliveira, unveiling his first quarterly results since taking charge this month, said he had a positive first impression but urged the company to do better.
"We have strong foundations, but we are not translating them into consistent growth and winning with consumers and customers as often as we should," he said in a statement.
"There is more to do to sharpen execution, increase pace, and build a stronger performance culture, with greater accountability across the business," he added.
Heineken has embarked on job cuts as part of efforts to bolster sales and profitability, with up to 6,000 posts of its roughly 85,000 jobs to be shed over the next two years.
The brewer no longer publishes quarterly net profit figures, unveiling these only in half-year or full-year reports.
The firm maintained its forecast of a full-year operating profit of between 2% and 6%.
Its net revenue in Q3 was €8.1 billion before exceptional items and amortisation, a gain of 4.6%.
Volumes were up across the board, with a return to growth in the Americas and Europe, managing a gain of 0.6%, helped by favourable weather.
