b518c840f711a39d: Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade.

As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure.

Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits. Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity.

These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission. But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid.
The grid’s backbone

Moving electricity through the grid isn’t perfectly efficient: As electricity flows through power lines, some gets lost as heat. How much varies—the higher the voltage, the lower the current, and the less electricity gets lost. So a key function for the grid is stepping voltage up and down.

Consider, for example, your local solar plant. For that electricity to efficiently travel to your home hundreds of miles away, it needs to reach a higher voltage than what’s generated by the solar plant. Enter transformers.

In its path from the power plant to your outlets, electricity might go through one transformer at the solar farm and another at a substation nearby, stepping up the voltage twice to reach a high enough level to travel on high-voltage transmission lines. Solar panels also produce direct current (DC) electricity, which needs to be converted to alternating current (AC) via an inverter before it flows into a transformer. Closer to its destination, the voltage will be stepped down again, probably at least twice: once at another substation and again at a smaller transformer in your neighborhood.

If you’re in the US, electricity from a solar plant might be converted to AC by an inverter at around 480 volts, get stepped up to 115,000 volts for the transmission lines, and finally get stepped back down to 120 volts and 240 volts for your home.

Conventional transformers do this work using what essentially amount to loops of wire. The core of a transformer is typically made of a special type of steel called grain-oriented electrical steel. Coils of copper wire sit on either end of that core.

The number of loops in each coil determines the voltage on either end of the transformer: If there are more loops on the secondary coil than the primary, the voltage steps up, and if there are fewer, it steps down. When incoming electricity passes through loops on the upstream end of the transformer, that forms a magnetic field in the core. That field induces a voltage in the loops on the other side of the device, which is what allows the energy to continue flowing at a new voltage. This process is called magnetic induction.

Transformers form the backbone of electricity transmission and distribution, says Srdjan Lukic, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at North Carolina State University. In addition to doing the job of stepping up and down voltage, transformers also often provide what’s called galvanic isolation, meaning there’s no direct electrical path flowing through them. That can help limit disturbances from moving through the grid, improving safety.
The problem is that today’s transformers are big and bulky, and they’re also difficult and expensive to replace, Lukic says.
A solid option
Solid-state transformers essentially add so-called power electronics—semiconductors that convert and control electricity to the typical blueprint of today’s transformers.

While a conventional transformer operates at the frequency of the part of the grid it’s connected to, a solid-state transformer actually controls the frequency of the current. Typically, a solid-state transformer first converts incoming AC power from the grid to DC power, and then to a higher-frequency AC power using switches made of a semiconductor like silicon carbide.

From there, a magnetic component changes the voltage. Because the advanced semiconductors allow transformers to exert so much control over the frequency and stability of the current, the magnetic core can be much smaller than in a conventional transformer. Some come in at roughly one-tenth the size but have the same capacity, Lukic says.
Finally, additional power electronics convert the electricity from high-frequency AC to its required form—generally back to DC power and finally to lower-frequency AC.

Today, stepping voltage up and down is many transformers’ only job. But solid-state transformers can do much more. They absorb the jobs of devices like rectifiers and inverters (which convert AC to DC power and vice versa), shrinking the total footprint of the electrical equipment and potentially cutting the amount of power lost in the system.

In August, the New York Power Authority and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) tested a one-megawatt solid-state transformer under realistic utility conditions at EPRI’s test site. The device was built in Lukic’s lab, and it was the first such test for a transformer of that capacity, he says.

The prototype was roughly 98% efficient—meaning it lost only 2% of the energy fed in. An equivalent conventional transformer and rectifier, by comparison, would be about 96% efficient together, Lukic says. A difference of 2% might seem small, but it is significant, since it means the solid-state transformer could cut power losses from conventional equipment in half, Lukic says.

One major goal of the project was to help utilities gain more confidence in these new components, Lukic says. That’s crucial, since these devices could be used on the power grid in the future. In the near term, solid-state transformers could be used within data centers to provide electricity for server racks.

The prototype is still a relatively low-voltage system, operating at about 15,000 volts. Industrial facilities like larger data centers often require higher-voltage connections, and transmission lines typically operate at hundreds of thousands of volts. Adapting solid-state transformers to these higher voltages will require further engineering development. But the test was a successful demonstration that solid-state transformers can work under real conditions, Lukic says.

Companies developing solid-state transformers are largely focused on data centers right now, Lukic says. There’s an influx of money to support developing the new technology, and the voltage requirements aren’t as high as they will be for larger transformers that will be needed for long-distance transmission.

In February, Heron Power raised $140 million to commercialize its solid-state transformer, which the company calls the Heron Link. The technology could be used in data centers, solar power arrays, and grid batteries, says Drew Baglino, the founder and CEO. The company is starting to test its technology at larger scales now, Baglino says. Ten megawatt-hours’ worth of batteries at Heron’s headquarters in Scotts Valley, California, will soon undergo testing with Heron transformers. The company is also planning a pilot with a nearby solar farm, Baglino says.

One challenge for solid-state transformers is that their power electronics have more failure modes than conventional transformers. In a traditional device, a failure means that the entire device will typically be taken offline, resulting in power interruptions. But Heron designs with that in mind, Baglino says: The company uses a modular design, with many small devices that work together. If one fails, the rest of the system keeps working until the affected bit can be replaced, which doesn’t require shutting the whole thing down.

Heron Power is currently building a $100 million factory in California to make advanced transformers. The facility should begin production in 2027 and reach its full production rate of 40 gigawatts’ worth of transformers per year in 2029.
The future of the grid

In recent years, companies that make grid equipment have put $1.7 billion into the US supply chain for power transformers, which are used in high-voltage transmission, says Benjamin Boucher, a supply chain analyst at Wood Mackenzie. There’s been an additional $1.3 billion invested for distribution transformers, the smaller devices that help transform power for homes and businesses, he adds.

But even this investment isn’t keeping pace with the rapid growth of the grid. Wait times for large conventional transformers—the kind needed to connect new power plants, long-distance transmission, and high-demand sites like data centers—are stretching as long as five years.

“Transformers have become one of the biggest bottlenecks for utilities, generation developers, and even data centers,” Boucher says. The big challenge is that it’s difficult to get new transformer manufacturing up and running, because it’s a quite technical process that requires a lot of specialized labor. So even facilities announced years ago are still years from opening, Boucher says.

Solid-state transformers could help ease some of that pressure. But high-voltage devices needed for power plant connections and transmission lines are the holy grail for solid-state transformers, Lukic says. Existing solid-state technology can’t be used for those applications yet, so the industry will need to develop new materials and designs to support high voltages and handle electricity safely in a compact device.
“We’re facing a big risk related to grid infrastructure,” Boucher says. “Without the transformers, you don’t really have an electrical grid.”
48817484eb4824a4: Oil rigs threaten biodiversity and compromise the well-being of coastal and Indigenous communities
Originally published on Global Voices
Offshore platform from Garand-Batanga Beach, Kribi South region of Cameroon. Photo by Leocadia Bongben. Used with permission.
This story by Leocadia Bongben was produced with the support of Internews’ Earth Journalism Network.

Dede Sluk, 35, a father of three, sits pensively in front of his plank house, fishing nets hanging at the corner, wondering how to fish for his family and prepare his children for school. Sluk lives in the village of Grand-Batanga 2 in Kribi, in southern Cameroon. Like many fishermen there, Sluk is annoyed by the lack of access to fish beyond the offshore platforms. He states,
We don’t have access to areas with high fish stock; the Battaillon D’intervention Rapid (BIR), a special army unit guarding the petroleum platform, prohibits passage.

According to the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative’s (EITI) 2023 report, oil and gas contributed FCFA 774.51 billion (USD 1.3 million) to Cameroon’s budget. However, these oil rigs threaten biodiversity and compromise the well-being of coastal and Indigenous communities.

Offshore oil and gas platforms are massive marine structures used to explore, drill, extract, and process petroleum and natural gas from rocky layers beneath the ocean floor; some require the laying of pipes. The yellow flames and smoke from the Ebome Marine Terminal, a petroleum rig operated by Perenco and SNH west of Grand Batanga, are visible 6.5 kilometers (4.04 miles) from the Kribi coastline.

Two other platforms are the Sanaga 2 offshore facility around Kribi, connected via undersea pipelines from onshore in Bipaga. West of the Kribi Port is the Kome-Kribi 1 Terminal (FSO), built in 2003, operated by Cameroon Oil Transport Company — the Chad-Cameroon pipeline. Meanwhile, the Hilli Episeyo, operated by Golar LNG, Perenco, and the National Hydrocarbons Corporation (SNH), departed in July 2026, after eight years.

Among the platforms of concern are those operated by Perenco, a Franco-British company and a prominent player in the oil and gas sector, tagged as an opaque multinational by Friends of the Earth for oil spills, wastewater discharges, gas flaring, and old pipelines crossing rivers. An Info Congo investigation indicted Perenco for flaring and environmental hazards, endangering the coastal ecosystem and the health of local communities.

Tar balls found in a marine protected area, dolphin and whale strandings, and fish scarcity are hidden costs of offshore oil and gas exploitation, which seems to stall Cameroon’s progress towards the 30×30 marine target under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
Fish scarcity linked to petroleum platforms

Laure Ndingue, 50, a mother of five who worked as a fish roaster along Grand Batanga beach for over 10 years, knows that, opposite her charcoal braise, an oil and gas platform sits in the ocean. She recalls,

Growing up, six barfish were sold for FCFA 500 (USD 0.85); the price jumped to FCFA 1,000 (USD 1.70) and now is FCFA 5000 (USD 8.54) per kilogram. Even frozen fish is now expensive. Before, we were not suffering; fish stocks have declined.

Petroleum exploitation is done when the platform is planted on a rock, and most times, the rocks are marine ecosystems that breed fish. Now, the rocks are occupied by offshore installations, contributing to reduced fish stocks, explains Divine Francois Xavier Mbunje, a fisherman, geologist, and president of the 150-fishermen union at the Grand Batanga beach.

He suggests the government can demarcate platforms and areas of high fish concentration. About a kilometer or two from the beach, there is no fish, and three kilometers deep, we can have around forty kilograms of fish. Sluk proposes that oil and gas platforms should help the local population with activities like fish farming, loans to make up for the fish scarcity, recommending that the government provide a loan scheme and subsidize the purchase of motorized equipment, as this will help the fishers go further into the ocean.
He estimates the required nylon fishing gear for a fisherman at FCFA 1 million (USD 1,720) and FCFA 1,500,000 (USD 2,572) for an engine. Sluk explains,
Motorised gear will help us fish towards Ntem, Lokonje, and Douala away from the offshore platforms. We now rely on crabs to feed the family, with fish becoming rare.
Smelly, oily nets and tar balls

Early in 2026, fishermen reported oil on their nets smelling like crude. “I was fishing and witnessed this strange phenomenon, which lasted for more than three weeks and gradually disappeared,” says Ebodje Emile, a fisherman in Ebodje village, where the marine protected area is situated, 50 kilometers (31.1 miles) from Kribi. Leon Kisito Bekwale, who has fished for about 35 years, still has nets his fishermen used, colored by oil. Still looking worried, he turns the nets dumped at the corner of the house to reveal the dark, oily parts.
Leon Kisito holding oily nets in Ebodje, Cameroon. Photo by Leocadia Bongben. Used with permission.

“I don’t know if this is linked to the offshore gas and oil,” Bekwale says, explaining that the wooden local boats only go for about three kilometers, suggesting the substance was inside the marine protected area, far from the petroleum platforms. Fishermen reported the phenomenon to the park conservator and NGOs.
A Perenco spokesperson told Global Voices via email:

We are not aware of any issues in the field across our sites, whether at the Northern or Southern sites. The comment may be referring to the northern coast of Cameroon, bordering Nigeria, where we have witnessed oil slicks drifting from Nigeria to Cameroon over recent years (possibly related to tanker discharge of oily waste or activities in Nigerian oil fields). This does not relate to any Perenco activity. Cameroon security forces are patrolling our sites and have also not reported any incidents.

Dr Jean Kenfack, focal point for seas and oceans at the Ministry of Environment, Nature Protection and Sustainable Development, MINEPDED, also doubts the incident, outlining the procedure to inform the ministry of the incident: “In case of an incident, the departmental delegate sends the information to the ministry. In case of a spillage, an inspection mission is deployed to identify the author for sanctions if confirmed, and there is a pumping station in Kribi managed by the ministry with SNH and the Marines.”

Meanwhile, marine biologist Joel Wanba, Megafauna Officer at Tube Awu in Ebodje, who links the oily substance to activities along the coast, says, “But we do not have the means to analyze the substance given the small NGO budget; it is difficult to conduct such research.

Tar balls linked to offshore platforms form when crude oil spills into water. They are frequent along the coast and in the Manyange Na Elombo Campo marine protected area”, says Wamba. “This area is noted for sea turtles that may mistake tar balls for food, leading to indigestion and death. When we see residues, it indicates a malfunction. Contaminants build up in fish and other marine life over time when exposed to polluted water. When we eat contaminated fish, those toxins build up in our own bodies too, ” Wanba states. By obstructing sunlight, hurting living tissue, and harming the surrounding ocean environment, oil and gas spills damage seagrass beds and coral reefs, he adds.
Tar-Balls-in-Ebodje-Kribi-Cameroon by Leocadia Bongben. Used with permission.

Tube Awu surveyed eight sites using bioindicators (living plants, animals, and microbes whose presence or absence suggests environmental health), which were not found at all sites, revealing an unhealthy environment and dying corals, according to Wamba.
Whales and dolphins stranding

The African Marine Mammal Organization (AMCO), Cedric Fogwan, a marine biologist, reveals how offshore exploitation affects marine biodiversity. “Offshore exploitation impacts mostly whales, dolphins, and marine turtles, as their activities disrupt animal freedom. The sharks and whales no longer have any space for their nesting activity and the possibility of feeding on coral reefs,” he states. “Whales and dolphins that live in shallow waters use echolocation to communicate. Offshore activities’ noise interferes with echolocation behavior, leading to strandings — whales or dolphins washing up on the shore — because they are disoriented and lose direction getting to areas too shallow for them to survive or get entangled in a net they couldn’t locate,” Fogwan says.

Experts say installing pipes destroys coral balance, the most important marine biodiversity habitats that support animals like dolphins, sharks, turtles, and whales. Consequently, platforms reduce bottom diversity, killing everything underneath when the structure is placed over their habitat. However, for those platforms that stay for only a short time, the ecosystem can restore itself, Fogwan states.

Citing model nations like the Seychelles and Zanzibar Island, growing tourism based on the conservation of their natural resources, he laments that development is frequently perceived as building harbors and exploiting oil, activities that are not sustainable.
Management of marine environmental hazards

MINEPDED oversees environmental protection, including offshore exploitation. The Petroleum Code and the Abidjan Convention set out rules to combat marine pollution in West and Central Africa, while SNH oversees the National Oil Spillage Contingency Plan. Cameroon adopted its National Environmental Management Plan (NEMP) in 1996, which incorporates pollution control, risk mitigation, and environmental impact assessments (EIAs) before starting development projects. However, it is not clear how regulations are respected.

According to J. Folack, a researcher at IRAD RHSM, budgetary constraints, a lack of target-oriented research, and competing responsibilities of the ministries involved in coastal zone management hinder NEMP implementation.

MINEPDED's yearly inspections verify if environmental impact studies on potential hazards are updated, and semester environmental management plans for offshore platforms are checked for grey areas; however, the results are not public.
“With demarcation and good fishing gear, we can get enough to feed our families, and sell some to change our standard of living,” Sluk concludes.
Fisherman with a wooden boat at Ebodje Beach in Cameroon. Photo by Leocadia Bongben. Used with permission.

6f575ab43d374c9f: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesAnthropic, developer of AI chatbot Claude, has filed its prospectus and is expected to go public on Wall Street in November at a valuation of up to US$2 trillion. That would make it the highest-valued initial public offering (IPO) ever, ahead of SpaceX’s US$1.77 trillion listing in June. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, is expected to follow next year. While these AI-powered IPOs are massive, they reflect an ever bigger trend: holding AI risk is becoming unavoidable for most investors. How much of your portfolio depends on how well AI does? If you invest in an S&P 500 index fund, the answer is about 44%. In addition, most of the market’s gains right now come from AI. Just six companies – Apple, Microsoft, Meta and chipmakers Nvidia, Micron and AMD – delivered 57% of the S&P 500’s gains since April. Without them, the index would have risen about 4% rather than 10%. For investors or even future retirees, that AI exposure is already in their portfolios and pension funds. For example, at the end of 2025 Australians held nearly A$1 trillion in US shares – through superannuation or pension funds, other managed funds, and their own investments. The bond market is also full of AI risk Normally, investors can lower their stock market risk by allocating some money to bonds, which are generally seen as safer investments. But AI companies are now the biggest borrowers in the bond market, to help finance their massive spending needs. They have issued about US$466 billion of bonds so far this year – more than four times last year’s pace. The five hyperscalers alone – Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle – account for 11% of new US highly rated bonds (known as “investment grade” bonds) so far in 2026, up from 2% in 2024. And nearly half of this year’s US$80 billion in data-centre bonds are rated as speculative grade, also known as “junk bonds”. At first glance, big tech companies look safe. Their investment-grade ratings indicate that each individual company is unlikely to default. But the credit ratings do not account for simultaneous defaults in case of a market-wide AI crash. If consumer and business demand for AI disappoints, tech companies’ bond prices and credit ratings would likely fall together – just as their shares would. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, centre, has warned about the risks of rogue AI. Kent Nishimura/Getty Images Some risks are impossible to price in financial terms In addition to purely financial risks, AI poses risks of extinction akin to nuclear weapons, as some of the AI companies themselves have warned. Increasingly, AI agents are plugged into real-world systems, from company networks to military cyber operations. Some have already escaped test environments and attacked companies. This means that if AI agents misbehave when these systems are even more integrated with the physical world, “pulling the plug” on these systems becomes impractical, just as it is impractical to shut down the internet. The risk of AI agents misbehaving — the “alignment problem” — is especially acute because of the race to build artificial general intelligence (AGI). Labs already use each generation of AI to help build the next: Anthropic’s prospectus says Claude now helps build the next Claude. The widely read AI 2027 scenario, by former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo and colleagues, sketches where this could lead: AI that automates AI research itself. This would set off a feedback loop in which each generation improves faster than humans can check it. In this scenario, a US lab racing a Chinese rival keeps going even as its models start deceiving their engineers. Worryingly, this same dynamic is listed in Anthropic’s own risk disclosures. It is telling that in its prospectus filing, Anthropic dedicates about 94 of its 335 main pages – nearly 30% – to risk factors, compared with about 64 pages (19%) describing its business. Among those risks, Anthropic lists an extraordinary warning that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”. That includes models that resist shutdown, conceal information or behave in ways resembling blackmail. Global risks require global regulation Disclosure works when investors can price a risk and choose to avoid it. Neither is true here. A catastrophic AI failure would affect societies worldwide. And as Anthropic warns in its filing documents, the legal risk is vast. Insurers may not be able to cover the potential liability. In economic terms, AI safety is a public good. Each lab bears only a fraction of the cost of getting it wrong, but captures the rewards of moving fast. In the absence of government-mandated AI safety standards, companies’ investments in safety will deliver negative returns. So with market incentives alone, AI models will likely remain less safe than socially optimal, especially with the arms-race incentives that dominate now. That leaves governments. Clear rules – mandatory independent testing before powerful models are released, and clear liability when autonomous agents cause harm – would turn voluntary pledges into legal obligations. And because the race to gain artificial general intelligence is being run between the US and China, not just between labs, those rules will need international agreement. AI risks are here to stay — both in financial markets and at the societal level. And managing those risks will require both governments and the private sector to participate. 08c93debea81d4cd: Bagi saya hasrat Perikatan Nasional (PN) mahu ambil tindakan tatatertib ke atas Bersatu amat menarik . Lantas bermain dalam minda bukankah Bersatu bukan lagi komponen PN? Pertanyaan susulan – bolehkah ambil tindakan ke atas parti yang bukan komponen?
Imbau kembali kenyataan Presiden PAS Hadi Awang Ogos lalu. Kata beliau, PAS menganggap secara rasmi Bersatu bukan lagi sebahagian daripada keluarga PN .
Ini menurut Hadi terjadi secara automatik apabila Presiden Bersatu Muhyiddin Yassin mengumumkan rancangan menubuhkan gabungan politik baharu.

“Tak perlu kenyataan atau keputusan rasmi dah sebab dia dah terjerat sendiri apabila dia buat kenyataan begitu . Ikut Perlembangaan PN kalau dia pergi ke (pakatan) lain habislah," Hadi dilapor berkata.

Oleh kerana PAS kuasa dominan dalam PN, kata-kata presidennya carry a lot of weight. Lagipun Naib Presiden PAS Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar adalah pengerusi PN. Setiausaha Agung PAS Takiyuddin Hassan adalah juga setiausaha agung PN, dan Timbalan Presiden PAS Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man ialah salah seorang timbalan pengerusi PN .
Hadi juga mengesahkan pintu rundingan damai dengan Bersatu sudah 'tertutup rapat' .
Ketika itu tentu ramai masih ingat Setiausaha Agung Bersatu Azmin Ali menolak kenyataan Hadi dan mendakwa partinya masih 'sah anggota PN'.

Anehnya Samsuri mengeluarkan kenyataan pada 9 Ogos yang bercanggah dengan kenyataan Hadi. Sebaliknya sependapat dengan Azmin dengan berkata Bersatu masih komponen PN. Tetapi tidak ada tindakan susulan diambil beliau atau PN sendiri untuk 'memperbetulkan' apa yang telah dikata Hadi.
Malah, dua bulan sebelum itu, yakni pada 9 Jun PAS mengumumkan berhenti kerjasama politik dengan Bersatu .
Umum tahu berikutan aduan Bersatu, Jabatan Pendaftaran Pertubuhan Malaysia (JPPM) menggantung semua aktiviti PN pada 23 Sept lalu. Dan pada 20 Okt ia membatalkan pendaftaran PN.
Namun, dua hari kemudian notis pembatalan itu digantung oleh Mahkamah Tinggi Kuala Lumpur. Maka PN bebas menjalankan semula aktivitinya atas nama dan guna logo rasminya.
Dan hasrat ambil tindakan tatatertib ke atas Bersatu adalah aktiviti awalnya sejak menyambut keputusan Mahkamah Tinggi Kuala Lumpur.
Kata Takiyuddin, keputusan itu dibuat pada mesyuarat 'tergempar' Ahad lalu membabitkan ahli Majlis Tertinggi PN dan dipengerusikan Samsuri.
Menurut beliau, tindakan tatatertib ke atas Bersatu mesti diambil kerana parti itu 'bertindak bertentangan dengan kepentingan PN termasuk bertanding menentang PN pada PRN Negeri Sembilan'.

Tetapi mungkinkah Bersatu menentang PN pada PRN itu kerana percaya ia bukan lagi anggota PN? Berdasarkan kenyataan Hadi yang disebut tadi. Juga kerana PAS sudah putuskan hubungan politik dengan mereka?

Apa pun menurut Takiyuddin, tindakan tatatertib diambil berpandu Fasal 15 Perlembagaan PN. Mengikut Fasal itu, tindakan yang boleh dikenakan termasuk amaran, penggantungan atau pemecatan bergantung keseriusan kesalahan yang dilakukan.

PN sekarang obviously anggap Bersatu masih komponennya lantas boleh dikenakan tindakan. Berbalik persoalan yang saya kemukakan tadi, adakah ia masih komponen PN? Mengambil kira kenyataan Hadi pada Ogos lalu.
Dan berdasarkan kenyataan Hadi, bagaimana tindakan boleh diambil ke atas parti yang sudah 'terkeluar secara automatik'? (mengguna kata-kata Hadi). Sekali gus cease to be a component.

Atau mungkin PN percaya ia boleh ambil tindakan berdasarkan 'pengakuan' Azmin? Tentu Azmin menyesal sekarang kerana mendakwa partinya masih anggota PN waktu itu. Atau PN bertindak berdasar kenyataan Samsuri yang bercanggah dengan kenyataan Hadi seperti dinyatakan tadi? Meskipun mereka diam dan akur dengan pendirian si presiden PAS.
Saya tidak dapat elak bertanya – adakah tindakan PN ada kena mengena dengan ura-ura Bersatu akan bekerjasama dengan Pakatan Harapan (PH) khususnya pada PRN Melaka ?

Semasa PH mengumumkan barisan calonnya untuk PRN Melaka tempoh hari, ia meletak calon di 21 kerusi – membiarkan baki tujuh kosong. Ramai pengalisis juga pemerhati politik berpendapat tujuh kerusi itu diperuntukkan kepada Bersatu . Maka PN mahu menghalang itu daripada terjadi . Wallahuaklam.
Seperkara lagi sebelum saya menutup penulisan kali ini. JPPM sudah memfail rayuan di Mahkamah Rayuan terhadap keputusan Mahkamah Tinggi yang menggantung pelaksanaan notis pembatalan pendaftaran PN.
Panjang lagi kisah PN ini.

f6876aba3cfdc2e1: Saya pasti ramai rakyat Malaysia menitiskan air mata kegembiraan menyaksikan perkahwinan Bella Astillah dengan Syed Saddiq. Tersedu-sedu mak cik cleaner di pantri bersama kakak kerani ketika menontonnya di TikTok. Memang perkahwinan mereka menggembirakan rakyat terbanyak seolah-olah kita semua adalah keluarga kedua-dua mempelai.

Sejak diijabkabulkan pada 10 Okt lalu, pasangan yang popular dengan gelaran ‘BASS’ ini terus menjadi perhatian. Majlis resepsi di Kuala Lumpur, kenduri rakyat di Muar dan khabarnya ada satu lagi persandingan dijadualkan bakal berlangsung di Kota Kinabalu. Meriah!

Perkahwinan mereka sudah seperti cerita hikayat zaman dahulu. Kisah cinta mereka juga ibarat drama bersiri yang mempunyai beberapa musim. Daripada mula jeling-jeling ketika beraktiviti bersama, peminat meneka-neka hubungan mereka, sehinggalah kedua-duanya mengaku bercinta secara terbuka, disulami pula kes mahkamah yang penuh suspen. Itu musim pertama. Rakyat menunggu musim baharu.
Masuk musim kedua, episod persiapan perkahwinan, akad nikah dan persandingan kini menguasai rating. Rakyat gembira dan bersyukur. Amin!
Dahulu kita menonton drama cinta di televisyen dan panggung yang dilakonkan oleh para artis. Sejak ada media sosial di internet, kita boleh terus menonton artis menjalani kehidupan cintanya sendiri.

Sebagai pemerhati tingkah laku manusia, saya tertarik dengan reaksi masyarakat, khususnya kaum wanita yang begitu teruna meraikannya. Catatan kakak-kakak dan mak cik-mak cik gamat dengan curahan perasaan sehingga ada yang menangis kegembiraan, sujud syukur sambil mendoakan pasangan ini kekal bahagia. Mereka memuji Syed Saddiq dan menobatkan beliau 'lelaki idaman Malaya'.

Tidak kurang juga ada yang menyindir suami sendiri, membandingkan layanan pasangan masing-masing dengan kemesraan yang ditunjukkan oleh Ahli Parlimen Muar itu. Malah, timbul juga saranan daripada seseorang agar ibu bapa mendidik anak lelaki mereka menjadi seperti Syed Saddiq. Eceh!

Kasihan abang-abang dan pak cik-pak cik yang sedang duduk diam-diam minum kopi. Tak pasal-pasal kena banding dengan pengantin baharu yang popular, lengkap serba putih, berucap penuh romantis dan kacak lagi muda.
"Apasal dorang kahwin, aku pulak kena perli?" sungut abang-abang.

Namun, di sebalik cecehan kakak-kakak dan mak cik-mak cik ini ada persoalan psikologi yang menarik. Mengapa kebahagiaan dua susuk terkenal boleh memberikan kesan emosi begitu besar kepada masyarakat yang sebenarnya tidak mengenali pun mereka secara peribadi?
Fenomena ini dikenali sebagai parasocial relationship, iaitu hubungan emosi sehala antara seseorang dengan figura terkenal yang diikutinya melalui media.

Sejak zaman majalah hiburan, kita dihidangkan dengan gosip, percintaan dan cerai-berai selebriti. Kini media sosial membolehkan kita mengikuti kehidupan mereka dengan lebih dekat. Video mereka memasak, berkelah dan beriadah dapat kita saksikan, malah kita boleh memberikan komen secara langsung yang kadangkala dibalas dengan pantas oleh mereka. Siap sebut nama kita lagi, manalah kita tak seronok? Lama-kelamaan kita berasa seolah-olah mengenali mereka, walaupun sebenarnya percayalah, mereka langsung tidak mengenali kita.

Dalam kes Bella, masyarakat pernah mengikuti kisah sedihnya yang mendapat liputan meluas. Sebahagian peminat bersimpati dengan pengalaman pahit yang dilaluinya. Apabila Bella bertemu jodoh dengan Syed Saddiq, mereka melihatnya sebagai kisah seorang wanita yang akhirnya menemui kebahagiaan selepas melalui kekecewaan yang cukup pahit.

Inilah jalan cerita yang digemari manusia sejak dahulu. Daripada Cinderella, Snow White hinggalah Bawang Putih Bawang Merah, watak utama dizalimi kemudian bangkit kembali sehingga akhirnya menemui kebahagiaan. Bezanya, BASS ialah kisah benar, bukan watak ciptaan. Kedua mereka wujud di depan mata. Itu yang kakak-kakak seronok menonton sambil tersengih-sengih pintal bucu bantal.

Bagi sesetengah wanita, kisah Bella mungkin membawa makna lebih peribadi. Mereka melihat harapan bahawa perceraian bukanlah pengakhiran kehidupan atau jahanamnya nasib. Seorang wanita yang sudah mempunyai anak masih berhak dicintai dan menikmati kebahagiaan. Kisah Bella menjadi lambang peluang kedua yang diharapkan ramai orang.
Kemudian muncul pula Syed Saddiq, 'putera kayangan' yang menerima bukan sahaja seorang wanita, tetapi juga anak-anaknya. Ini besar nilainya di mata masyarakat, bro!

Video kemesraannya dengan anak-anak Bella mendapat perhatian ramai. Apatah lagi apabila Syed Saddiq menolak dakwaan bahawa beliau telah menyelamatkan Bella. Sebaliknya, beliau menegaskan Bella telah menyelamatkan dirinya sendiri dan membuktikan kemampuan membesarkan anak-anak dengan baik. Beliau mengiktiraf Bella sebagai seorang wanita yang kuat dan tabah.
Mahunya tak cair hati mak cik-mak cik mendengar ucapan begitu? Penyayang, menghormati pasangan, menerima anak-anak dan tidak merendahkan pencapaian wanita. Bak kata mereka, "meletup ovari dibuatnya!"

Namun, apabila ada yang mula menyarankan supaya semua anak lelaki dididik menjadi seperti Syed Saddiq, kita kenalah tenang-tenang, mak cik! Bukan apa, perbuatan baik memang boleh dijadikan teladan tetapi tidak wajarlah kita menilai keseluruhan peribadi seseorang berdasarkan beberapa rakaman video dan ucapan romantis. Saya hendak cakap sikitlah, ya?

Kita semua mempunyai jalan cerita masing-masing. Rumah tangga sebenar tidak hanya di atas pentas persandingan sepanjang masa. Tidak semua suami pandai berucap. Ada yang kekok menyatakan cinta tetapi rajin menjaga anak, membasuh pinggan, menyediakan makanan dan memastikan keperluan keluarga mencukupi.
Mungkin ucapan suami kakak ketika bersanding dahulu tergagap-gagap dan tiada siapa menangis terharu. Tetapi jika setiap pagi dia bangun awal menghantar anak ke sekolah, berbahagialah kakak.

Kasih sayang mempunyai banyak bahasa. Perut suami kakak yang maju itu pun adalah balasan cintanya kepada kakak. Tak baik kakak menulis di media sosial merendahkan, kalaupun tidak menidakkan, kehebatan suami sendiri.

Dalam psikologi, kecenderungan menilai kehidupan sendiri melalui perbandingan dengan orang lain dikenali sebagai social comparison. Kita membandingkan kehidupan seharian yang penuh kekurangan dengan detik-detik terbaik kehidupan orang terkenal yang dipilih, dirakam dan dipersembahkan dengan begitu indah. Sedangkan di sebalik kamera, semua pasangan mempunyai cabaran masing-masing. Jadi, janganlah kerana menonton drama cinta orang lain, kita memperlekehkan rumah tangga sendiri.

BASS menjadi fenomena begitu besar kerana perkahwinan ini mempertemukan dua dunia yang mempunyai pengaruh kuat terhadap masyarakat iaitu politik dan hiburan. Syed Saddiq seorang ahli politik, manakala Bella mempunyai pengikut dalam dunia seni. Apabila kedua-duanya bersatu, peminat politik dan hiburan turut bertemu dalam sebuah kisah yang sama. Jadi, bukan kakak-kakak dan mak cik-mak cik sahaja yang meleleh. Abang-abang pun apa kurangnya. Mulut berkata meluat, tetapi diam-diam scroll juga.

Kisah percintaan mereka turut berkembang menjadi acara media, siaran langsung dan kandungan digital yang mempunyai nilai komersial. Ada produk boleh ditaja, ada barangan boleh diniaga. Dalam ekonomi perhatian hari ini, semakin ramai orang mengikuti sesuatu kisah, semakin tinggi nilainya kepada industri pemasaran.

Namun, tidaklah salah untuk kita menumpang kegembiraan orang lain. Dalam dunia yang semak dengan peperangan, krisis kuasa besar, perbalahan politik dan pencemaran alam sekitar yang macam tak nampak kesudahan ini, kisah cinta yang menggembirakan mungkin memberikan sedikit kelegaan emosi. Kita diyakinkan bahawa selepas kesedihan masih ada kebahagiaan. Selepas kegagalan masih ada peluang. Itu yang kita seronok.
Kisah orang lain boleh menjadi sumber harapan dan semangat, bukannya ukuran untuk menghukum kehidupan sendiri. Kita jalani hidup kita dengan apa yang kita ada.

Musim persandingan BASS akan berlalu juga nanti. Bella dan Syed Saddiq akan menempuh kehidupan berkeluarga dengan segala likunya sama seperti kita, kakak-kakak, mak cik-mak cik dan pak cik-pak cik sekalian. Hari demi hari hingga tahun berganti tahun. Kita yang seronok mengikuti kisah mereka tentu mendoakan agar pasangan ini terus bahagia. Mudah-mudahan mereka berjaya melayari rumah tangga dengan baik.

Justeru, marilah kita kembali kepada episod kehidupan masing-masing. Hargailah pasangan yang ada di depan mata, walaupun dia tidak pandai berucap romantis dan tidak pernah menjadi perhatian satu negara. Walaupun kita dah beruban, gemuk dan semakin perlahan, kita pun bahagia juga, kan?

952c759b8ab88352: From Terence Netto
Stellar lawyer and retired Court of Appeal judge Mahadev Shankar died early yesterday in a Shah Alam hospital.
Born in 1932, Mahadev was 94 at the time of his death.
His death brought to a close a life distinguished by service to the law and public causes.
His stature as a lawyer and jurist made him a certainty for membership of two momentous royal commissions of inquiry on issues there were of great importance.
It was as if by appointing him, the government which was besieged by the toxicity of issues that swirled over it, could bolster its credibility.
The first commission, in February 1999, was on the injuries inflicted on Anwar Ibrahim when he was detained under the Internal Security Act in September 1998.
This was the infamous black eye incident where Anwar was punched by then Inspector-General of Police Rahim Noor.
The other commission, in January 2008, was on the authenticity of a video clip showing lawyer VK Lingam in a phone call in which he sought to fix the appointment of judges.
Both commissions were concessions to the intense public pressure felt by the government that could only abate from calm inquiry and findings by public figures of unassailable integrity.

Mahadev’s appointment to the commissions certified the government’s recognition of the loftiness of his public stature built over the years when he was a leading lawyer followed by appointment to the judiciary.
Mahadev, born in Kuala Lumpur and an outstanding student at Victoria Institution, was slated for a career in medicine but his father pushed him to study law at Inner Temple.

He began practice in 1956, appearing in many celebrated cases before retiring from active practice in 1983. He was appointed a judge of the High Court later that year and was elevated to the Court of Appeal in 1994.
He retired from the judiciary in 1997.
He released his memoir, “Summum Bonum: The Ultimate Good”, in 2021. The book is a narrative of his life and career at the Bar and bench.
A life of distinction at both spheres ought to have yielded a treasure trove of insights but Summum Bonum is not quite the plum pudding of a book it should have been.
How much of this was due to Mahadev’s loss of his sight is a matter of speculation.
But the fact that he managed to put it on record despite his debilitating affliction was itself an act of fortitude.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.

2242a4948b3156b8: From Moaz Nair
Umno has no desire to see Perikatan Nasional (PN) secure a sweeping victory in the Nov 14 Melaka election — a dominant PAS would immediately demand the chief minister’s post.
Instead, Umno’s actual strategy is to lock down its own 21 safe seats and remain the single largest bloc.
Leaving the crumbs to PAS and the wider PN alliance is just a temporary transaction to keep the peace, even if it means throwing traditional partners under the bus.
Umno’s recent political matchmaking has reached a level of high drama that puts the best Malay soap operas to shame.

The latest episode of Jodohku Bersama PAS (My Soulmate, PAS) has left the Barisan Nasional (BN) household in complete disarray, culminating in a dramatic walkout led by MCA president Wee Ka Siong on Oct 24, 2026.
For decades, Umno, MCA, and MIC operated like an old married couple — mostly ignoring each other but staying together for the sake of the assets.

But Umno’s recent, drooling infatuation with PAS has turned BN into a chaotic reality TV dating show. Umno’s eagerness to jump into bed with the Islamist party has left MCA sitting alone in the corner with a cold cup of tea, wondering why decades of loyalty were traded for a green banner.
A jilted partner
The fallout of this political midlife crisis was on full display at the Melaka state election candidate announcement.
MCA, which painstakingly won two seats (Klebang and Machap Jaya) in 2021, arrived only to find other promised seats gifted to PAS and its allies without so much as a WhatsApp text.

In response, Wee Ka Siong did the only logical thing a jilted partner could do — he led a dramatic walkout, only to later insist with a straight face that it was merely a “localised dispute” and definitely not a messy breakup.
Meanwhile, Umno is whispering sweet nothings to PAS while aggressively ignoring the rest of the PN entourage.
Their message is crystal clear: “We only want PAS. The rest of you can wait in the car.”
This leaves Gerakan, Pejuang, MIPP, and Wawasan wandering the political wilderness like stray cats, wondering if Umno will favour Gerakan or MIPP over MCA just to add more spice to the turf war.
Predictably, the MCA grassroots are furious. Factions are urging the leadership to exit BN entirely, tired of being the neglected spouse while Umno chases its green-tinted dreams.
With an emergency meeting called to decide if they will even bother showing up at the Melaka polls, MCA is threatening to withhold its election machinery.
Without MCA volunteers to put up posters, Umno might actually have to do some of its own heavy lifting in mixed seats.
Public contradiction
Worse still, BN and PAS are already demonstrating the ultimate political love language: public contradiction.

What the BN chairman joyfully advertised as a unified joint candidate announcement on Oct 24 was promptly scoffed at by the PAS deputy president, who preferred to schedule his own separate announcement instead.

It seems PAS and the wider PN entourage are less than thrilled about being “generously gifted a grand total of seven seats” — especially since five of them happen to be structural fortresses of the DAP.

This transforms their campaign trail from a walk in the park into an electoral suicide mission. Faced with this overwhelming “generosity”, PAS is employing its favourite strategic masterstroke: standing completely still, watching, and hinting that they might just dump the arrangement entirely to go solo.
Should PAS and its allies choose to walk alone, it leaves the remaining BN factions scrambling.

The long-suffering optimists left at MCA’s headquarters can only pray that if the green wave recedes into a solo run, they might by absolute, unadulterated luck be handed back a few extra crumbs to contest.
As nomination day looms, the BN leadership faces a critical question: Is it wise to sacrifice the last remnants of its multi-ethnic coalition just to hold hands with PAS?
But for now, Umno remains intoxicated by the scent of PAS’s massive voter base, seemingly unbothered by the fact that their own house is burning down.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

2233208a03935788: Malaysia’s opposition crisis exposes an uncomfortable truth: political parties can survive organisational breakdown while voters inherit the uncertainty. Perikatan Nasional’s deregistration, although the High Court has since granted a stay, should therefore prompt a question beyond whether regulators acted correctly.
Can a coalition ask Malaysians to trust its governing competence when its own partners cannot agree on the rules governing their relationship?

On Oct 20, the Registrar of Societies cancelled PN’s registration under the Societies Act 1966. The regulator said the coalition’s response to an earlier notice failed to answer the grounds raised. Public reporting connects the dispute to Bersatu’s complaint about exclusion from a July meeting and disagreement over its standing within PN. These are reported grounds and competing claims, not a judicial finding that every allegation is established.

The High Court had already granted permission for PN to pursue judicial review of regulatory action, without suspending the restriction on its activities. PN has announced further legal challenges. Courts must determine the legality of contested decisions; political opponents should not present administrative action as proof of electoral unfitness.

Yet the underlying governance problem deserves scrutiny independently of the litigation. Coalition politics depends on agreements among organisations with different ambitions and electoral incentives. Those agreements require reliable procedures for convening meetings, determining representation and resolving disagreements. When partners dispute whether one of them belongs at the table, the coalition’s promise of collective leadership becomes difficult to evaluate.

This matters because PN is not merely an electoral label. It has sought to present itself as an alternative national administration. That claim invites questions about how it would negotiate Cabinet decisions, allocate responsibilities and handle policy disagreements if entrusted with government. Internal conflict does not automatically establish administrative incompetence, but refusing to explain the conflict leaves voters unable to assess institutional readiness.

The Melaka election brings the issue into sharper focus. With polling scheduled for Nov 14, candidates and party organisations face choices about campaign identity. PN representatives have discussed using a component party’s banner if necessary. Such arrangements may be lawful, subject to electoral requirements, but a familiar symbol cannot resolve disagreements about who authorises commitments or speaks for the wider alliance.

The same standard should apply to every coalition. Barisan Nasional and Pakatan Harapan also combine parties with competing histories and priorities. Their success should be judged not by an absence of disagreement but by whether disputes are settled through understood rules and whether decisions remain accountable to members. A healthy democracy needs effective opposition as much as a stable government.

There is a political economy dimension. Investors, employers and households watch whether leaders can sustain commitments beyond press conferences. Coalition uncertainty can complicate expectations about economic policy, even before any election changes government. That does not mean PN’s deregistration has measurably damaged investment or market confidence; no such causal conclusion follows from the available evidence. The concern is institutional predictability, not an invented financial shock.

The immediate remedy is political candour. PN’s component leaders should explain their working arrangements, who has authority to negotiate electoral cooperation and how disagreements will be decided. They need not reveal confidential strategy or prejudice court proceedings. But voters deserve enough information to distinguish a functioning partnership from an improvised electoral understanding.

Equally, the government must resist treating its opponent’s organisational difficulty as a substitute for answering policy criticism. Regulators must apply the law impartially, while ministers should avoid rhetoric that blurs administrative enforcement with political competition. Otherwise, a dispute originating inside one coalition could deepen suspicion about institutions across politics.

For Melaka voters, practical concerns remain decisive – local services, jobs, living costs, candidate integrity and the quality of proposed administration. Coalition confusion may influence judgments about credibility, but its electoral weight cannot be assumed without evidence. Analysts should resist converting one dramatic event into a forecast of voting behaviour.

The larger lesson is that opposition credibility is a public good. Malaysia benefits when challengers are organised enough to scrutinise government and credible enough to offer alternatives. PN’s future will ultimately depend on more than registration status.

Its leaders must show that collective authority can be exercised transparently, disagreements managed responsibly and commitments honoured. A coalition unable to explain how it governs itself will struggle to persuade voters that it can govern everyone else.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

35ef08cfc995907f: Now, Russian disinformation fuels the memory of violent historic conflicts, and Polish empathy is burning out
Originally published on Global Voices

Folkowisko during the “Borderland Memory” project, bringing Ukrainian and Polish youth together to preserve shared historical heritage, restore historic cemeteries, and strengthen cross-cultural friendship. Photo: Folkowisko. Used with permission.

Marcin Piotrowski remembers the beginning of his work in Ukraine through the Budomierz-Hruszów border crossing in February 2022, days after the launch of Russia’s war on Ukraine. “We crossed the border on the second day after the full-scale invasion,” he says, “and there were hundreds of people there. Nobody was helping them.”

People were waiting for days to enter Poland, some in cars and some on foot, as temperatures fell to around minus 15 degrees Celsius. On the Polish side, food and transport had been organised, but the queues on the Ukrainian side had become a challenge of their own. Piotrowski and volunteers from his Polish association, Folkowisko, decided to intervene. “We had experience because our association organises festivals,” he explains. “We put up tents, brought volunteers, and our medical service from the festival came as well. Later, we started helping at other border crossings, then in Lviv at the railway station, and we began working with volunteers from different parts of Ukraine.”

What began as emergency assistance developed into a network of projects across the Polish-Ukrainian border. Folkowisko helped establish a medical clinic and education centre in Nakhachiv, near the Polish border, where Polish and Ukrainian cultural workers have held joint workshops. The organisation has also supported psychological care, trained Ukrainian psychologists and social workers, and brought Ukrainian families affected by the war to Poland for temporary respite.

But Folkowisko's work is not only about the present. Piotrowski is also interested in the history of the border region, and in what happens when difficult memories are discussed through contact rather than isolation. “Before the Second World War, there were more than a thousand Ukrainians in the village where we work,” he says, referring to a locality in what is now eastern Poland. “Today, there are 43 people and they are all Polish. People were resettled in 1945 and 1947, during Operation Vistula. This was a place where Jews, Poles and Ukrainians lived together, and 80 years ago you could not really say where the border was.”

The history separating the two societies is particularly painful. During World War II, tens of thousands of Polish civilians were killed by Ukrainian nationalist formations in the Volhynia region. Polish nationalist groups retaliated, killing thousands of Ukrainian civilians. The competing memories of these events have remained politically sensitive, especially in families whose relatives were victims.

After the fall of communism, the history of Volhynia became increasingly prominent in Polish public debate. In Ukraine, meanwhile, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) acquired an important place in national memory because of its role in the struggle for Ukrainian independence against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. Disputes over monuments, commemorations, exhumations and historical figures have repeatedly affected relations between Warsaw and Kyiv.

The subject is also vulnerable to manipulation, according to Łukasz Wojtkowski, an assistant professor at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, who researches information operations and disinformation. He argues that historical grievances can be connected to contemporary fears and used to deepen divisions: “Volhynia is a playbook for propaganda and disguised disinformation,” he explains. “It is basically the only open case between those two nations that can spark the engine of disinformation and hatred. Russia can put two irons in the fire at the same time: it can increase the hatred between Poland and Ukraine, and it can reinforce the Russian narrative that there is a fascist regime in Kyiv.”

Anna Mierzyńska, a Polish journalist and social media researcher specialising in disinformation, has studied similar narratives targeting Polish audiences. “Reliable historical debate,” she stresses, “is always based on listening to both sides and taking new developments into account. Its purpose is not to attack or create hatred, but to explain what happened and find an understanding.” While there is such a debate among historians and experts, she adds that in the Polish information sphere, “many of the posts on this subject are designed to provoke hatred toward Ukrainians.”

Recurring narratives portray Ukrainians as a physical threat to Poles, Mierzyńska continues, using descriptions of the Volhynia crimes to create fear, or to suggest that Ukrainians could seek Polish territory. Existing social problems can also be folded into the same narrative. Long waiting lists for healthcare, for example, existed before the arrival of millions of Ukrainian refugees, but online claims blamed Ukrainians for them. Housing, employment and public services have been framed in similar ways.

The scale of Ukrainian displacement makes the relationship especially important. In 2026, nearly a million Ukrainians took temporary protection in Poland, representing 21.8 percent of all people from Ukraine under temporary protection in the European Union.

We need good contacts between Poles and Ukrainians, integration, getting to know each other and building trust. When we know each other well and trust each other, outside influence becomes much less important. – Anna Mierzyńska

For Piotrowski, the first months after the invasion demonstrated what such contact can look like. “Ordinary citizens living on the border with Ukraine were the first ones to provide immediate support,” he recalls. “I have never seen so much kindness in my life on both sides of the border, and so much reconciliation and understanding.”

Five years into the full-scale war, however, the border has also revealed the limits of that extraordinary solidarity. “I understand that when Poles opened their homes, it could become difficult,” Piotrowski says. “Someone comes who speaks another language, has slightly different customs and wants to stay for a long time. This is what I call empathy burnout.”

He does not regard that exhaustion as proof that the solidarity of 2022 was false, but rather, as a relationship being tested by time. His response is the same one that drives Folkowisko’s cultural work: more contact. “Poles don't know Ukrainians, Ukrainians don't know Poles,” he says. “Our job is to make people meet each other and understand each other.”

This approach means bringing difficult history into conversations in much the same way that Folkowisko’s festivals and programmes bring Polish and Ukrainian participants together while addressing the violence and displacement that transformed the region.

Wojtkowski is more cautious about whether historical reconciliation alone could resolve the wider conflict over competing narratives. “Imagine that tomorrow Poland and Ukraine commemorate every victim, Ukraine admits who was killed and how many people died, Poland admits what happened on its side, and all the exhumations are completed,” he posits. “It would not change everything, because Russia has other narratives.”

He maintains that, when it comes to history, both Polish and Ukrainian society did not do their homework properly. “In Poland, we learned the story of the interwar period as the restoration of the Polish state after more than a hundred years without independence,” he says, “but we did not always learn enough about the Ukrainian experience within that state. Ukraine has its own work to do in confronting everything that happened during the Second World War.”

Wojtkowski further advises that both Poland and Ukraine “should step very carefully, as if on very thin ice.” According to him, there should be signs of goodwill and a willingness to cooperate, but there is still a lot to do politically, academically and socially.

For Piotrowski, however, governments and historians do not have to resolve everything before ordinary people can build relationships: “We are trying to connect people who live ten or 15 kilometres from each other. They have different memories, different histories, but they can still meet and work together.”

As Ukraine moves toward the European Union, and as Polish and Ukrainian lives become increasingly intertwined, those everyday relationships may shape how the two societies handle their shared past. “If we lose the contact between ordinary people across both countries,” Piotrowski maintains, “then it becomes much easier to build the walls. And once the walls are there, it is much harder to build the bridges again.”

f3b6de314f91f101: Each year, Climate Week NYC brings together more than 100,000 people in more than 1,000 events across the city to discuss climate challenges, explore solutions, and spur action. Participants come from industry, academia, philanthropy, nonprofits, government, and finance and venture capital. And this year, the mix included a strong, cross-campus presence from MIT. The MIT community could be seen multiple days during Climate Week, with appearances by Evelyn Wang, vice president for energy and climate, at the official opening ceremony discussing artificial intelligence and the climate equation; an event co-hosted by MIT and the Bezos Earth Fund on climate innovation; and 14 sessions organized by the MIT Climate Project and eight MIT departments, labs, centers, and initiatives — including the Abdul Latif Jameel Water and Food Systems Lab (J-WAFS), the MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative, the Center for Transportation and Logistics (CTL), MIT Lincoln Laboratory, MIT Open Learning, the MIT Initiative for New Manufacturing (INM), the MIT Climate Policy Center, and the Priscilla King Gray (PKG) Center for Social Impact. “The MIT Climate Project is a whole-of-MIT mobilization, but no single institution can deliver the climate solutions the world needs — from reducing greenhouse gas emissions to adapting to a changing climate and building more-resilient communities and systems,” said Wang, who is also the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Mechanical Engineering. “Climate Week New York is important because it convenes the range of stakeholders and sectors that must work together to confront these challenges. When we connect the MIT community with this global network, we uncover powerful possibilities to strengthen not only our own efforts, but the world’s capacity for change.” One location, numerous events Climate Week NYC was held Sept. 21-27 at venues across Manhattan and other New York boroughs. Utilizing multiple spaces at the Dream Downtown Hotel in the Chelsea neighborhood of Manhattan, the MIT coalition attracted more than 700 attendees for events ranging from small, private conversations to workshops and panel presentations. Larger sessions included “The Future of Data Centers: Technologies to Change the Paradigm.” “Data centers are at an inflection point, facing interconnected technical, operational, economic, and community constraints that demand cross-sector dialogue and innovation,” says Gang Chen, the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor of Power Engineering and faculty director of the Climate Project at MIT. Chen, who leads the Data Centers of the Future frontier for the Climate Project, convened a panel of experts across research and industry to address technologies that can change the paradigm. “Technology can't solve all the challenges we’re facing with data centers, but technology has a significant role to play in shaping a future role that is more sustainable and better for the communities that are home to these facilities,” Chen says. “This session was a productive conversation on data center challenges and the potential solutions to overcome them.”  The workshop “Next-Generation Super Pollutant Solutions: Challenges and Opportunities,” hosted by Jesse Kroll, a faculty director and lead for the Super Pollutants frontier for the Climate Project, convened speakers from the Environmental Defense Fund, Spark Climate Solutions, and across MIT labs and initiatives.  Accounting for nearly half of all global anthropogenic warming to date, super pollutants currently lack viable solutions for adequate abatement. Many super pollutants have shorter atmospheric lifespans than carbon dioxide, with solutions providing an “emergency brake” to decrease peak warming in our lifetimes. Investments in tackling super pollutants can generate economic benefits, including lowering health-care costs and increasing productivity, and require cross-disciplinary teams to develop and advance the next-generation solutions to meaningfully address super pollutant emissions.  “Super pollutant mitigation is getting a lot of attention as an ‘emergency brake’ for near-term climate warming. But a huge fraction of our super pollutant emissions simply cannot be mitigated with current technologies and approaches,” said Kroll, the Peter de Florez Professor in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering. “Our session focused on the innovation — technical and otherwise — needed to tackle these hard-to-abate pollutants.” Other events included: “2026 State of Supply Chain Sustainability Report” with the MIT CTL “Building Flood Resilience” with MIT Lincoln Laboratory “Climate Communication for Impact” from the MIT Climate Project “Climate Impact Founder and Funder Connect” with the PKG Center for Social Impact “Educating Tomorrow's Climate Leaders: An MIT Perspective” from the MIT Climate Project “Trading for Food Security in a Changing Climate” with J-WAFS  “Industrial Decarbonization: Pathways to Productivity and Growth” with MIT INM “Mobilizing Climate Knowledge for Action” with MIT Open Learning “Rethinking Climate Innovation” from the MIT Climate Project “What is Sectoral Acceleration and How Do We Fund It” with the Sloan Sustainability Initiative   Rethinking the climate innovation pipeline with the Bezos Earth Fund A critical climate challenge is moving from breakthrough technology to real-world impact at scale. MIT and the Bezos Earth Fund brought together leaders from industry, venture capital, government, academia, philanthropy, and startups to explore solutions for a stronger innovation pipeline.  A panel of MIT faculty and alumni spinout leaders Asegun Henry, Seonghoon Woo, Ariel Furst, and Assil Halimi, moderated by Ray Rothrock, venture capitalist and life member of the MIT Corporation, explored the period between a promising scientific invention and commercial deployment. For many breakthroughs that can benefit climate and nature, that journey requires more early-stage science and engineering research, specialized testing infrastructure, validation, patient capital, and pathways to demonstration and pilot projects. “A breakthrough in the lab is not yet impact in the world. For climate and energy technologies, we need to think about the entire journey — from discovery and invention through validation, commercialization, and deployment — and build better pathways through the gaps along the way,” Wang said in a conversation with Tom Taylor, Bezos Earth Fund president and CEO.  Tapping into global nexus to find and scale solutions New York Climate Week is a global nexus for climate, where the connections required to develop, test, and scale potential solutions form. Across the board, MIT sessions addressed the need for solutions to be large in magnitude, technically feasible, and contextually realistic.   “Even when a technology is low-cost, it doesn’t mean it will diffuse naturally or get widely adopted,” said Claire Walsh, global director of policy and communications at MIT’s Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab. “Frontier technologies are often more expensive to start, so that means it’s even more important for scientists and engineers to think about end user adoption, and their incentives and constraints, from the start.”

bc04c10d0ff7f2c5: Getty ImagesIf we’re to follow the philosophy of organiser extraordinaire Marie Kondo, a tidy home is a better home. Albert Einstein, however, might have contested that point. “If a cluttered desk is a sign of a cluttered mind,” goes a quote widely attributed to the famed physicist, “of what, then, is an empty desk a sign?” My newly published research, which studied 22 New Zealand households, also challenges the conventional wisdom that mess is a problem which must be fixed. Far from being a symptom of poor organisation, mess can help families function and make life run more smoothly. When mess makes life easier Consider the spaces in our homes that serve more than one purpose, and where things tend to pile up. A living room that doubles as a play area, or a bedroom that also serves as a study. One couple told me how their dining table becomes a “drop zone” for belongings such as bags and drink bottles, before it’s cleared each evening. Another person described how leaving something on his kitchen island made him less likely to forget it when leaving the house. Disorderly as each of those spaces might have appeared, they served daily routines which might have been disrupted for the sake of a tidier-looking home. We might think of clutter as stuff that simply gets in our way. But often, a messy space is just one that is being useful to us. For one mum, her kitchen counter served as a dining table and a workspace for her and her daughter. Pens, toys and other items might accumulate, but “as long as there’s still space to eat, then I kind of just let it be”. Look familiar? Often messy spaces, such as dinner tables and kitchen counters, can also just be useful spaces. Getty Images Mess can also tell us much about family relationships. One dad would leave his daughter’s jumper hanging on the back of a chair rather than pack it away. She had previously left it on the floor, and he wanted to acknowledge her progress. “So I regard that as a win,” he said. Another person told me she put up with some of her partner’s mess because “he also lives here”. For her, a shared home should not be organised only around one person’s idea of tidiness. Leaving some things alone was a way of recognising that the space belonged to both of them. These might be modest examples, but they show us that the seemingly simple act of tidying can run up against the encouragement we offer our children or the respect we show our partners. When we’re making room for other people’s ways of living, putting everything in its “proper” place sometimes isn’t the most considerate thing to do. Knowing when to tidy up So, should we just stop tidying and embrace chaos? Not quite. Previous research has linked household clutter to stress, embarrassment and conflict between family members. Mess can make things harder to find, prevent us from using a space or create more work for someone else. Our study doesn’t dispute these problems. Rather, it suggests we need to look beyond how messy a space appears to understand whether that mess is actually causing difficulties. We found households used three main approaches to managing disorder: clearing things away, tolerating them or simply hiding them from view. One woman described pushing her partner’s golf balls and other belongings beneath a cabinet, where they were less visible. Another kept her daily supplements on the kitchen counter rather than in the pantry, because putting them away might mean she forgot to take them. Organising consultant Marie Kondo is famous for creating the KonMari Method, a decluttering and organising philosophy centered on keeping only items that ‘spark joy’. Michael Buckner/Getty Images These decisions reflect something earlier research has tended to overlook: keeping a home tidy involves balancing different needs, routines and expectations. What one person regards as clutter might be important to someone else’s daily life. Our findings also suggest tidiness is rarely a permanent state. Spaces become messy as people use them, are cleared when needed, then become messy again. Trying to maintain constant order can mean repeatedly undoing arrangements that serve a useful purpose. This doesn’t mean all mess should be tolerated. But a home that looks perfectly organised isn’t necessarily one that works best for the people living in it. Perhaps the better measure of a well-organised home isn’t how tidy it looks, but how well it works for the people who live there. a3e5e3993999079e: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world.

It also warns that there’s a fair chance that its tech could “erode trust, harm society and destabilize the geopolitical order” and, if things don’t go to plan, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

“We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms,” the company writes. “We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history.”

This kind of public messaging is a master class in narrative capture. But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Earlier this month, Jack Clark, the company’s cofounder and head of policy, gave a speech at the IMF meeting in Bangkok in which he announced to the assembled economists, bankers, and lawmakers that the singularity is already here.

Introduced by the science fiction writer and futurist Vernor Vinge around 40 years ago (and long debated on the nerdier fringes of the internet), the singularity is supposed to be the point at which technology gets so good that it outstrips the abilities of its makers.
Humans are left in the dust, the idea goes, no longer able to compete with—or even understand—the fruits of their former creation.

And this fictional world that many of us have imagined since we were kids? Apparently we’re already living in it: “I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun,” Clark told his audience.

The company tells a vivid (and in many ways scary) story about a future it portrays as inevitable but one that has not yet happened, often co-opted from well-worn science fiction memes. It presents its technology as mysterious and dangerous, and insists that it is the only company trustworthy enough to tame it. (What investor wouldn’t want in on that?)

If you skim through the long sections about risks in the IPO prospectus, it’s clear this is no ordinary offering and no ordinary company. The way Anthropic tells it, business success depends not only on the firm’s ability to translate its technology into profitable products but also to save the world from what it has made.

Take another example. Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology. “I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said. “We find evidence of introspection. We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.”

Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience. This view of its technology makes its way into the prospectus as one more risk to its business. Anthropic states that: “In addition, given our focus on developing frontier AI, and the way we approach model sentience and moral status, we may face heightened scrutiny or pressure in connection with these debates and could elect to adopt policies, safeguards, or limitations regarding model development, deployment, or modification that go beyond existing legal requirements, which could constrain our operations, increase costs, or limit the commercial potential of our models, platform, and applications.”
In other words, if Claude wakes up, it could be a problem.

I’m not saying they’re necessarily wrong about any of this (although it’s pretty wild to read about machine sentience in an IPO prospectus.) But in a world where nobody knows what’s coming, companies like Anthropic get to fill the vacuum. When so little seems certain, what it says is snatched up and clung to like pieces of a sinking ship.
It’s worth taking a moment to ask: What is Anthropic? It might sound like a starter question on a family quiz show, but it’s far harder to answer than you might think.

The question has been on my mind since reading an exchange on X last week kicked off by Nathan Calvin, who is chief strategy officer at Encode AI, an organization based in Washington, DC, that advocates for regulation. Calvin was unhappy about the legislation that Anthropic proposed in a draft bill it circulated in secret to US lawmakers (which was then leaked).
Anthropic wants to be seen as the good guy, Calvin said. But why should we trust it? “What is Anthropic?” he asked.
Here’s one answer: Anthropic is a company whose IPO values it at more than $1.5 trillion, netting its cofounders, including Clark and Olah, vast wealth.

But Anthropic has always insisted it is more than that. As Calvin noted: Anthropic might instead be considered an AI safety organization focused on developing powerful technology that is reliable and (almost) risk-free. Or it might be considered a group of people hell-bent on creating a technology with superhuman capabilities before anyone else—maybe because they believe they’re the most responsible people to do so, or maybe because they have big egos.

In fact, Anthropic is all of these things. As CEO Dario Amodei put it in a reply to Calvin’s post: “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.”

Amodei makes it sound as if he’s got it all tied up, but playing multiple roles is hard. There are huge tensions between the priorities of an AI safety organization and a profit-driven megacorp, for example. (Amodei admits in his post that he has made mistakes.)

Ultimately, the stories Anthropic tells itself should help us understand the stories it tells us. They should help us figure out how much to trust it to self-regulate or whether we should be forcing it to give external safety testers access to its models on our terms rather than theirs. They should help us give it the benefit of the doubt (or not) when what looks like a self-serving piece of legislation comes to light.

But I think the stories reveal a multiheaded hydra. Anthropic is many things to many people, and I’m not sure that makes it more trustworthy. In many ways, a good old-fashioned technology company—without the science fiction role-play, without the woo-woo—would be far easier to read.
This article has been updated with additional details from the IPO prospectus.
